Q9_preprocessing.justification: Pre-processing steps (cropping, resizing, intensity clipping, normalization) are described, but no post-processing is mentioned.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or model is publicly available; data availability statement indicates data not available.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Multiple metrics used: Dice, Jaccard, false negative/positive, surface distance, Hausdorff distance, volume differences, HU differences, and radiomic features.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: 95% confidence intervals reported for key metrics; statistical analysis is present.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Results are reported separately for lungs and lesions, including per-center breakdowns in supplemental tables.

detailed_extraction.title: COLI-Net: Deep learning-assisted fully automated COVID-19 lung and infection pneumonia lesion detection and segmentation from chest computed tomography images

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Development of COLI-Net, a deep learning-based automated framework for whole lung and COVID-19 pneumonia lesion segmentation from chest CT, using transfer learning from a large multicentric lung dataset to lesion segmentation, and evaluated on multiple external datasets.
contribution_summary.novelty: Use of a large, diverse training dataset (2368 CT exams for lung, 190 for lesions) and transfer learning from lung to lesion segmentation; comprehensive evaluation including radiomic feature analysis; robust performance across multiple centers and scanners.
strengths: Large and diverse training dataset from multiple centers and scanners
External validation on independent datasets from different countries
Comprehensive evaluation with multiple metrics including radiomics
Transfer learning approach to overcome limited lesion data
High Dice scores (0.98 for lung, 0.91 for lesions) and low volume errors
weaknesses: No code or model publicly available
Only one architecture (ResNet) evaluated; no comparison with other architectures on same data
No post-processing steps described
Loss function choice not justified in detail
No direct head-to-head comparison with state-of-the-art on identical test sets

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training set consists of only 18 patients (dual-energy set), with 15 used per fold in cross-validation, which is below the 50-subject threshold.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Dataset sources are clearly described: dual-energy set from CLARITY study, single-energy set from routine clinical care and orCaScore study, with scanner details, patient demographics, and acquisition parameters.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Six-fold cross-validation is clearly described with 3 patients per fold for validation/testing and 15 for training. An independent multi-vendor multi-center set of 290 patients is used for external qualitative testing.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Reference segmentations were obtained on CCTA using an automatic method followed by manual correction by medical students and verification by a resident. The process is detailed.

Q5_external_validation.justification: External validation on an independent multi-vendor multi-center set of 290 NCCT images from four different scanners and centers.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Network architecture is fully described in Table 2, including layer types, filter sizes, strides, channels, and activation functions.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Training details are provided: optimizer (Adam), learning rate (0.001) with decay, 10,000 iterations, batch size 32, sub-image size, and ensemble of three CNNs.

Q8_loss_function.justification: The loss function is stated as negative sum of soft Dice coefficients, but no justification or comparison to alternative losses is provided.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Pre-processing (Gaussian smoothing, intensity normalization, resampling) and post-processing (connected component labeling) are clearly described.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No mention of code or model availability.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Multiple metrics used: DSC and ASSD for VNC images; volume comparison via Bland-Altman and t-test for NCCT.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: 95% confidence intervals and p-values are reported for volume differences; inter-observer agreement is quantified with Cohen's kappa.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparison with related works is provided in Table 5, but not on the same dataset; the authors acknowledge this limitation.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-structure DSC and ASSD are reported in Table 4, and per-structure volume differences are given.

Q15_limitations.justification: Failure cases (prosthetic valves, anatomical variations) are discussed, along with limitations such as quantitative evaluation on VNC not NCCT and volume underestimation.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Patient selection is clearly defined for both datasets; the single-energy set is consecutive and no images were excluded.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes are assessed consistently using quantitative metrics and a standardized five-point grading scale by two observers with kappa agreement.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes (DSC, ASSD, volumes, qualitative grades) are reported, and limitations are discussed.

detailed_extraction.title: Deep Learning from Dual-Energy Information for Whole-Heart Segmentation in Dual-Energy and Single-Energy Non-Contrast-Enhanced Cardiac CT
detailed_extraction.authors: Steffen Bruns, Jelmer M. Wolterink, Richard A. P. Takx, Robbert W. van Hamersvelt, Dominika Suchá, Max A. Viergever, Tim Leiner, Ivana Išgum

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Developed a deep learning method for whole-heart segmentation in non-contrast-enhanced CT (NCCT) by training on virtual non-contrast (VNC) images derived from dual-energy CT, thereby avoiding the need for manual annotation in NCCT.
contribution_summary.novelty: Leverages dual-layer detector CT to generate perfectly aligned VNC images from contrast-enhanced acquisitions, enabling transfer of high-quality CCTA reference segmentations to the NCCT domain without inter-modality registration.
strengths: External validation on a large multi-vendor, multi-center dataset (290 patients) demonstrating generalizability.
Clear and reproducible methodology with detailed architecture and training parameters.
Quantitative evaluation on VNC images with high Dice scores and multiple metrics.
Discussion of failure cases and limitations.
weaknesses: Small training set (18 patients) may limit robustness.
Quantitative evaluation is performed on VNC images, not directly on NCCT images.
Systematic volume underestimation in NCCT compared to CCTA.
No code or model publicly available.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The method could enable quantification of cardiac measures (e.g., ventricular mass, atrial volumes) from NCCT scans acquired for coronary calcium scoring, potentially improving cardiovascular risk prediction without additional contrast-enhanced imaging.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: The training dataset for the underlying model is described as 1390 prostate mpMRI scans from two institutions, which is adequate (>50). The paper itself does not train a new model but uses this pre-trained model.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: The patient population is clearly described: two prospective cohorts from a single institution, with specific clinical protocols (NCT03354416 and NCT00102544) and inclusion criteria. The original training data source is also mentioned (two institutions).

Q3_train_test_split.justification: The paper does not describe a train/validation/test split because it does not perform training. The original model used 5-fold cross-validation, but this is not detailed in the current paper.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: The reference standard is described as expert radiologist interpretation for Phase 1 and biopsy results for Phase 2. However, the annotation process (e.g., how lesions were contoured, criteria) is not detailed in this paper.

Q5_external_validation.justification: This study is a single-center deployment; no external validation is performed. The paper mentions prior external validation studies of the model, but not in this study.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: The network architecture is not described in detail. It only references a cascaded AI pipeline with organ and lesion segmentation operators, but no specifics on layers, model types, or parameters.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: No training hyperparameters, optimizer, or training details are provided because the model was pre-trained. The deployment process is described, but not the training process.

Q8_loss_function.justification: The loss function used in the original training is not mentioned or justified.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Pre-processing steps are clearly described: series selection via regex rules, resampling of ADC and high-b-value images to T2W spacing, organ mask cropping, and thresholding of probability maps. Post-processing includes DICOM output generation (overlays, RTSTRUCT).

Q10_code_availability.justification: The models are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/Project-MONAI/research-contributions/tree/main/prostate-mri-lesion-seg). The deployment framework uses MONAI Deploy Express, which is open-source.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Multiple metrics are reported: sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, accuracy, cancer detection rate (CDR), and runtime. These cover both detection and clinical outcomes.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: A Pearson correlation is reported for runtime vs. prostate volume, but no confidence intervals or p-values are provided for the main performance metrics (sensitivity, CDR, etc.). No formal statistical comparison between AI and radiologist is performed.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: The paper compares AI performance to the radiologist as reference, but does not compare to other state-of-the-art AI segmentation methods. It references prior validation studies but not direct comparisons.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: The study focuses on prostate organ and lesion segmentation. Results are reported at scan-level and lesion-level, including per-lesion CDR by PIRADS category, which is organ-specific.

Q15_limitations.justification: Failure cases are discussed (one scan failed due to missing high b-value series). Limitations are discussed in the Discussion section, including low specificity and the need for further validation.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Patient selection is clearly defined with consecutive cohorts and explicit inclusion criteria. No exclusions were applied in Phase 1, and Phase 2 exclusions are documented.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes were assessed consistently: a single expert radiologist interpreted all images, and a single pathologist reviewed all biopsy specimens.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes are reported, including failures and negative results. The paper provides detailed metrics for both phases.

detailed_extraction.title: Research-based clinical deployment of artificial intelligence algorithm for prostate MRI
detailed_extraction.authors: Stephanie A. Harmon, Jesse Tetreault, Omer Tarik Esengur, Ming Qin, Enis C. Yilmaz, Victor Chang, Dong Yang, Ziyue Xu, Gregg Cohen, Jeff Plum, Testi Sherif, Ron Levin, Alexander Schmidt-Richberg, Scott Thompson, Samuel Coons, Te Chen, Peter L. Choyke, Daguang Xu, Sandeep Gurram, Bradford J. Wood, Peter A. Pinto, Baris Turkbey

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Demonstrates the feasibility of real-time deployment of a deep learning-based prostate and lesion segmentation pipeline directly into a clinical PACS environment using MONAI Deploy Express, with prospective evaluation in two phases (diagnostic imaging and biopsy planning).
contribution_summary.novelty: The novelty lies in the integration of a publicly available AI model into a clinical PACS workflow, enabling point-of-care utilization by radiologists without leaving the familiar PACS interface. The study also shows downstream use of AI outputs for biopsy target selection.
strengths: Prospective, real-world deployment in a clinical setting
Successful execution in 57/58 and 40/40 cases with median runtime of 33 seconds
Integration with biopsy planning software and demonstration of cancer detection rates
Use of open-source tools (MONAI) and publicly available models, promoting reproducibility
Clear description of the deployment framework and DICOM workflow
weaknesses: No training details or architecture description (pre-trained model only)
Single-center study with no external validation in this work
Low specificity (22.2%) and PPV (35.6%) in Phase 1, indicating high false-positive rate
Limited statistical analysis (no confidence intervals or hypothesis testing for main metrics)
No comparison with other state-of-the-art AI segmentation methods
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The study shows that AI segmentation can be integrated into clinical PACS for prostate MRI, potentially improving biopsy targeting. The AI-assisted workflow may increase cancer detection rates, especially for lesions missed by radiologists (AI+/Rad- lesions had 47.8% PCa CDR). However, the high false-positive rate and need for radiologist review suggest it should be used as a decision support tool rather than a standalone diagnostic.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training set consists of 70 patients (first 70 of 100 manually segmented), which exceeds the 50-subject threshold.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Single tertiary care center, patients from 2010-2020, inclusion criteria clearly described.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Clear split: first 100 consecutive patients used for training (70) and validation (30); remaining 227 used for testing.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Manual segmentation performed using LIFEx software; process described, though number of annotators not specified.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external independent dataset used; validation only on internal split and same-center cohort.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: U-Net architecture from MIScnn library mentioned, but no detailed layer/filter specifications provided.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Hyperparameters partially reported (300 epochs, Tversky loss, Keras callbacks, preprocessing), but optimizer, learning rate, batch size not specified.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Tversky loss used but no justification or rationale provided.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing (resampling, clipping, Z-score normalization, augmentation) and postprocessing (largest connected region) clearly described.

Q10_code_availability.justification: Open-source library MIScnn used, but trained model or specific code not publicly released.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Dice score for segmentation, Bland-Altman plot for volume comparison, and clinical metrics (survival, AUC) used.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: P-values, hazard ratios with 95% CIs, Kaplan-Meier with log-rank, ROC with AUC reported.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: No comparison with other segmentation methods or state-of-the-art algorithms; only comparison with 2D measurements.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Spleen-specific results reported (Dice, visual grading, volume) for the single organ.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Inclusion criteria clearly defined, consecutive patients, and exclusions documented.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Standardized definitions for outcomes (ALBI increase, survival) and consistent assessment.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes (OS, TTP, TTUP, decompensation) and segmentation failures reported.

detailed_extraction.title: Fully automated AI-based splenic segmentation for predicting survival and estimating the risk of hepatic decompensation in TACE patients with HCC
detailed_extraction.authors: Lukas Müller, Roman Kloeckner, Aline Mähringer-Kunz, Fabian Stoehr, Christoph Düber, Gordon Arnhold, Simon Johannes Gairing, Friedrich Foerster, Arndt Weinmann, Peter Robert Galle, Jens Mittler, Daniel Pinto dos Santos, Felix Hahn

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Developed a deep learning algorithm for fully automated splenic volume assessment from CT scans and validated its prognostic value for survival and hepatic decompensation in HCC patients undergoing TACE.
contribution_summary.novelty: First study to assess prognostic role of splenic volume in a Western cohort of TACE patients, and first to identify splenic volume as a predictor for hepatic decompensation.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training cohort size is only 29 subjects, below the threshold of 50.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Dataset sources clearly described: Sheffield ASPIRE registry (UK) and Stanford ILD cohort (USA), with scanner details and protocols.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Split methodology clearly described: model development (n=49) divided into training (29), validation (8), testing (12); separate radiological evaluation set (n=176).

Q5_external_validation.justification: External validation performed on independent Stanford cohort (n=28) with heterogeneous scans.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: nnU-Net architecture fully described, including two-stage cascade, patch size, and diagram provided.

detailed_extraction.title: External validation, radiological evaluation, and development of deep learning automatic lung segmentation in contrast-enhanced chest CT
detailed_extraction.authors: Krit Dwivedi, Michael Sharkey, Samer Alabed, Curtis P. Langlotz, Andy J. Swift, Christian Bluethgen

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Development of a 3D nnU-Net-based lung segmentation model specifically for contrast-enhanced CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA), with clinical radiological evaluation and external validation in two diverse cohorts (pulmonary hypertension and interstitial lung disease).
contribution_summary.novelty: First model trained specifically on CTPA in PH patients; includes a novel clinical scoring system (RadSeg) for radiological evaluation of segmentation outputs and detailed failure analysis.
strengths: External validation on independent heterogeneous cohort
Clinical evaluation by radiologists with consensus scoring
Failure analysis identifying common error causes (consolidation, atelectasis, effusion)
Use of state-of-the-art nnU-Net architecture
High technical performance (DSC 0.990, NSD 0.983) with no segmentation failures
weaknesses: Small training set (n=29) below recommended threshold
Training cohort limited to PH patients, potentially reducing generalizability
Loss function not explicitly described or justified
Code/model not publicly available
No formal statistical comparison with other methods on same dataset
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: Intended for lung volume quantification, parenchymal disease severity assessment in pulmonary hypertension, and potentially other CTPA-based quantitative analyses. The model shows promise for clinical translation but is currently limited to PH patients pending further validation.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: The study uses training-validation sets up to 300 images, which exceeds 50 subjects for training. Although smaller sizes are tested, the largest dataset size is adequate.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Dataset sources are clearly described: internal CT from nephrectomy registry, internal MR from radiology database, and external KiTS21 open-source dataset. Inclusion/exclusion criteria are provided.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: The split methodology is explicit: 80-20 training-validation split for each dataset size, with 50 held-out test images for internal datasets and 60 for KiTS21. Fivefold cross-validation is also described.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Annotation process is detailed: manual segmentations by trained analysts, reviewed by experts, and for MR, automated segmentation with manual refinement. Tools like ITK-Snap are mentioned.

Q5_external_validation.justification: External validation is performed on the KiTS21 dataset, which is independent of the internal CT and MR datasets.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: The nnU-Net framework is used, but the paper does not fully describe the architecture details; it refers to the public GitHub for instructions. Only the configuration (3d_fullres, 2D) is specified.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Training process is not fully reproducible as hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, epochs, etc.) are not listed; the paper defers to nnU-Net's default settings.

Q8_loss_function.justification: The loss function is not explicitly mentioned or justified. nnU-Net typically uses a combination of Dice and cross-entropy, but this is not discussed.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing steps are described: CT images are cropped around kidneys and resampled to 256x128, with zero padding. MR images are T2-weighted with fat-saturation. Post-processing includes majority voting ensemble.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or trained models are provided. The paper only references the public nnU-Net GitHub, but not their own implementation.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Multiple metrics are used: Dice, Jaccard index, true positive rate (TPR), mean surface distance (MSD), plus Bland-Altman and linear regression for volume agreement.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Paired Student's t-tests are performed to compare dataset sizes, with p-values reported. Standard deviations are also provided.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: The study compares performance to inter-observer variability and compares 2D vs 3D nnU-Net architectures, but does not directly compare with other state-of-the-art methods on the same datasets.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Results are reported separately for kidney and tumor, and for CT and MR modalities.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations are discussed, including differences in processing between CT and MR, inclusion of partial nephrectomy patients, lack of additional MR images, and the need for representative test sets. Qualitative failure cases are also shown.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Patient selection is clearly defined with inclusion/exclusion criteria for both CT and MR datasets, and random selection of 350 cases per modality.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes are assessed consistently using the same metrics and test sets across all models.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes (Dice, Jaccard, TPR, MSD, volume agreement) are reported, including per-organ results and failure cases.

Q8_loss_function.justification: No loss function for segmentation is specified; only registration loss functions (MI, NCC) are mentioned.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing steps (intensity clipping, normalization, resampling) are described, but post-processing steps are not mentioned.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No mention of code or model availability; data is not public.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Both Dice Similarity Coefficient and Hausdorff Distance are used.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Only mean ± std reported; no confidence intervals, p-values, or statistical tests.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Compares three state-of-the-art segmentation models (ResU-Net, 3D U-Net, Swin UNETR) and multiple registration strategies.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-label results reported for kidney, stone, artery, cortex, medulla, collecting system, and parenchyma.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations discussed (slow registration, small stones), but no explicit failure case analysis.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Medium - Patient selection from a single hospital with no explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria; dataset may be skewed toward kidney stone patients (61.6%).
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Consistent annotation and evaluation protocols applied across all models and phases.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes (per-label Dice and HD) are reported for all models and registration strategies.

detailed_extraction.title: Comprehensive 3D Analysis of the Renal System and Stones: Segmenting and Registering Non-Contrast and Contrast Computed Tomography Images
detailed_extraction.authors: Zhuo Chen, Chuda Xiao, Yang Liu, Haseeb Hassan, Dan Li, Jun Liu, Haoyu Li, Weiguo Xie, Wen Zhong, Bingding Huang

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Develops an ensemble framework that combines deep learning segmentation and rigid registration to reconstruct a comprehensive 3D model of the kidney, including stones, arteries, cortex, medulla, collecting system, and parenchyma, from three-phase CT scans (non-contrast, corticomedullary, and excretory).
contribution_summary.novelty: First system to simultaneously utilize both contrast and non-contrast CT scans and integrate segmentation and registration for complete 3D kidney reconstruction and stone localization.
strengths: Large, well-annotated dataset (464 patients, 1392 scans) with diverse pathologies.
Comprehensive evaluation of three state-of-the-art segmentation models.
Detailed registration evaluation with multiple strategies and loss functions.
Clinically relevant application for preoperative planning in percutaneous nephrolithotomy.
weaknesses: No external validation on independent datasets.
Lack of statistical significance testing.
Segmentation loss function not specified.
Code not publicly available.
Registration process is slow (44.5s per sample).
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The framework shows potential for improving diagnosis and preoperative planning in percutaneous nephrolithotomy by providing detailed 3D visualization of renal anatomy and stone location, but requires further validation and speed optimization for routine clinical use.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training set size is 41 or 44 volumes, which is below the threshold of >50 subjects for training.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Dataset source clearly described: 50 planning CT scans of breast cancer patients from University Medical Center Groningen, with scanner model, slice thickness, and contrast settings specified.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Split methodology is clear: first stage uses 44 training/3 tuning/3 validation; second stage uses 41 training/3 tuning/6 validation, with explicit rationale for re-splitting to balance slice thickness.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Annotation process described: manual contours by experienced cardiac radiologist and physician assistant, based on Feng et al. atlas, by consensus.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation on an independent dataset; only internal validation on 6 volumes.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Network architectures fully described: InceptionResNetV2 for slice classification, UNet3+ for segmentation (three parallel networks for axial, coronal, sagittal views), with details on depth and pretraining.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Training details provided: batch sizes, epochs, early stopping, learning rates, optimizer (Adamax with beta values), and loss functions.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss functions justified: binary cross-entropy for classifier; hybrid loss (dice + focal) for segmentation, with focal loss weighted twice to improve hard slices.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Pre-processing described: conversion to NUMPY, mediastinum windowing (W:350, L:50), no further preprocessing; post-processing: multiplication of binary masks from three views.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No mention of code or model being publicly available.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Multiple metrics used: Dice coefficient, 95% Hausdorff distance, and volume ratio.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No formal statistical analysis (no confidence intervals or p-values); only descriptive statistics (median and quartiles) are reported.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparison with state-of-the-art methods (Choi et al., Harms et al., Jung et al., Luo et al.) presented in Table 3.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-organ results reported for whole heart, right/left ventricle, and right/left atrium.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations discussed: difficulties in cranial/caudal slices, poor atria performance, thick slices, lack of ECG triggering, and potential ground truth variability.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Patient selection clearly defined (breast cancer patients, no abnormalities, from a single center), though limited to a specific cohort.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes assessed consistently using the same metrics and ground truth protocol for all cases.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes (per-organ metrics, volume ratios) and limitations are reported.

detailed_extraction.title: Automatic Cardiac Structure Contouring for Small Datasets with Cascaded Deep Learning Models
detailed_extraction.authors: L. B. van den Oever, D. S. Spoor, A. P. G. Crijns, R. Vliegenthart, M. Oudkerk, R. N. J. Veldhuis, G. H. de Bock, P. M. A. van Ooijen

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Development of a two-stage cascaded deep learning pipeline for automatic cardiac structure contouring (whole heart, ventricles, atria) on low-dose non-contrast planning CT scans using a small dataset (50 scans). The pipeline uses a slice classifier (InceptionResNetV2) to identify slices containing the heart, followed by three UNet3+ networks (axial, coronal, sagittal) that segment structures and are combined via multiplication. Achieves good Dice scores for whole heart and ventricles, but lower for atria.
contribution_summary.novelty: The cascaded approach with 2D networks addresses class imbalance and small dataset constraints, and the combination of three orthogonal views improves boundary segmentation. The focus on local small datasets for clinical implementation is a practical contribution.
strengths: Clear and reproducible methodology with detailed hyperparameters
Comparison with state-of-the-art methods
Use of multiple evaluation metrics (Dice, 95% HD, volume ratio)
Discussion of limitations and failure cases
Fast inference (<30 seconds) suitable for clinical workflow
weaknesses: Small training dataset (41 volumes) and no external validation
No code or model publicly available
Poor segmentation performance for atria (Dice ~0.80, volume ratios 0.80-0.84)
No statistical significance testing
Only non-contrast CT with thick slices, limiting generalizability
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The pipeline can be used for radiotherapy planning, cardiac volume assessment, and as an intermediate step for coronary artery calcium scoring. It is feasible for local centers with small datasets, but atria accuracy needs improvement before clinical implementation.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: 430 patients total, 70% used for training (301 cases), well above 50.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Single institution (Tohoku University Hospital), scanner model and acquisition parameters specified.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: 70/10/20 split for training/validation/testing, random division, same for both models, and fivefold cross-validation for hyperparameter tuning.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Ground truth obtained via urethral catheter and contoured by experienced radiation oncologists; process described.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation; test set from same institution and same patient cohort.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: 2D and 3D U-Net architectures fully described in Table 1 (residual units, channels, strides, dropout).

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Hyperparameters (loss, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, epochs, early stopping) and data augmentation are specified.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Dice Cross Entropy Loss used but no explicit justification for choice over other losses.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Detailed preprocessing: conversion from DICOM RT to binary, resampling to 1mm, grayscale assignment, 2D projection, cropping; post-processing: circle creation and resampling.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or model publicly available; data also not released.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Used CLD and PWR, but no Dice coefficient, which is explicitly required by the criterion.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Reported p-value (p=0.834) for 2D vs 3D comparison, but no confidence intervals.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Compared with Cubero et al., Belue et al., and their own multi-atlas method.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: CLD reported for whole, top, middle, and bottom thirds of the prostate.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations discussed: catheter-induced deformation, cases with asymmetrical urethra, and potential clinical errors.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Patient selection clearly defined (all localized prostate cancer patients treated with IMRT at a single institution over a defined period).
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes assessed consistently using the same metrics and ground truth for all cases.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes (CLD, PWR, per-region) reported, and limitations discussed.

detailed_extraction.title: Development of deep learning-based novel auto-segmentation for the prostatic urethra on planning CT images for prostate cancer radiotherapy
detailed_extraction.authors: Hisamichi Takagi, Ken Takeda, Noriyuki Kadoya, Koki Inoue, Shiki Endo, Noriyoshi Takahashi, Takaya Yamamoto, Rei Umezawa, Keiichi Jingu

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Developed a deep learning-based method to estimate the prostatic urethra position from bladder and prostate contours (without CT images) for patients undergoing external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), achieving a mean centerline distance of ~2.05 mm with a large test set (86 cases).
contribution_summary.novelty: Uses only contour information (not CT) to avoid catheter visibility, and applies to EBRT patients (previous deep learning studies focused on brachytherapy). Also demonstrates scalability with a larger dataset compared to prior work.
strengths: Large dataset (430 patients) with clear split and cross-validation
Detailed methodology and reproducible training conditions
Comparison with state-of-the-art methods and per-region analysis
Discussion of limitations and failure cases
weaknesses: No external validation on independent dataset
No Dice coefficient used for evaluation
Loss function choice not justified
Code/model not publicly available
Potential bias from catheter-induced deformation of the urethra
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: Could potentially replace invasive urethral catheter placement for dose-sparing in prostate radiotherapy, reducing patient burden and enabling urethral dose constraints to minimize urinary toxicity. However, further validation and improvement for asymmetric cases are needed before clinical use.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: The DL model for whole heart segmentation was trained on 300 CT scans (150 breast, 150 lung), which is well above 50. The substructure model used 30 scans for development, but the primary training data for the DL component is 300.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Dataset source is clearly described: local clinical RT database, with specific patient cohorts (breast and lung cancer) and treatment years (2014-2018). Imaging parameters (resolution, slice thickness) are also provided.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: For the DL model, 5-fold cross-validation on 300 scans is described. For substructure segmentation, a leave-one-out approach is used to ensure independence between atlas and test cases. Three atlas sets are defined and evaluated.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Annotation process is described: whole heart contours by radiation therapists/oncologists; substructure contours by three independent observers (medical students) for breast cases and one radiation oncologist for lung cases, all verified by a cardiologist.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation on an independent dataset from another institution. The authors explicitly state that evaluation was performed on data from a single centre, limiting generalizability.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: The nnU-Net framework is used, and four model variants (2D, 3D low-res, 3D full-res, ensemble) are described. The framework is well-known and the paper provides sufficient details on the overall architecture and its components.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Training parameters are set to nnU-Net defaults, and the number of epochs (1000) and cross-validation scheme are specified. For the atlas mapping, registration parameters (resolution levels, iterations, optimization) are given. Code is open-source, enabling reproduction.

Q8_loss_function.justification: The loss function is not explicitly mentioned or justified. The paper relies on nnU-Net's default loss (Dice + cross-entropy) without discussion or rationale.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: No pre-processing is required, as stated. Post-processing steps are clearly described: connected components filter, morphological hole filling, overlap correction, and probability threshold optimization.

Q10_code_availability.justification: The code is publicly available as open-source software (PlatiPy package and nnU-Net), with links provided in the paper.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Four metrics are used: Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), Mean Distance to Agreement (MDA), Hausdorff Distance (HD), and volume ratio.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests are used to compare model performance and threshold optimization effects, with p-values reported. Median and median absolute deviation are also provided.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: The paper compares its results with several state-of-the-art methods (Jin et al., Morris et al., van Velzen et al., Haq et al., etc.) and discusses relative performance.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Results are reported for each of the 18 cardiac substructures individually, with detailed figures and tables showing per-structure metrics.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations are discussed: single-centre data, different observers for lung cases, motion blur effects, potential sex differences, and the geometric nature of valve definitions. Failure cases are also illustrated.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Medium - Patient selection is described but not fully randomized; the 30 substructure cases were specifically chosen to include challenging variations (artefacts, contrast, anatomy). This may introduce selection bias, but the authors acknowledge it.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Medium - Outcomes were assessed consistently using the same metrics, but manual contours were created by different observers (three for breast, one for lung), which could introduce variability. The authors note this and provide inter-observer variability measures.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes are reported, including per-structure results, failure cases, and limitations. No evidence of selective reporting.

detailed_extraction.title: Open-source, fully-automated hybrid cardiac substructure segmentation: development and optimisation
detailed_extraction.authors: Robert N. Finnegan, Vicky Chin, Phillip Chlap, Ali Haidar, James Otton, Jason Dowling, David I. Thwaites, Shalini K. Vinod, Geoff P. Delaney, Lois Holloway
detailed_extraction.venue: Physical and Engineering Sciences in Medicine

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Development of a fully-automated, open-source hybrid segmentation method that combines deep learning (nnU-Net) for whole heart segmentation, a novel whole-heart-guided multi-atlas mapping for chambers and great vessels, and geometric modelling for small structures (valves, coronary arteries, conduction nodes). The method segments 18 cardiac substructures on CT scans and is designed to handle variable imaging conditions.
contribution_summary.novelty: The hybrid approach leverages the strengths of DL for large structures and geometric modelling for small, low-contrast structures, achieving anatomically consistent results with only 10 atlas cases. The whole-heart-guided registration with distance-preserving regularisation is a novel contribution, and the geometric definitions for valves and conduction nodes are new.
strengths: Open-source code available, facilitating reproducibility and clinical translation.
Comprehensive set of 18 cardiac substructures, more than most existing methods.
Robust to variations in imaging (contrast, artefacts, 4DCT, breath-hold) and patient anatomy.
Requires minimal training data (10 atlases) compared to deep learning approaches that need hundreds of cases.
Performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, with per-structure metrics reported.
weaknesses: No external validation on independent datasets from other institutions.
Evaluation limited to 30 cases from a single centre.
Segmentation time is relatively long (9-23 minutes per case), which may hinder real-time clinical use.
Low Dice scores for small structures (valves, coronary arteries) due to inherent imaging limitations and manual contouring variability.
Geometric parameters (e.g., valve thickness) are fixed for all patients, not individualised.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The tool enables retrospective analysis of cardiac substructure doses in large radiotherapy datasets, supporting the development of improved cardiotoxicity risk models. It can be integrated into radiotherapy planning workflows to provide consistent and anatomically accurate delineations, potentially improving cardiac sparing. The open-source nature allows widespread adoption and further validation.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training set comprises 104 CT volumes from multiple databases (3D-IRCADb:20, LiTS:45, KMC:39), exceeding 50 subjects.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Three databases clearly described: 3D-IRCADb, LiTS, and internal KMC Manipal, with details in Table 1.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Training/validation split ratio 78:22 described, manual split for diversity; test sets are separate (CHAOS and internal KMC) with no overlap.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Ground truth for KMC generated using ITK-SNAP under guidance of experienced radiologist; public datasets have publicly available annotations.

Q5_external_validation.justification: External validation on CHAOS dataset (independent) and internal test set, demonstrating robustness.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Network architecture fully described with encoder-decoder pairs, ASPP module, leaky ReLU, and detailed layer-wise table (Table 3).

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Hyperparameters provided: SGDM optimizer, momentum 0.7, minibatch size 2, initial LR 0.1, decay factor 0.1 every 50 epochs, 150 epochs; augmentation details given.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Cross entropy loss used but no justification for choice; no comparison with other loss functions.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing steps clearly described (HU conversion, 8-bit, cropping, resizing, augmentation), but post-processing steps are not mentioned.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or model publicly available; data availability statement indicates institutional restrictions.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Five metrics used: Dice Coefficient, Jaccard Index, MCC, Absolute Volume Difference, and Average Surface Distance.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No confidence intervals, p-values, or statistical tests reported; only average values.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparison with SegNet, UNet, DeepLab v3+, and other recent works on CHAOS dataset.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-case results reported for internal dataset (Table 4) and CHAOS (Table 5), including per-phase averages.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations discussed: failure to identify IVC, sensitivity to image format (DICOM vs NIFTI), and challenging cases where other models fail.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Medium - Patient selection for internal dataset not explicitly defined, but training data includes diverse cases from multiple sources; no clear inclusion/exclusion criteria.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes assessed consistently using same metrics across all models and datasets.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes reported, including per-case results and multiple metrics.

detailed_extraction.title: Automatic Liver Segmentation from Multiphase CT Using Modified SegNet and ASPP Module
detailed_extraction.authors: P. Vaidehi Nayantara, Surekha Kamath, Rajagopal Kadavigere, Kanabagatte Nanjundappa Manjunath

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Developed a modified SegNet architecture incorporating an ASPP module and leaky ReLU layers for automatic liver segmentation from multiphase CT volumes, achieving high Dice coefficients (>96% on portal venous phase and CHAOS dataset) with reduced learnable parameters compared to standard SegNet.
contribution_summary.novelty: Combines SegNet with ASPP to capture multiscale features without increasing parameters, and uses leaky ReLU to improve generalizability; addresses multiphase CT segmentation (plain, arterial, portal venous, delayed) which is rarely explored.
strengths: Robust performance on challenging cases (unusual shapes, heterogeneous intensity, low contrast)
Lower computational complexity (17.1M parameters) compared to SegNet, UNet, DeepLab v3+
Ablation study validates contribution of each component
External validation on independent CHAOS dataset with multiple scanners
Per-phase results demonstrate effectiveness across all CT phases
weaknesses: No code or model publicly available
Loss function choice not justified
No statistical analysis (confidence intervals, p-values)
Post-processing steps not described
Sensitivity to image format (better on DICOM than NIFTI)
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The method shows promise for integration into computer-aided diagnosis (CADx) systems for liver cancer, as it accurately segments the liver across multiple CT phases, which is essential for clinical workflow. However, lack of code and limited external validation beyond one public dataset may hinder immediate adoption.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training set consists of only 12 patients (development set), which is far below the threshold of 50 subjects for training.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Dataset source clearly described: retrospective study of 1602 consecutive TAVI work-up patients at Amsterdam UMC, with inclusion/exclusion criteria, scanner details, and acquisition parameters provided.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Clear split: development set (12 patients) and test set (1497 patients), with leave-one-patient-out cross-validation in development. Test set used for independent evaluation.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Annotation process described: 3D reference segmentations in development set obtained via automatic segmentation with manual correction by a radiology resident; 2D reference segmentations in 81 test patients by a medical student and verified by a radiology resident. Tools (3D Slicer) specified.

Q5_external_validation.justification: External validation performed on the publicly available MM-WHS challenge dataset (20 training, 40 test), with results compared to state-of-the-art.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Network architecture fully described: 3D CNN with encoding path (strided convolutions), residual ResNet blocks, decoding path (transposed convolutions), batch normalization, and softmax output. Detailed layer table provided.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Training process reproducible: optimizer (Adam), initial learning rate (0.001) with decay, early stopping, batch size (8), patch size (128^3), number of iterations, and training time are specified. No data augmentation.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss function justified: negative sum of soft Dice coefficients, chosen for equal weighting of structures of different sizes.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing: resampling to 0.8 mm isotropic resolution and linear rescaling of CT numbers to [0,1]. Post-processing: averaging probability maps across patches and retaining largest connected component.

Q10_code_availability.justification: Code publicly available at https://github.com/qurAI-amsterdam/cardiacSegmentationCCTA.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Multiple metrics used: Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), average symmetric surface distance (ASSD), and Bland-Altman analysis for volumes.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Statistical analysis includes Spearman rank-order correlations with p-values for qualitative assessments, and Bland-Altman limits of agreement. However, no confidence intervals or p-values are reported for the primary segmentation metrics (DSC/ASSD).

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparison with state-of-the-art: external evaluation on MM-WHS challenge dataset, achieving DSC 0.915 vs. best challenge method 0.908.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-organ results reported for LV cavity, LV myocardium, RV, LA, and RA in both quantitative (figures) and qualitative (tables) evaluations.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations discussed: small training set, low contrast enhancement issues, 2D vs 3D evaluation, lack of true 4D CNN, and potential for improved contrast protocols.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Patient selection clearly defined: consecutive TAVI work-up patients with explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes assessed consistently using the same metrics and protocols; inter-observer agreement reported for qualitative grading.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes reported, including per-structure, per-phase, and external validation results; limitations acknowledged.

detailed_extraction.title: Deep learning-based whole-heart segmentation in 4D contrast-enhanced cardiac CT
detailed_extraction.authors: Steffen Bruns, Jelmer M. Wolterink, Thomas P.W. van den Boogert, Jurgen H. Runge, Berto J. Bouma, José P. Henriques, Jan Baan, Max A. Viergever, R. Nils Planken, Ivana Išgum

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Developed and evaluated a deep learning-based method for automatic whole-heart segmentation (LV cavity, LV myocardium, RV, LA, RA) in 4D contrast-enhanced cardiac CT, using a large clinical dataset of TAVI patients. The method produces clinically useful segmentations across the cardiac cycle, enabling potential assessment of cardiac function.
contribution_summary.novelty: The study evaluates a 3D CNN trained on both end-systolic and end-diastolic images to handle temporal variation, and provides a comprehensive evaluation on a very large clinical dataset (1497 test patients) with both quantitative and qualitative assessments. strengths: Large test set (1497 patients) with real-world clinical variability
External validation on independent dataset (MM-WHS)
Code publicly available for reproducibility
Detailed per-structure and per-phase evaluation
Qualitative assessment on full test set with inter-observer agreement
Clear description of architecture and training details

Limited statistical analysis on primary segmentation metrics (no confidence intervals)
Contrast enhancement issues in right heart affect segmentation quality

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Dataset includes 98 patients with 137 CT scans, exceeding the >50 threshold for validation purposes.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Source clearly described: MedAustron, CT scanner model, acquisition protocol, immobilization details, and patient demographics.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: No formal train/validation/test split since this is a validation study; however, a subset of 20 scans was used for qualitative and DVH analyses, but the split methodology is not fully described.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Manual segmentations by radiation oncologists and technologists, following standard delineation guidelines; interobserver variability referenced.

Q5_external_validation.justification: The commercial model was trained on external data (RaySearch) and validated on an independent dataset from MedAustron.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Only mentions '3D CNN U-net type' without detailed architecture (layers, filters, etc.).

Q7_reproducibility.justification: No training hyperparameters, optimizer, or learning rate provided; model is commercial and not reproducible.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss function not mentioned or justified.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Post-processing described (smoothing, noise removal, overlap resolution), but pre-processing details are limited.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or model publicly available; commercial software.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Uses DSC, HD95, and surface DSC, providing multiple geometric metrics.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Statistical tests (Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank) with Bonferroni correction; ICC for inter-observer agreement.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Compares to interobserver variability from literature, but not directly to other deep learning models; discussion mentions similar studies but no head-to-head comparison.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-OAR results reported for all 16 OARs in figures and supplementary data.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations discussed: no replanning, no time quantification, poor performance in non-HFS orientations, and need for model improvement.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Patient selection clearly defined (treated at MedAustron, specific time period, tumor types, orientations).
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Medium - Outcomes assessed consistently for geometric analysis, but qualitative and DVH analyses only performed on a subset (20 scans in two orientations), potentially introducing bias.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes reported, including per-organ results and limitations; no evidence of selective reporting.

detailed_extraction.title: Validation of a deep-learning segmentation model for adult and pediatric head and neck radiotherapy in different patient positions
detailed_extraction.authors: Linda Chen, Patricia Platzer, Christian Reschl, Mansure Schafasand, Ankita Nachankar, Christoph Lukas Hajdusich, Peter Kuess, Markus Stock, Steven Habraken, Antonio Carlino
detailed_extraction.venue: Physics and Imaging in Radiation Oncology

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Validation of a commercial deep-learning segmentation model for 16 head and neck OARs across eight patient orientations, using geometric, qualitative, and dose-volume analyses, and implementation for clinical use in HFS straight and hyperextended positions.
contribution_summary.novelty: Focus on multiple patient orientations relevant to particle therapy with fixed beam lines, and inclusion of pediatric patients, which is rarely addressed in validation studies.
strengths: Comprehensive evaluation with multiple metrics (DSC, HD95, sDSC) and comparison to interobserver variability.
Includes both adult and pediatric populations, showing no significant differences.
Clinical implementation decision based on qualitative scoring and DVH analysis.
Clear discussion of limitations and future improvements.
weaknesses: No training details or code availability (commercial model).
Qualitative and DVH analyses limited to only two orientations (HFS straight and hyperextended).
No replanning with autocontours; only dose recalculated on existing plans.
No direct time-saving quantification.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: For HFS straight and hyperextended scans, 13/16 OARs are deemed clinically suitable, leading to up to 20% time reduction. For other orientations, the model is not yet suitable without major corrections.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: No training performed; evaluation on 15 patients (60 CTs) is small for robust conclusions, and the criterion specifically addresses training dataset size.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Dataset source clearly described: patients from a clinical trial at a single center, CT scans on Siemens SOMATOM Drive, 2 mm slice thickness, treatment position, etc.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: No train/validation/test split is described because pre-trained commercial models were used; no split methodology is reported.

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation with both quantitative (DICE, HD, meanDTA) and qualitative (Likert scale) metrics.

detailed_extraction.title: Medical imaging deep learning with differential privacy
detailed_extraction.authors: Alexander Ziller, Dmitrii Usynin, Rickmer Braren, Marcus Makowski, Daniel Rueckert, Georgios Kaissis

contribution_summary.main_contribution: The paper presents deepee, an open-source PyTorch framework for differentially private deep learning, implementing a parallelized DP-SGD algorithm that is compatible with any neural network architecture. It demonstrates the framework on medical image classification (chest radiographs) and semantic segmentation (liver CT), showing that strong privacy guarantees can be achieved with minimal performance loss in segmentation.
contribution_summary.novelty: The key novelty is the parallelized execution of per-sample gradient computation, which improves efficiency and memory usage compared to existing frameworks, along with automatic architecture modification and privacy accounting based on Gaussian Differential Privacy (GDP).
strengths: Open-source and well-documented framework
Efficient and memory-conscious implementation
Compatibility with arbitrary network layers (e.g., transposed convolutions)
Demonstrates excellent segmentation performance under strict privacy (ε=0.12)
Tighter privacy accounting using GDP compared to RDP
weaknesses: Not focused on 3D organ segmentation; uses 2D slices from CT volumes
Only evaluates on a single organ (liver) and does not compare with state-of-the-art segmentation methods
Lacks detailed description of ground truth annotation and loss function
No external validation on independent datasets
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The framework enables privacy-preserving training of deep learning models for medical imaging, which is crucial for clinical deployment where patient data cannot be shared. The demonstrated segmentation performance suggests that DP can be applied to organ segmentation tasks without significant utility loss, facilitating multi-institutional collaborative learning while protecting patient privacy.

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Describes and evaluates a commercially available deep image-to-image network (DI2IN) algorithm for automatic contouring of organs at risk (lungs, heart, bladder, rectum) in CT for radiation treatment planning, demonstrating high agreement with manual contours.
contribution_summary.novelty: The algorithm combines deep reinforcement learning for anatomical landmark detection to define ROIs, followed by a DI2IN segmentation network. strengths: Large independent evaluation cohort (237 thoracic, 102 pelvic patients)
Comprehensive geometric evaluation with multiple metrics (DSC, HD95, JCI, etc.)
Per-organ results reported
Comparison with state-of-the-art atlas-based and deep learning methods
Clinically relevant as the algorithm is commercially available and certified
weaknesses: No statistical analysis (no confidence intervals or p-values)
Code not publicly available
Loss function choice not justified
Only one human reader for ground truth, limiting inter-observer variability assessment
Thoracic evaluation only on female patients

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training set includes 118 cases, which is >50 subjects.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Uses Dice, precision, recall, and relative volume difference (RVD).

detailed_extraction.title: Automated quantitative assessment of pediatric blunt hepatic trauma by deep learning-based CT volumetry

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Developed an end-to-end deep learning framework for automated segmentation of liver and trauma regions in pediatric blunt hepatic trauma CT, enabling calculation of liver trauma volume and LPDI for severity assessment.
contribution_summary.novelty: First study to apply deep learning specifically for quantitative assessment of pediatric blunt hepatic trauma, using a two-stage dynamic UNet (nnU-Net based) with preprocessing to enhance trauma regions.
strengths: Clear methodology and adequate training dataset (118 cases)
Comprehensive evaluation with multiple metrics and statistical analysis
High correlation with AAST grade and good AUC for severity discrimination
Discussion of limitations and comparison with prior adult studies
weaknesses: Single-center study with no external validation
No code or model release
Incomplete hyperparameter details and lack of loss function justification
Lower segmentation accuracy for small trauma regions (low AAST grades)
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: Could serve as an automated tool to quantify liver trauma severity in pediatric patients, potentially reducing inter-observer variability and aiding in treatment decisions, but requires multicenter validation before clinical adoption.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Dataset source is clearly described: mice bred at Duke University Medical Center, with detailed genotype, diet, and sex breakdown, and IACUC approval.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Split methodology is clear: 186 segmentations for training, 38 for validation, 22 for testing, with random shuffling before separation.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Ground truth annotation process is described: user-guided 3D segmentations using ITK-Snap with snake-based region growing.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation on an independent dataset; all data comes from the same study cohort.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Network architecture is only described as 'U-Net with 3D convolution operations similar to [28]' without detailed layer/filter specifications, though input/output size (128^3) is given.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss function is stated as sum of binary cross entropy and 1 - Dice, but no explicit justification for this choice is provided.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Pre-processing includes normalization (mean 0, std 1) and data augmentation; post-processing includes thresholding at 0.5 and an optimal threshold selection based on precision-recall balance.

Q10_code_availability.justification: Code and models are publicly available via a GitLab repository (https://gitlab.oit.duke.edu/aja54/pcct-cardiac-pipeline).

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Multiple metrics reported: Dice, precision, recall, and AUC.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No statistical analysis (confidence intervals, p-values) is performed on segmentation performance; only means and standard deviations are reported.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: No comparison with state-of-the-art segmentation methods; only internal comparison between two CNN variants (CT vs iodine input).

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Results are reported for the left ventricle specifically, which is the organ of interest.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations are discussed (e.g., label bias from CT images, potential for improvement with material maps), but no explicit failure cases are analyzed.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Patient selection is clearly defined with detailed inclusion criteria (genotype, diet, sex) and outlier removal based on age.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes are assessed consistently using the same imaging protocol, reconstruction, and segmentation pipeline for all subjects.

Good segmentation performance (Dice 0.91) with publicly available code.
Use of advanced PCCT technology enabling material separation and plaque detection.
Large cohort (123 mice) with diverse genotypes and diets.
weaknesses: No external validation on independent datasets.
Segmentation evaluation lacks statistical analysis and comparison with state-of-the-art methods.
Only left ventricle segmentation; no multi-organ segmentation.
Small test set (22 segmentations) for segmentation evaluation.
Network architecture not fully detailed.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss function is not mentioned or justified, as no training is performed.

contribution_summary.novelty: Application of deep learning to analyze positional lung changes and correlate them with pulmonary function, providing a potential imaging biomarker for ILD.
strengths: Automated segmentation and registration enable quantitative analysis of lung volume and movement.
Correlation with clinical data (FVC) adds clinical relevance.
Clear description of preprocessing and registration pipeline.
weaknesses: Relies on pre-trained models without validation of their performance on this specific cohort.
Small sample size and single-center retrospective design.
High exclusion rate (50%) due to registration/segmentation failures.
No comparison with other segmentation or registration methods.

Comprehensive evaluation with multiple geometric and dosimetric metrics
Statistical analysis with effect sizes and confidence intervals

Ground truth annotation process not fully described

The method uses Kaiming initialization, Leaky ReLU, and R2 regularization to improve performance.

strengths: Clear description of the U-Net architecture and hyperparameters.

No external validation on an independent dataset.

No need for network retraining or hyperparameter retuning.
Clear training algorithm and reward function design.
weaknesses: Only evaluated on liver CT from a single dataset (LiTS), limiting generalizability.
Only Dice metric used; no other evaluation metrics or statistical analysis.
No comparison with other state-of-the-art efficient segmentation methods.
Preprocessing details and code are not provided, hindering reproducibility.
Method relies on residual block independence, which may not hold for all architectures.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The method can reduce computational burden of 3D segmentation networks, potentially enabling real-time clinical use on standard hardware. However, further validation on diverse organs and datasets is needed before clinical adoption.

detailed_extraction.title: Applying a novel two-step deep learning network to improve the automatic delineation of esophagus in non-small cell lung cancer radiotherapy
detailed_extraction.authors: Fuli Zhang, Qiusheng Wang, Na Lu, Diandian Chen, Huayong Jiang, Anning Yang, Yanjun Yu, Yadi Wang

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes a two-step deep learning framework for automatic segmentation of thoracic OARs, with a specific focus on improving esophagus delineation. The first step uses DenseNet67 to segment five OARs, and the second step uses a residual attention network on a cropped region around the trachea to refine the esophagus segmentation. The method is evaluated both geometrically (DSC, HD95, ASD) and dosimetrically (IMRT plan comparison).
contribution_summary.novelty: The two-step approach leverages the anatomical relationship between the trachea and esophagus to focus attention on the esophagus region, using a spatial and channel cascaded attention residual network to handle small, low-contrast organs. This is a novel strategy for improving esophagus segmentation in CT.
strengths: Dosimetric evaluation demonstrates clinical feasibility (no significant differences in most dose parameters).
Per-organ results reported, showing improvement over U-Net for esophagus and other organs.
Statistical analysis with p-values included.
Clear description of dataset and annotation process.
weaknesses: Small training dataset (39 patients) limits generalizability.
No external validation on independent dataset.
Lack of training details (loss function, hyperparameters) hinders reproducibility.
No code or model publicly available.
Comparison limited to U-Net baseline; no quantitative comparison with state-of-the-art methods.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The study suggests that the automatic segmentation can produce treatment plans similar to manual delineation, with no significant differences in most dosimetric parameters. The esophagus DSC of 0.73 is considered to have preliminary clinical significance (>0.70). However, the small sample and lack of external validation mean further validation is needed before clinical adoption.

detailed_extraction.title: Deep Learning-Augmented Head and Neck Organs at Risk Segmentation From CT Volumes
detailed_extraction.authors: Wei Wang, Qingxin Wang, Mengyu Jia, Zhongqiu Wang, Chengwen Yang, Daguang Zhang, Shujing Wen, Delong Hou, Ningbo Liu, Ping Wang, Jun Wang

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes SEB-Net, a deep learning framework that combines a Siamese ensemble strategy with shared weights across three orthogonal CT planes and a boundary loss to improve segmentation accuracy of head and neck organs at risk, particularly small organs.
contribution_summary.novelty: The integration of a shared-weight ensemble across three planes (2.5D approach) with a boundary loss that penalizes distance to ground truth boundaries, addressing both inter-slice information loss and class imbalance.
strengths: Significant improvement in segmentation accuracy for small organs (e.g., lens, optic nerve) compared to state-of-the-art methods.
Clinical evaluation demonstrates substantial time savings (81.36% reduction in contouring time) and high acceptance rate (81.92% of organs required no revision).
Ablation studies validate the contribution of each component (shared weights and boundary loss).

Code and data not publicly available, limiting reproducibility.
Single-center study with relatively small training dataset (133 patients).

Q1_dataset_size.justification: The clinical dataset includes 58 ICU patients (>50 subjects) for training, which meets the criterion. The pig dataset has 18 subjects, but the primary training for the final model (u2NetTransfer) uses the human dataset with 58 subjects.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Dataset sources are clearly described: experimental data from two studies (Güldner et al., 2014 and an unpublished study) and clinical data from two studies (Ball et al., 2016 and Ball et al., 2021), with details on scanners, resolutions, and protocols.
