detailed_extraction.title: Deep Learning-Based Adrenal Gland Volumetry for the Prediction of Diabetes
detailed_extraction.authors: Eu Jeong Ku, Soon Ho Yoon, Seung Shin Park, Ji Won Yoon, Jung Hee Kim

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Developed a 3D nnU-Net model for automated adrenal gland segmentation and volumetry from CT scans, and demonstrated that adrenal gland volume (AGV) is associated with current glycemic status and predicts incident type 2 diabetes in a large longitudinal cohort.
contribution_summary.novelty: First study to use deep learning-based adrenal volumetry in a large cohort to show a prospective association with diabetes development, with sex-specific cutoffs.
strengths: Large clinical cohort (9,708 participants) with long-term follow-up (median 7 years)
External validation of segmentation model on independent dataset
Sex-specific analysis and adjustment for multiple confounders
Clear description of model training and evaluation
weaknesses: Moderate segmentation performance on external dataset (Dice 0.71)
Observational design, cannot establish causality
Lack of hormone measurements (ACTH, cortisol) to link AGV to HPA axis
Single ethnicity (Korean) limits generalizability
No code or model publicly available
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: AGV measured via deep learning could serve as an imaging biomarker for diabetes risk stratification, potentially aiding early intervention. Sex-specific cutoff values (7.2 cm³ for men, 5.5 cm³ for women) may be used for risk assessment, but need validation in other populations.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training primarily on LiTS (131 subjects) which exceeds 50; 3D-IRCADb has 20 but is used for secondary training and cross-validation.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: LiTS, 3D-IRCADb, and MSD-Liver are clearly described with acquisition details and provenance.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Explicit 80/20 train/validation split for LiTS and 3D-IRCADb; cross-dataset validation also described.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Mentions that datasets have annotations but does not describe the annotation process or inter-observer variability.

Q5_external_validation.justification: External validation on MSD-Liver and cross-dataset testing between LiTS and 3D-IRCADb.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Architecture fully described with equations, figures, and component details (encoder, ASPP-gated skip, CBAM, decoder).

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Hyperparameters provided but inconsistent (Adam vs AdamW, learning rate discrepancy); missing some details like weight decay.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Dice loss chosen and justified; ablation with BCE and Focal loss also performed.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing steps (slice elimination, windowing, CLAHE, resizing, normalization) and augmentation are clearly described.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or model availability mentioned.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Uses Dice, IoU, Recall, Precision, F1, Accuracy.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Reports mean ± SD across 3 runs, p-values with Bonferroni correction, and paired t-tests.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Compares with U-Net variants and multiple state-of-the-art models (QAU-Net, DefED-Net, SAR-U-Net, etc.).

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Single-organ (liver) segmentation, so per-organ results are inherently reported.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations section discusses dataset diversity, CT-only training, small lesion sensitivity, and domain shift.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Patient selection is based on public datasets with clear inclusion criteria; no private data used.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Consistent evaluation metrics and protocols applied across all models and datasets.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes (multiple metrics, ablations, cross-dataset) are reported; no obvious selective reporting.

detailed_extraction.title: PAFU-Net: A Pyramidal Attention-Fortified U-Net for Precise Liver Segmentation in Abdominal CT scans
detailed_extraction.authors: Andrews Jose, Sujitha Juliet, J. Anitha
detailed_extraction.venue: KSII Transactions on Internet and Information Systems

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes PAFU-Net, a lightweight U-Net variant integrating ASPP-gated skip connections, channel attention in encoder, CBAM at bottleneck, and spatial attention in decoder for precise liver segmentation from CT scans.
contribution_summary.novelty: Novel use of ASPP within attention gates on skip connections to suppress background leakage and enhance multi-scale feature fusion; pyramidal hybrid attention design.
strengths: High Dice scores (0.9824 on LiTS, 0.9277 on 3D-IRCADb) outperforming several SOTA models.
Lightweight and efficient: ~9.8M parameters, 24.5 GFLOPs, 42 ms inference per slice.
Comprehensive ablation studies and cross-dataset validation demonstrate robustness.
Detailed preprocessing pipeline (windowing, CLAHE) improves input quality.
weaknesses: No code availability, limiting reproducibility.
Inconsistency in reported hyperparameters (Adam vs AdamW, learning rate).
Training on 3D-IRCADb uses only 20 subjects, which may limit generalizability for that dataset.
Only CT modality considered; no MRI or multi-phase validation yet.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The model's high accuracy and computational efficiency make it suitable for real-time clinical use in liver segmentation for surgical planning and diagnosis, though further validation on diverse clinical cohorts and integration with DICOM workflows are needed.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training set of 80 patients (>50) used for model training.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Dataset source clearly described: 100 prostate cancer patients treated with TomoTherapy, MVCT images acquired weekly.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Explicit split: 80 training, 10 validation, 10 testing.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Manual contouring by two radiation oncologists with review process described.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external independent dataset; test set is from the same cohort.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: FC-DenseNet architecture described with block diagram, growth rate, and depth specified.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Hyperparameters (optimizer, learning rate, patch size, augmentation) provided.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss function (cross-entropy + dice) mentioned with brief justification for expediting optimization, but not deeply justified.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing (resampling, intensity normalization, augmentation) described; post-processing not mentioned.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or model publicly available; commercial software used.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Used DSC, MSD, centroid differences, and volume differences.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No confidence intervals, p-values, or statistical tests reported.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Compared with one previous non-deep-learning method (Chan-Vese) and with/without augmentation, but not with current deep learning SOTA.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Results reported separately for body outline, rectal balloon, and Blad+Pros.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations discussed, including image quality issues, gas in rectum, and need for larger dataset.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Medium - Patient selection criteria not fully detailed; only states 100 prostate cancer patients treated with TomoTherapy.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Consistent manual contouring protocol with two oncologists and review; outcomes assessed uniformly.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes (DSC, MSD, centroid, volume, HU) reported; no obvious selective reporting.

detailed_extraction.title: Feasibility of artificial intelligence-driven interfractional monitoring of organ changes by mega-voltage computed tomography in intensity-modulated radiotherapy of prostate cancer
detailed_extraction.authors: Yohan Lee, Hyun Joon Choi, Hyemi Kim, Sunghyun Kim, Mi Sun Kim, Hyejung Cha, Young Ju Eum, Hyosung Cho, Jeong Eun Park, Sei Hwan You

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Demonstrated the feasibility of using a commercial AI-based FC-DenseNet model for auto-segmentation of organs-at-risk (body, rectal balloon, bladder+prostate) on low-quality daily MVCT images in prostate cancer radiotherapy, achieving high Dice scores (>0.88) and low mean surface distances (<1.43 mm). Also showed the model's utility for interfractional monitoring of organ changes across six MVCT scans.
contribution_summary.novelty: Application of deep learning auto-segmentation to low-quality MVCT images for interfractional monitoring, which is not commonly addressed; uses a commercial platform with custom training.
strengths: Clear description of dataset and training methodology
Use of multiple evaluation metrics (DSC, MSD, centroid, volume)
Per-organ performance reported
Discussion of limitations and future work
weaknesses: No external validation on independent dataset
Small test set (10 patients)
No statistical analysis (no confidence intervals or p-values)
No code or model publicly available
Limited comparison with state-of-the-art deep learning methods
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: Could enable efficient automated monitoring of interfractional organ changes during radiotherapy, potentially guiding adaptive replanning and reducing manual contouring workload in clinics with limited resources.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: LiTS17 dataset has 116 sets for training/validation, which is >50 subjects. 3DIRCADb has only 12 sets, but the primary training is on LiTS17, so adequate.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Both datasets (LiTS17 and 3DIRCADb) are publicly available and URLs are provided.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Split methodology is clearly described: 3:1 ratio for training/validation, and separate test sets (15 for LiTS17, 8 for 3DIRCADb).

Q4_ground_truth.justification: No description of how ground truth annotations were obtained; only mentions the datasets are used.

Q5_external_validation.justification: Validation on 3DIRCADb, an independent dataset from LiTS17, serves as external validation.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Network architecture fully described with encoder (ResNet-34), decoder, scSE modules, L-ASPP, and CCM, including figures and tables.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Hyperparameters (optimizer Adam, lr=0.003, max iterations=200, batch size=4, input channels=3) and loss function are specified.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss function (BCE+Dice) is stated but not justified or explained why it was chosen.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing steps (windowing, resolution adjustment, histogram equalization) are described, but no post-processing is mentioned.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No mention of code or model being publicly available.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Uses multiple metrics: Dice, VOE, RVD, ASSD, RMSD (and MSD mentioned but not reported in tables).

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Paired t-test with p<0.05 used, and significant differences are marked with asterisks in tables.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Compares with FCN, UNet, MiniSeg, Attention UNet, HFRU-Net, and FRA-UNet.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Results are reported separately for liver and tumor.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations are briefly mentioned (only tested on liver CT, need robustness tests on other organs), but no detailed failure case analysis.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Medium - Patient selection not explicitly defined; uses public datasets with random splits, but no inclusion/exclusion criteria described.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes assessed consistently using the same metrics across all methods.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant metrics (Dice, VOE, RVD, ASSD, RMSD) are reported, though MSD is omitted from tables.

detailed_extraction.title: 2.5D cascaded context-based network for liver and tumor segmentation from CT images
detailed_extraction.authors: Rongrong Bi, Liang Guo, Botao Yang, Jinke Wang, Changfa Shi

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes CCLNet, a 2.5D network combining cascaded context module (CCM) and Ladder Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (L-ASPP) for automatic liver and tumor segmentation from CT, balancing accuracy and computational cost.
contribution_summary.novelty: Introduces a 2.5D approach to overcome limitations of 2D and 3D methods; integrates CCM for multi-scale context capture and L-ASPP with depthwise separable convolutions to enlarge receptive field while reducing parameters.
strengths: Good performance on two public datasets (LiTS17 and 3DIRCADb) with multiple metrics.
Ablation study demonstrates contribution of each module.
Comparison with several state-of-the-art methods.
Statistical significance testing performed.
weaknesses: No code or model publicly available.
Limited external validation (only one independent dataset).
Small training set for 3DIRCADb (only ~9 subjects).
No post-processing steps described.
Loss function choice not justified.
Limited discussion of failure cases and limitations.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The method shows potential for clinical assistance in liver and tumor segmentation, but further validation on larger and more diverse datasets is needed before clinical deployment.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training set consists of only 16 subjects (from SLiver07), which is below the threshold of 50.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Datasets (LiTS17 and SLiver07) are clearly described with acquisition details, resolutions, and number of scans.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Split methodology is explicit: 16 training, 2 validation, 10 test (8 from LiTS17, 2 from SLiver07), with random selection described.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Ground truth is mentioned as provided by the datasets, but no details on annotation process (e.g., number of annotators, protocol) are given.

Q5_external_validation.justification: External validation is performed on LiTS17 test set (8 volumes) which is independent from the training set (SLiver07).

Q6_architecture_description.justification: The iResU-Net architecture is fully described with figures, residual modules, skip connections, and 3D variant.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Optimizer (Adam), learning rate (0.03), and framework (Keras) are given, but batch size, epochs, and other hyperparameters are not specified.

Q8_loss_function.justification: The choice of Dice loss over cross-entropy is justified for class imbalance, and morphological weighting is explained.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing (intensity windowing, normalization, data augmentation) is described, but no post-processing steps are mentioned.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or model is publicly available.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Multiple metrics used: Dice (global and per case), VOE, RVD, ASD, MSD.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Mean ± standard deviation are reported, but no confidence intervals or significance tests (p-values) are provided.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparison is limited to baseline models (U-Net, ResU-Net, FCN) and not with other state-of-the-art liver segmentation methods.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-case results are reported for the liver (the only organ), including Dice per case and other metrics.

Q15_limitations.justification: Challenging cases (low contrast, noise, pathology) are analyzed qualitatively, and limitations of the 3D variant are discussed.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Medium - Patient selection is based on public datasets but only a subset is used (16 training from SLiver07, 8 test from LiTS17), and the random selection process is not fully detailed.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - All models are evaluated consistently using the same metrics and test set.

detailed_extraction.title: An improved residual U-Net with morphological-based loss function for automatic liver segmentation in computed tomography
detailed_extraction.authors: Peiqing Lv, Jinke Wang, Xiangyang Zhang, Chunlei Ji, Lubiao Zhou, Haiying Wang

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes an improved residual U-Net (iResU-Net) for liver CT segmentation, incorporating residual modules, batch normalization, a Dice-based loss with morphological weighting, and data augmentation. Also extends the method to 3D.
contribution_summary.novelty: The morphological-based weighting of the Dice loss to emphasize liver edges and small structures, combined with residual connections and a 3D variant, is the key novelty.
strengths: Clear architectural improvements (residual modules, BN) that accelerate convergence.
Morphological weighting effectively improves edge segmentation.
Ablation study and comparison with baselines demonstrate incremental gains.
Qualitative analysis on challenging cases (low contrast, noise, pathology) shows robustness.
weaknesses: Very small training set (16 subjects) limits generalizability.
No code or model released, hindering reproducibility.
Comparison lacks state-of-the-art methods from the literature.
No statistical significance testing; only mean ± std reported.
3D variant has rough edges due to bilinear upsampling.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The method shows potential for automated liver segmentation in CT, but requires validation on larger, more diverse datasets and further refinement for clinical deployment.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: LiTS17 training set has 116 subjects (>50), but SLiver07 and 3DIRCADb have only 12 training subjects each (<50). Overall, the study uses one large dataset and two small ones, so partial adequacy.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: All three datasets (LiTS17, SLiver07, 3DIRCADb) are publicly available and their URLs are provided, making sources clearly described.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: For LiTS17, they mention a 3:1 train/validation split within 116 training cases and 15 test cases. For SLiver07 and 3DIRCADb, they only state random selection of 12 training and 8 test cases without specifying validation split. Methodology is partially clear.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: The paper does not describe how ground truth annotations were obtained, who annotated them, or any annotation protocol. It only relies on public dataset annotations.

Q5_external_validation.justification: The model is trained and tested on the same datasets separately; no cross-dataset training/testing is performed, so there is no external validation on independent datasets.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: The network architecture is described in detail with figures (Figure 1, 2, 3) and text, covering residual blocks, LSSC, attention module, and deep supervision.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Hyperparameters are provided: Adam optimizer, initial learning rate 0.001, decay schedule (γ=0.1 at epochs 400/650), 800 epochs, batch size 1, input size 16×256×256, and preprocessing details.

Q8_loss_function.justification: The combination of BCE and Dice loss is justified: BCE preserves boundary information, Dice handles class imbalance. Deep supervision weights are also specified.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing steps are described (windowing to [-200,200] HU, resampling z-axis to 1mm, removing non-liver slices, adding 20 slices). However, no post-processing steps are mentioned.

Q10_code_availability.justification: Source code is publicly available at a GitHub link (https://github.com/ZhangXY-123/Model/blob/master/MAD-UNet.py).

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Five metrics are used: Dice, VOE, RVD, ASD, and RMSD, satisfying the requirement of Dice plus at least one other.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Paired t-tests are performed on Dice and ASD with p<0.05, and statistical significance is indicated with asterisks in tables.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparison is made with four state-of-the-art methods: 3D UNet, VNet, 3D ResUNet, and 3D DenseUNet.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: The study focuses on liver segmentation only, and results are reported specifically for the liver across three datasets, which qualifies as per-organ reporting.

Q15_limitations.justification: A dedicated 'Limitation' section discusses failure cases (blood vessels, large tumors) and provides visual examples, acknowledging weaknesses.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Medium - Patient selection is not explicitly defined; random splits from public datasets are used, but no inclusion/exclusion criteria are described, which may introduce bias.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes are assessed consistently across all methods and datasets using the same evaluation metrics and protocols.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes (metrics, training time, parameters, limitations) are reported transparently.

detailed_extraction.title: Multi-scale attention and deep supervision-based 3D UNet for automatic liver segmentation from CT
detailed_extraction.authors: Jinke Wang, Xiangyang Zhang, Liang Guo, Changfa Shi, Shinichi Tamura

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes MAD-UNet, a 3D UNet variant that integrates multi-scale attention and deep supervision for automatic liver segmentation from CT. The network replaces pooling with convolution, uses residual blocks, long-short skip connections (LSSC), and an attention module to aggregate multi-scale features, while applying deep supervision with a combined BCE and Dice loss.
contribution_summary.novelty: The combination of LSSC, multi-scale attention, and deep supervision in a 3D UNet is novel for liver segmentation. The LSSC preserves edge details, the attention module fuses multi-scale contextual information, and deep supervision improves learning of both shallow and deep features.
strengths: Comprehensive evaluation on three public datasets (LiTS17, SLiver07, 3DIRCADb) with high Dice scores (0.9727, 0.9752, 0.9691).
Ablation study demonstrates the contribution of each component (LSSC, attention, deep supervision).
Statistical significance testing (paired t-tests) is performed.
Code is publicly available, enhancing reproducibility.
Detailed discussion of limitations and failure cases.
weaknesses: Small training sets for SLiver07 and 3DIRCADb (12 each) may limit generalizability.
No external validation (training and testing on the same dataset).
Ground truth annotation process is not described.
Only liver segmentation is addressed; no multi-organ capability.
Post-processing steps are not mentioned.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The method shows high accuracy and could assist radiologists in liver segmentation for clinical workflows, but further validation on larger, more diverse datasets and external cohorts is needed before clinical deployment.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: The Synapse CT dataset has only 30 patients total, with 18 for training, which is below the threshold of 50. The ACDC dataset has 100 patients, but the primary CT dataset is inadequate.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Both datasets are clearly identified with references: Synapse multi-organ dataset [30] and ACDC dataset [31], including number of patients and organs.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: For Synapse, 18 cases for training and 12 for testing are specified, but no validation split is mentioned. For ACDC, a 7:1:2 ratio is given. The split is clear but incomplete for Synapse.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: The annotation process is not described; the paper only references the public datasets without detailing how ground truth was generated.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation on an independent dataset is performed; the model is trained and tested on the same datasets (Synapse and ACDC) separately.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: The network architecture is thoroughly described with figures, equations, and detailed explanations of encoder, decoder, attention blocks, and components.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Training details are provided: PyTorch, NVIDIA RTX A6000, batch size, epochs, SGD optimizer, learning rate, momentum, weight decay, and data augmentation.

Q8_loss_function.justification: The loss function (dice loss and cross entropy) is mentioned but not justified; no rationale is given for the choice or weighting.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Pre-processing includes normalization and data augmentation (random rotation and flipping), but post-processing steps are not described.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or model is publicly available; the paper does not mention any repository or release.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Two metrics are used: Dice coefficient and 95% Hausdorff distance (95HD).

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No statistical analysis such as confidence intervals, p-values, or significance tests is reported.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: The method is compared with state-of-the-art models including Unet, Transunet, Unetr, and UTnet.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-organ results are reported for Synapse (8 organs) and per-structure results for ACDC (RV, MYO, LV).

Q15_limitations.justification: The discussion focuses on ablation studies but does not explicitly address failure cases or limitations of the proposed method.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Patient selection is based on public datasets with predefined inclusion criteria, though not explicitly described.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes are assessed consistently using the same metrics across all methods.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant metrics (Dice, 95HD) and per-organ results are reported, though no negative results are discussed.

detailed_extraction.title: Hierarchical volumetric transformer with comprehensive attention for medical image segmentation
detailed_extraction.authors: Zhuang Zhang, Wenjie Luo

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes a novel 3D segmentation framework that hierarchically integrates convolution, transformer, and attention mechanisms, including a double transformer structure, local multi-channel attention (LMCA), and global multi-scale attention (GMSA) with deep supervision.
contribution_summary.novelty: Introduces a volumetric transformer block with learnable relative position encoding, a double decoder that uses both encoder features and skip-connected key/value vectors, and attention modules that adaptively enhance effective features at channel and scale levels.
strengths: Comprehensive architecture description with clear figures and equations.
Strong performance on two public datasets (Synapse and ACDC) compared to four baselines.
Ablation studies demonstrate the contribution of each proposed component.
Uses both Dice and Hausdorff distance for evaluation.
weaknesses: Small training set for CT (Synapse) limits generalizability.
No external validation on independent datasets.
Loss function choice not justified.
No statistical analysis or confidence intervals.
No code availability.
Limitations and failure cases not discussed.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The method shows potential for automated multi-organ CT and cardiac MR segmentation, but further validation on larger, diverse datasets and clinical settings is needed before deployment.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: The study uses two datasets (CHAOS with 40 patients and SLiver07 with 20 training scans) totaling 60 subjects, which exceeds the 50-subject threshold for training adequacy.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Both datasets are clearly identified: CHAOS challenge and SLiver07 challenge, with details on resolution, spacing, and patient characteristics.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: No explicit train/validation/test split is described; the datasets are simply merged and used for the model without specifying how data is partitioned.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: The annotation process for ground truth liver masks is not described; only the existence of ground truth is implied.

Q5_external_validation.justification: The two datasets are merged into one for training and testing; no independent external dataset is used for validation.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: The SegCaps architecture is referenced and partially described (convolutional layers, capsule layers, skip connections), but full layer details, dimensions, and routing specifics are not provided.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Learning rate (0.1) and epochs (150) are given, but optimizer, batch size, loss function, and other hyperparameters are missing, making full reproduction difficult.

Q8_loss_function.justification: No loss function is mentioned or justified; the paper only reports evaluation metrics.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing steps (median filter, anisotropic diffusion, intensity windowing, normalization, contrast stretching) and post-processing (thresholding at 0.6) are clearly described.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or model is publicly available.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Three metrics are used: Accuracy, Dice coefficient, and Jaccard index.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No confidence intervals, p-values, or other statistical tests are reported.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparison is made with U-Net and FCN, which are common baselines but not necessarily state-of-the-art for liver segmentation in 2020.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: The study focuses solely on liver segmentation, so results are per-organ (liver) and not averaged across multiple organs.

Q15_limitations.justification: No failure cases or limitations are discussed; the paper only claims a 'promising' result without addressing weaknesses.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: High - Patient selection criteria are not defined; the study merges two datasets without explaining inclusion/exclusion rules.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Medium - Outcomes are assessed consistently using the same metrics, but the training of comparison models (U-Net, FCN) is not described, potentially introducing bias.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Medium - Multiple metrics are reported, but no per-case results, failure cases, or additional relevant outcomes (e.g., surface distance) are provided.

detailed_extraction.title: Liver Segmentation: A Weakly End-to-End Supervised Model
detailed_extraction.authors: Youssef Ouassit, Soufiane Ardchir, Reda Moulouki, Mohammed Yassine El Ghoumari, Mohamed Azouazi
detailed_extraction.venue: International Journal of Online Engineering (iJOE), Vol. 16, No. 9

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes an end-to-end liver segmentation model based on an improved SegCaps network, incorporating selective preprocessing, data augmentation, and post-processing to handle limited annotated data.
contribution_summary.novelty: Application of capsule networks to liver segmentation, with hand-crafted filter initialization (Laplacian, Sobel) to improve generalization and reduce overfitting.
strengths: Use of capsule networks which are robust to limited data and spatial transformations
Comprehensive preprocessing and augmentation pipeline
Clear post-processing thresholding
Comparison with U-Net and FCN baselines
weaknesses: Low Dice score (0.66) compared to state-of-the-art methods
No loss function specified
No statistical analysis or confidence intervals
No external validation on independent dataset
No code availability
Incomplete description of architecture and training details
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The model could potentially assist in liver volumetry and surgical planning, but its low accuracy (Dice 0.66) limits clinical adoption; further improvements are needed for reliable use.

detailed_extraction.title: Spatial Aggregation of Holistically-Nested Convolutional Neural Networks for Automated Pancreas Localization and Segmentation
detailed_extraction.authors: Holger R. Roth, Le Lu, Nathan Lay, Adam P. Harrison, Amal Farag, Andrew Sohn, Ronald M. Summers

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes a two-stage cascaded deep learning framework for pancreas localization and segmentation using holistically-nested convolutional networks (HNNs) on three orthogonal views. Localization uses multi-view max-pooled HNN probability maps to generate a bounding box, and segmentation combines interior and boundary cues via superpixel aggregation with random forests. Achieves state-of-the-art DSC of 81.27% on 82 CT scans with 4-fold cross-validation.
contribution_summary.novelty: Uses the same HNN architecture for both localization and segmentation, and introduces multi-view pooling (meanmax) to fuse probability maps from axial, sagittal, and coronal views. Also integrates organ boundary and interior mid-level cues through superpixel-based spatial aggregation, avoiding complex 3D CNNs and multi-atlas registration.
strengths: High segmentation accuracy (DSC 81.27%) with low standard deviation compared to prior methods.
Efficient 2D-based approach that avoids the curse of dimensionality of 3D CNNs.
Comprehensive evaluation with multiple metrics and statistical analysis.
External validation on independent datasets demonstrates generalizability.
Simplified pipeline using only HNNs and random forests, no need for hand-crafted features or atlas registration.
weaknesses: No code or trained models released, limiting reproducibility.
Training hyperparameters not fully specified (e.g., batch size, epochs).
Ground truth annotation process not detailed.
Performance on external datasets drops significantly (62-65% DSC) without fine-tuning.
Dataset size is relatively small (82 patients) for deep learning.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The method can be used for automated pancreas segmentation in abdominal CT scans, potentially aiding in diagnosis, surgical planning, and radiotherapy. However, the drop in performance on external datasets suggests that fine-tuning on local data may be necessary for clinical deployment. The computational efficiency (2-3 minutes per scan) makes it feasible for clinical workflows.

strengths: High segmentation accuracy (Dice: 90% prostate, 95% bladder, 84% rectum, 95-96% femoral heads)
Fully automated, no manual intervention required
Comprehensive evaluation with multiple metrics and statistical significance testing
Comparison with state-of-the-art methods shows superior performance
Fast inference (few seconds per patient)
weaknesses: Single-institution dataset, no external validation
Code not publicly available, limiting reproducibility
Rectum segmentation accuracy lower due to high variability
Ground truth annotation process not fully detailed
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The method can be integrated into radiotherapy treatment planning for prostate cancer, providing fast and accurate organ delineation to reduce manual contouring time and inter-observer variability.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training sets are small: liver uses 22 scans (3Dircadb-01+02) with two-fold cross-validation, so ~11 per fold; vertebrae uses 10 scans. Both are far below 50 subjects.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Datasets are clearly identified: 3Dircadb-01 and 3Dircadb-02 for liver, CSI 2014 challenge train set for vertebrae, with details on resolution and slice thickness.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: For liver, two-fold cross-validation is described, and scans are assigned to train/test before sequence creation. For vertebrae, split methodology is not explicitly detailed.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Ground truth masks are mentioned as available, but the annotation process (who, how, criteria) is not described.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation on an independent dataset; models are trained and tested on the same datasets (with cross-validation).

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Architecture is fully described with a detailed table (Table I) listing layer types, input/output shapes, and filter sizes, along with a high-level diagram.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing steps (windowing, CLAHE, normalization, downsampling) and post-processing (thresholding, upsampling) are clearly described.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No public code or model release is mentioned.

detailed_extraction.title: Deep Sequential Segmentation of Organs in Volumetric Medical Scans
detailed_extraction.authors: Alexey A. Novikov, David Major, Maria Wimmer, Dimitrios Lenis, Katja Bühler

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes Sensor3D, a U-Net-like architecture with bidirectional C-LSTM and time-distributed layers that processes volumetric scans sequentially, enabling segmentation of slabs of slices without requiring full volume input, thus overcoming memory and resizing limitations.
contribution_summary.novelty: Integration of bidirectional C-LSTM into a U-Net framework for sequential slice processing, allowing variable input sizes and real-time segmentation during acquisition.
strengths: Handles variable input sizes and does not require full volume at once.
Memory efficient due to sequential processing.
Competitive performance on liver and vertebrae segmentation tasks.
Detailed architecture description and ablation studies (2D variants, unidirectional, capacity).
weaknesses: Small training datasets (22 liver, 10 vertebrae) limit generalizability.
No external validation on independent datasets.
Code not publicly available.
Loss function justification is brief.
Ground truth annotation process not described.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: Could be used for real-time segmentation during CT scanning, as it processes slices sequentially, and is suitable for large volumes where memory is constrained.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training set consists of only 33 subjects (25 + 8 additional), which is below the threshold of 50 for adequate training size.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Dataset source is clearly described: PDDCA dataset from MICCAI 2015 Challenge, provided by Dr. Gregory C. Sharp, originating from RTOG 0522 clinical trial.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: The official train/test split is used (33 training, 15 testing), but no validation set is described, making the split methodology incomplete for hyperparameter tuning.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Ground truth is described as manually segmented by experts, but no details on annotation protocol, inter-observer variability, or quality control are provided.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation on an independent dataset is performed; evaluation is only on the MICCAI 2015 Challenge test set.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: The 3D U-Net architecture is fully described: analysis path with two 3x3x3 convolutions, batch normalization, ReLU, max pooling; synthesis path with up-convolutions and skip connections; 17 convolutional layers total.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Hyperparameters are partially specified: cross-entropy loss, Adam optimizer with 'recommended parameters', mini-batch size 1, 200 iterations. Learning rate and other details are not given, but implementation in Keras and GPU are mentioned.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Cross-entropy loss is used but no justification is provided for choosing it over other segmentation losses (e.g., Dice loss).

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing steps are clearly described: resampling to 1mm isotropic, cropping to 384x384x224, downsampling for LocNet, bounding box determination, and postprocessing to remove small isolated regions (<10% of total volume).

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or model is publicly released; only implementation in Keras is mentioned without any link or repository.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Multiple metrics are used: Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), 95% Hausdorff Distance (95HD), Positive Predictive Value (PPV), and Sensitivity (SEN).

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No statistical analysis is performed; only means and standard deviations are reported, with no confidence intervals, p-values, or significance tests for comparisons.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparison with state-of-the-art methods is extensive, including MICCAI 2015 Challenge participants (VU, UC, IM, UB) and other deep learning methods (Tong et al., AnatomyNet).

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-organ results are reported for all nine OARs in tables, not just averages.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations are discussed: lack of training data, low contrast, inaccurate localization, and potential overfitting. Failure cases are also illustrated.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Patient selection is clearly defined: the PDDCA dataset from RTOG 0522 clinical trial, with a subset chosen to ensure image quality and minimal tumor overlap.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes are assessed consistently using standard metrics (DSC, 95HD, PPV, SEN) across all methods and organs.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes (per-organ metrics) are reported, and comparisons with state-of-the-art are transparent.

detailed_extraction.title: Organ at Risk Segmentation in Head and Neck CT Images Using a Two-Stage Segmentation Framework Based on 3D U-Net
detailed_extraction.authors: Yueyue Wang, Liang Zhao, Manning Wang, Zhijian Song

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes a two-stage segmentation framework for head and neck OARs, decomposing the task into localization (LocNet) and segmentation (SegNet) using dedicated 3D U-Nets. This approach improves accuracy, especially for small organs, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MICCAI 2015 Challenge dataset.
contribution_summary.novelty: The two-stage decomposition with separate 3D U-Nets for bounding box localization and local segmentation is novel, addressing the challenge of segmenting small structures in large volumes while maintaining a large field of view with limited memory.
strengths: Significant improvement in boundary-based metric (95HD) for most organs.
Effective handling of small organs (e.g., optic nerves, chiasm) compared to single-stage methods.
Comprehensive comparison with multiple state-of-the-art methods.
Clear description of preprocessing and postprocessing steps.
weaknesses: Small training dataset (33 subjects) limits generalizability.
No external validation on independent datasets.
No statistical significance testing for comparisons.
Loss function choice not justified; no code released.
No validation set used for hyperparameter tuning.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The method shows potential for clinical use in radiotherapy treatment planning by automating OAR segmentation, reducing manual delineation time. However, further validation on larger, multi-center datasets and integration into clinical workflows are needed before adoption.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training set uses only 7 acquisitions (subjects), far below the threshold of 50 subjects.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Source clearly described: contrast-enhanced abdominal CT from St. Michael's Hospital, with ethics board approval, equal male/female subjects aged 25-50.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Split clearly stated: 7 acquisitions for training, 3 for validation, 10 for test, with slice counts provided.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Annotation process described: manual outlining by trained personnel, standard protocol, quality assured by two board-certified radiologists.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation on an independent dataset; only internal split used.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Architectures (AlexNet, GoogLeNet, FCN variants) are referenced but not fully detailed; standard models assumed.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Hyperparameters provided: Adam optimizer, sigmoid decay LR, momentum 0.9, L2 regularization 1e-4, early stopping, mini-batch sizes, learning rates, and 10-fold cross-validation.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss function not explicitly stated or justified.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Cylindrical transform sampling described, and augmentation for FCNs (rotation, scaling, shifting, intensity) mentioned, but no post-processing steps.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No mention of code or model availability.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Multiple metrics used: DSC, precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC/AUC.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No statistical tests, confidence intervals, or p-values reported.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparison with FCNs (FCN-GoogLeNet, FCN-VGG-19) and reference to prior work with 86% DSC.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-class results reported for left kidney, non-kidney, and right kidney.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations discussed generally (limited annotated data, FCN challenges), but no explicit failure case analysis.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - patient selection clearly defined (20 normal abdominal CTs, equal gender, age range).
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - consistent evaluation using standard metrics and cross-validation.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - all relevant outcomes (per-class metrics, precision/recall, ROC) reported.

detailed_extraction.title: CYLINDRICAL TRANSFORM: 3D SEMANTIC SEGMENTATION OF KIDNEYS WITH LIMITED ANNOTATED IMAGES
detailed_extraction.authors: Hojjat Salehinejad, Sumeya Naqvi, Errol Colak, Joseph Barfett, Shahrokh Valaee
detailed_extraction.venue: IEEE Global Conference on Signal and Information Processing (IEEE GlobalSIP), California, USA

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes a cylindrical transform sampling method that converts 3D CT volumes into 2D images capturing spatial dependencies in both the x-y plane and along the z-axis, enabling training of classification DCNNs (AlexNet, GoogLeNet) for semantic segmentation instead of FCNs, with limited annotated data.
contribution_summary.novelty: The cylindrical transform is a novel augmentation/sampling technique that allows classification networks to perform segmentation by generating per-pixel representations from a volume, thereby leveraging 3D context without requiring fully convolutional architectures.
strengths: Achieves high DSC (98.40% with GoogLeNet) on a small dataset.
Demonstrates that classification networks can be used for segmentation with this transform.
Considers 3D spatial dependency along the z-axis.
Provides detailed experimental setup and comparison with FCNs.
weaknesses: Very small dataset (20 subjects total, 7 for training).
No external validation on independent data.
No statistical analysis (no confidence intervals or p-values).
Loss function not specified.
No code availability.
Inference may be computationally expensive as cylindrical transform is generated for every pixel.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: Potentially useful for kidney segmentation in CT scans when annotated data is scarce, reducing annotation burden. However, the small dataset and lack of external validation limit generalizability to broader clinical use.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training set comprises ~146 cases (two-thirds of 219), which is >50 subjects.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Source described: 219 liver CT volumes from surgery planning, acquired on different scanners, with contrast agent, including various pathologies and pre-resected cases.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Random assignment into three disjunct groups (training, validation, test) with two-thirds for training and 40 test cases clearly stated.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Annotation process described: slice-wise live-wire, shape-based interpolation, interactive correction, and expert review.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation on an independent dataset; only a single SLIVER07 case is shown as an example, not a full evaluation.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: U-net architectures (2D and 3D) are described in detail, including resolution levels, filter counts, padding, and a figure of the 2D U-net.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Optimizer (Adam) and loss functions are mentioned, but learning rate, number of epochs, and other hyperparameters are not specified; batch sizes are partially given.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Both cross-entropy and Dice loss are discussed, with justification for Dice in handling class imbalance, and empirical comparison.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing (resampling to isotropic voxel size with Lanczos/nearest neighbor) and post-processing (largest connected component, ensemble averaging) are clearly described.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No mention of code or model availability.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Multiple metrics used: VOE, volume error, mean/max/rms surface distances, and MICCAI score; Dice is also mentioned in abstract.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests are performed for pairwise comparisons, with p-values reported (e.g., p<0.05).

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparison is limited to different U-net variants; no quantitative comparison with other state-of-the-art methods (e.g., statistical shape models or other deep learning approaches) is provided.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: The study focuses on liver segmentation only, so results are inherently per-organ.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations discussed: issues with narrow fissures, GPU memory constraints, resampling effects, and differences in reference masks.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Patient selection is clearly defined (surgery planning cases, specific types, age/gender distribution) and random assignment to groups.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes are assessed consistently using the same metrics and reference segmentations for all methods.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes (multiple metrics, per-method results) are reported, and limitations are discussed.

detailed_extraction.title: Comparison of U-net-based Convolutional Neural Networks for Liver Segmentation in CT
detailed_extraction.authors: Hans Meine, Grzegorz Chlebus, Mohsen Ghafoorian, Itaru Endo, Andrea Schenk

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Systematic comparison of 2D and 3D U-net variants for liver segmentation in CT, including a novel ensemble of three orthogonal 2D U-nets that outperforms single 2D and 3D approaches under hardware constraints.
contribution_summary.novelty: Proposes an ensemble classifier based on softmax outputs from three orthogonal 2D U-nets, which is fully convolutional and efficient, and demonstrates its superiority over 3D U-nets given limited GPU memory.
strengths: Large dataset (219 CT volumes) with high-quality expert annotations
Comprehensive evaluation with multiple metrics and statistical tests
Clear description of architectures and preprocessing
Discussion of limitations and practical considerations
weaknesses: No external validation on an independent dataset
No code or model release
Limited comparison with other state-of-the-art methods
Incomplete hyperparameter details for reproducibility
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The proposed 2D ensemble approach is efficient and can be deployed in clinical environments without high-end hardware, potentially aiding liver surgery planning. However, further validation on diverse datasets is needed before clinical adoption.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Dataset has 68 3D CT images; with 4-fold cross-validation, 51 images are used for training, which exceeds the >50 threshold.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Source is clearly described: images acquired with a Siemens biograph 64 machine at Guangdong General Hospital; patient age range and image dimensions are provided.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Four-fold cross-validation is used with 17 test and 51 training images; split methodology considers CHD structures to ensure similar presence in training and testing.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Annotation process described: experienced radiologists labeled each image, taking 1-1.5 hours; labels include seven substructures with specific rules for vessels.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation on an independent dataset; only the internal dataset is used.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Architecture is partially described: 3D U-net for chambers/myocardium, 2D U-net for blood pool, and graph matching; details are given for input sizes, levels, and filters, but full architecture is referenced to [12] rather than fully specified.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Hyperparameters are partially provided: learning rate schedule, epochs, loss functions, data augmentation and normalization are mentioned, but optimizer, batch size, and other details are missing.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss functions (Dice and cross entropy) are mentioned but not justified or explained.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Pre-processing steps (RoI cropping, resizing, blood pool boundary class) are described, but post-processing details (refinement, graph matching specifics) are not fully elaborated.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or model is publicly available; only the dataset is mentioned as public.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Only Dice score is used; no other segmentation metrics (e.g., Hausdorff distance, IoU) are reported.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Mean and standard deviation are reported, but no confidence intervals, p-values, or formal statistical tests are performed.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparison with Seg-CNN [12], a state-of-the-art method for normal anatomy whole heart segmentation, is included.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Results are reported per CHD type, not per organ (LV, RV, LA, RA, Myo, Ao, PA); no per-substructure Dice scores are provided.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations are partially discussed: mis-segmentation between PA and LA, lower improvement for PuA due to severe variation, and need for manual refinement for 3D printing.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Medium - Patient selection is not explicitly defined; dataset is retrospective from a single hospital and may not be representative of all CHD cases.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes are assessed consistently using Dice score, and ground truth is provided by experienced radiologists.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Medium - All relevant outcomes are not reported (e.g., per-organ results, other metrics), and only mean Dice with standard deviation is given.

detailed_extraction.title: Accurate Congenital Heart Disease Model Generation for 3D Printing
detailed_extraction.authors: Xiaowei Xu, Tianchen Wang, Dewen Zeng, Yiyu Shi, Qianjun Jia, Haiyun Yuan, Meiping Huang, Jian Zhuang

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes a framework combining deep learning (3D U-net and 2D U-net) with graph matching for fully automated whole heart and great vessel segmentation in congenital heart disease (CHD) CT images, addressing the large structural variations typical of CHD.
contribution_summary.novelty: The key novelty is the integration of graph matching to classify great vessels based on connection information, overcoming the limitations of pixel-wise deep learning methods that fail when vessel connections are abnormal.
strengths: Addresses a clinically important problem (CHD segmentation for 3D printing) that is not well handled by existing methods.
Achieves 11.9% average Dice improvement over state-of-the-art Seg-CNN.
Dataset covering 14 types of CHD is made publicly available.
Demonstrates practical utility by 3D printing segmentation results with minor manual refinement.
weaknesses: Small dataset (68 images) and no external validation.
Only Dice score used; no other metrics or statistical significance testing.
No per-organ results reported, only per CHD type.
Code not released, limiting reproducibility.
Loss function choice not justified, and some hyperparameters are missing.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The method is intended for generating 3D printable models of CHD hearts, which can aid in surgical planning and education. The authors show that with minor manual refinement, the segmentation results are usable in clinical practice, as confirmed by experienced radiologists.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: The paper uses two datasets: KiTS19 (300 cases) for kidney and CHAOS (40 CT cases) for liver. The kidney dataset exceeds 50 subjects, but the liver dataset does not. Overall, the study includes one dataset with adequate size and one with insufficient size, so partial credit.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: The datasets are clearly identified: KiTS19 (Kidney Tumor Segmentation Challenge) and CHAOS (Combined CT-MR Healthy Abdominal Organ Segmentation Challenge), with references provided.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: The paper describes a 5-fold cross-validation strategy where folds are sorted by slice number to ensure test volumes have different slice counts than training, simulating worst-case clinical scenarios. The split methodology is explicit.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: The paper relies on ground truth annotations from the challenge datasets but does not describe the annotation process itself. No details on how annotations were created, verified, or by whom are provided.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation on an independent dataset is performed. The models are trained and tested on the same datasets (KiTS19 and CHAOS) using cross-validation, but no cross-dataset generalization is evaluated.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: The architectures (nnU-Net and MS-D Net) are described with key modifications (instance normalization, LeakyReLU, dilated convolutions), but full architectural details (e.g., layer counts, channel sizes) are not provided; they refer to original papers. Partial description.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Training details include batch sizes, optimizer (ADAM), loss function, augmentation probabilities, and hardware. However, specific hyperparameters like learning rate, weight decay, and number of epochs are not explicitly stated, making full reproduction difficult.

Q8_loss_function.justification: The loss function is a weighted combination of Tanimoto loss and categorical crossentropy (α=0.6, β=0.4). The choice is justified by the Tanimoto loss's suitability for class imbalance, a common issue in medical imaging.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing steps are clearly described: percentile-based windowing, z-score normalization, slice reduction to 16 slices, downsampling to 128x128, and augmentation techniques (noise, slice skipping, interpolation, range shift, rotation). Post-processing is not mentioned, but preprocessing is thorough.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or model weights are publicly released. The paper only mentions using open datasets, but the implementation is not shared.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Only the Dice score is used for evaluation. No other metrics (e.g., IoU, sensitivity, specificity) are reported.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: The paper reports mean and standard deviation but does not perform statistical significance tests (e.g., p-values) or provide confidence intervals.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: The paper compares their CT-specific augmentation framework against a state-of-the-art multidimensional image augmentation method from DeepMind, and also compares different architectures (nnU-Net vs MS-D Net) and 2D vs 3D variants.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Results are reported separately for kidney (including kidney and tumor classes) and liver, not just as an average across organs.

Q15_limitations.justification: The paper discusses challenging cases (e.g., small regions of interest) and notes that 3D CNNs do not always improve performance. However, a dedicated limitations section is absent, and potential issues like overfitting or dataset bias are not addressed.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Patient selection is based on publicly available challenge datasets with predefined inclusion criteria. The authors do not introduce additional selection bias, though they intentionally sort by slice number for cross-validation, which is a deliberate design choice to test robustness.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - All models are evaluated using the same Dice metric, same preprocessing, and same cross-validation scheme, ensuring consistent outcome assessment.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - The paper reports all primary outcomes (Dice scores for all models and tasks) and includes per-class results for kidney. No evidence of selective reporting.

detailed_extraction.title: Domain specific cues improve robustness of deep learning based segmentation of ct volumes
detailed_extraction.authors: Marie Kloenne, Sebastian Niehaus, Leonie Lampe, Alberto Merola, Janis Reinelt, Ingo Roeder, Nico Scherf

contribution_summary.main_contribution: The paper proposes a domain-specific preprocessing and augmentation framework for CT volumes that improves segmentation robustness (lower variance) while maintaining accuracy. The framework incorporates CT-specific knowledge such as Hounsfield unit windowing and slice reduction, and is shown to be architecture-independent. An ensemble model combining 2D and 3D networks further improves performance.
contribution_summary.novelty: The novelty lies in focusing on robustness and stability rather than just average performance, and in integrating radiological domain knowledge (windowing, slice handling) into the preprocessing pipeline. The systematic comparison of 2D vs 3D and different architectures under a robust evaluation scheme is also valuable.
strengths: Uses open datasets (KiTS19, CHAOS) for reproducibility.
Comprehensive comparison of multiple architectures and input dimensionalities.
Demonstrates that CT-specific preprocessing reduces variance by an order of magnitude compared to generic augmentation.
Proposes an ensemble that leverages complementary strengths of different models.
Clear description of preprocessing and augmentation steps.
weaknesses: Only uses Dice score as evaluation metric; lacks other metrics and statistical significance testing.
No external validation on independent datasets.
Code not publicly available, limiting reproducibility.
Ground truth annotation process not described.
Limited discussion of potential limitations and failure modes.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The framework aims to improve the reliability of automated segmentation in clinical workflows, where variability in slice thickness and volume size is common. By reducing prediction variance, the method could be more trustworthy for routine use, though further validation on diverse clinical data is needed.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training set per fold is less than 50 subjects (LCTSC: 48, PCT: ~34-35), so not adequate.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Both datasets (LCTSC and PCT) are publicly available and clearly described with references.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: 5-fold cross-validation is clearly described with group sizes.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Ground truth is manual segmentation from the datasets, but the annotation process is not detailed.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation on an independent dataset; only cross-validation within the same datasets.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: 3D U-Net architecture with residual blocks, encoder-decoder, and skip connections is fully described.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Hyperparameters (learning rate, optimizer, patch size, early stopping) are provided.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Weighted Dice loss is used, but no explicit justification for choosing it over other losses.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing (HU thresholding, normalization, cropping, resampling) and post-processing (patch merging, interpolation) are clearly described.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or model is publicly released.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Uses DSC for segmentation and RDE for dose calculation, providing two distinct metrics.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No confidence intervals, p-values, or formal statistical tests are reported.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Compares segmentation results with LCTSC challenge participants and dose results with population-average phantom method.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-organ DSC and RDE values are reported for all organs.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations are discussed, including small training data, poor performance on small organs, and lack of abnormality assessment.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Medium - Patient selection is from public challenge datasets, but inclusion/exclusion criteria are not described; potential selection bias from challenge design.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes are assessed consistently using the same metrics and cross-validation across all patients.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes are reported, though some organs are omitted from dose analysis due to phantom limitations, which is acknowledged.

detailed_extraction.title: A Method of Rapid Quantification of Patient-Specific Organ Dose for CT Using Coupled Deep-Learning based Multi-Organ Segmentation and GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo Dose Computing
detailed_extraction.authors: Zhao Peng, Xi Fang, Pingkun Yan, Hongming Shan, Tianyu Liu, Xi Pei, Ge Wang, Bob Liu, Mannudeep K. Kalra, X. George Xu

contribution_summary.main_contribution: First study to combine deep-learning-based multi-organ segmentation with GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo dose calculation for rapid patient-specific CT organ dose assessment, achieving clinically acceptable accuracy and efficiency.
contribution_summary.novelty: Integration of a 3D U-Net segmentation model with the ARCHER Monte Carlo dose engine in a parallel workflow, enabling near real-time patient-specific dosimetry.
strengths: High segmentation accuracy for most organs (DSC >0.9 for many organs).
Significant improvement in dose accuracy compared to population-average phantoms.
Fast processing: <5 seconds for segmentation and <4 seconds for dose calculation per patient.
Use of public datasets and clear methodology for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Small training datasets (especially for PCT) limit generalizability.
Poor performance on small, low-contrast organs (esophagus, duodenum).
No external validation on independent datasets.
No statistical analysis (confidence intervals, p-values).
Code not publicly available.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The method can be integrated into clinical workflows for personalized CT dose reporting, potentially enabling prospective scan parameter optimization and improved radiation risk assessment.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training set has 210 patients, well above the 50-subject threshold.

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes a compact multi-modal learning scheme for unpaired CT and MRI segmentation, using shared convolutional kernels with modality-specific normalization layers, and a novel knowledge distillation loss that aligns class-wise confusion matrices derived from pre-softmax activations.
contribution_summary.novelty: The combination of sharing all conv kernels while using separate normalization layers, and the KD-loss based on KL-divergence of semantic confusion matrices, is novel and parameter-efficient.

detailed_extraction.authors: Mohamed S. Elmahdy, Tanuj Ahuja, U. A. van der Heide, Marius Staring

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes a patient-specific fine-tuning approach for CNN-based segmentation in adaptive radiotherapy, where the model is adapted using imaging from previous treatment fractions to improve segmentation of daily CT scans.
contribution_summary.novelty: Introduces a personalized model adaptation strategy that accumulates anatomical knowledge over treatment sessions, unlike static deep learning models. Demonstrates significant improvement over a baseline model on an independent dataset.

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes a two-stage framework for CT prostate segmentation, with a multi-task UNet that integrates online voxel-wise metric learning to improve feature representation and boundary delineation.
contribution_summary.novelty: Introduces voxel-level metric learning with three online sampling strategies (random, focal hard negative, contour-aware) to model inter-voxel relationships, unlike conventional image-level metric learning.

Stage 2 uses a LeNet-based classifier on patches extracted from the segmented lung region to detect nodules.

detailed_extraction.title: Generalizable Cone Beam CT Esophagus Segmentation using Physics-Based Data Augmentation
detailed_extraction.authors: Sadegh R Alam, Tianfang Li, Pengpeng Zhang, Si-Yuan Zhang, Saad Nadeem

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Developed a physics-based data augmentation method that generates synthetic CBCTs (sCBCTs) from planning CTs by extracting scatter artifacts using Power-Law Adaptive Histogram Equalization (PL-AHE) and reconstructing with CBCT parameters. This enables training a 3D-UNet that generalizes across both pCT and CBCT for esophagus segmentation.
contribution_summary.novelty: Instead of improving CBCT quality to match pCT, the approach degrades pCTs to simulate CBCT artifacts, leveraging high-quality pCT contours. The use of PL-AHE for artifact extraction and the multi-objective loss tailored for tubular soft-tissue organs are novel.
strengths: Cross-modality generalization: model trained on sCBCTs performs well on both pCT and real CBCTs.
External validation on multiple independent datasets (MSK, LIDC, AAPM).
Dosimetric evaluation (mean dose, D5cc) adds clinical relevance.
Physics-based augmentation provides realistic noise/artifact spectrum, improving robustness.
weaknesses: No code or model publicly available, limiting reproducibility.
Limited statistical analysis (no confidence intervals or significance tests).
No direct comparison with state-of-the-art segmentation methods on the same datasets.
Only esophagus segmentation; applicability to other organs not demonstrated.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The model can potentially improve adaptive radiotherapy by enabling accurate esophagus segmentation on weekly CBCTs, facilitating real-time dose evaluation and reducing esophagitis risk. However, clinical adoption requires further validation and integration into clinical workflows.

detailed_extraction.title: 3D Graph Anatomy Geometry-Integrated Network for Pancreatic Mass Segmentation, Diagnosis, and Quantitative Patient Management
detailed_extraction.authors: Tianyi Zhao, Kai Cao, Jiawen Yao, Isabella Nogues, Le Lu, Lingyun Huang, Jing Xiao, Zhaozheng Yin, Ling Zhang

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes a novel Segmentation-Mesh-Classification Network (SMCN) that integrates 3D anatomy geometry with deep learning for pancreatic mass segmentation, differential diagnosis, and patient management using multi-phase CT. contribution_summary.novelty: Introduces a mask-to-mesh deformation approach that preserves anatomical correspondence, and a Graph-ResNet that pools features from the segmentation network onto mesh vertices, enabling anatomy-aware classification. strengths: Large dataset (661 patients) with five-phase CT and ten mass types.
Comprehensive evaluation with multiple metrics and comparison to strong baselines (nnUNet, radiomics, deep learning classifiers).

detailed_extraction.title: Multi-class probabilistic atlas-based whole heart segmentation method in cardiac CT and MRI
detailed_extraction.authors: Tarun Kanti Ghosh, Md. Kamrul Hasan, Shidhartho Roy, Md. Ashraful Alam, Ekras Hossain, Mohiuddin Ahmad

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes a probabilistic atlas-based whole heart segmentation framework using non-rigid registration and Bayesian inference, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the MM-WHS-2017 dataset (mVOE 14.5% for CT).
contribution_summary.novelty: Combines a multi-resolution non-rigid registration pipeline with a Bayesian framework for multi-class heart substructure segmentation, and integrates expectation-maximization for comparison. Also implements and compares three CNN variants for ablation.

Erdal, Vikash Gupta, Andres Diaz-Pinto, Andre Dourson, Lena Maier-Hein, Paul F. Jaeger, Michael Baumgartner, Jayashree Kalpathy-Cramer, Mona Flores, Justin Kirby, Lee A.D. Cooper, Holger R. Roth, Daguang Xu, David Bericat, Ralf Floca, S. Kevin Zhou, Haris Shuaib, Keyvan Farahani, Klaus H. Maier-Hein, Stephen Aylward, Prerna Dogra, Sebastien Ourselin, Andrew Feng

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Introduces MONAI, an open-source, community-supported PyTorch-based framework for deep learning in healthcare, providing domain-optimized tools for medical imaging, including network architectures, transforms, loss functions, and workflows.
contribution_summary.novelty: The novelty lies in the comprehensive, standardized, and modular framework that unifies fragmented healthcare AI development, with a focus on medical imaging and reproducibility.
strengths: Open-source and freely available (Apache-2.0 license).
Provides a wide range of domain-specific transforms, networks, and loss functions.
Designed to be PyTorch-native, ensuring ease of use and integration.
Strong community support and consortium-led development.
Includes utilities for reproducibility, determinism, and interpretability.
weaknesses: Not a specific organ segmentation study; lacks experimental validation on CT organ segmentation.
No quantitative results or comparisons with state-of-the-art segmentation methods.
No discussion of clinical applicability or performance on real-world datasets.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The framework itself is highly applicable for developing clinical segmentation models, but the paper does not demonstrate direct clinical applicability or validation.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training set sizes: 50 for CT (not >50), 60 for MRI, 1800 for endoscopy, 1000 for microscopy. The CT dataset is exactly 50, which is not >50, but other datasets have larger sizes, so partial.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: All datasets are clearly described: Abdomen CT from FLARE Challenge, Abdomen MRI from AMOS Challenge, Endoscopy from EndoVis Challenge, Microscopy from Cell Segmentation Challenge. Sources and origins are specified.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Train/test splits are clearly described for all datasets, but validation split is not explicitly mentioned; they likely use training data for validation or rely on nnU-Net's self-configuring, but not specified.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Annotation processes are described: CT annotations from AbdomenCT-1K and challenge organizers; MRI annotations generated by radiologists with MedSAM and ITK-SNAP; endoscopy and microscopy from official challenges.

Q5_external_validation.justification: All tasks use independent test sets: CT test from different centers, MRI test newly annotated, endoscopy test from unseen videos, microscopy test from challenge. External validation is performed.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: The U-Mamba block, encoder-decoder structure, Mamba block details, residual blocks, and overall network are fully described with a figure.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: They specify optimizer (SGD), loss function, epochs, patch size, batch size, but do not provide learning rate, momentum, weight decay, etc. They rely on nnU-Net's default hyperparameters, which are not fully detailed.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss function is unweighted sum of Dice and cross-entropy, justified by robustness across tasks (reference provided).

Q9_preprocessing.justification: They mention using default nnU-Net preprocessing and post-processing for instance segmentation (converting to semantic and then labeling), but do not describe the preprocessing steps in detail.

Q10_code_availability.justification: Code, models, and data are publicly available at https://wanglab.ai/u-mamba.html.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Uses DSC and NSD for semantic tasks, and F1 for instance segmentation, thus multiple metrics.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: They report mean ± standard deviation, but no confidence intervals or p-values.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Compares with nnU-Net, SegResNet, UNETR, and SwinUNETR, which are state-of-the-art methods.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-organ results are provided in Appendix Tables 5, 6, and 7 for CT and MRI.

Q15_limitations.justification: They discuss limitations such as training from scratch for Transformers, potential for ensemble, and future work, but do not explicitly analyze failure cases.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Patient selection is defined by public challenge datasets with clear inclusion criteria.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Consistent evaluation protocols, same preprocessing, and metrics across all methods; training from scratch is acknowledged.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes (DSC, NSD, F1) and per-organ results are reported.

detailed_extraction.title: U-Mamba: Enhancing Long-range Dependency for Biomedical Image Segmentation
detailed_extraction.authors: Jun Ma, Feifei Li, Bo Wang

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes U-Mamba, a hybrid CNN-SSM architecture that combines local feature extraction of CNNs with long-range dependency modeling of Mamba (SSM) for biomedical image segmentation, achieving superior performance over CNN and Transformer baselines on multiple tasks.
contribution_summary.novelty: Integrates Mamba blocks into a U-Net-like encoder-decoder, leveraging the linear scaling of SSMs to capture long-range dependencies efficiently. Inherits nnU-Net's self-configuring mechanism for automatic adaptation to different datasets.
strengths: Outperforms state-of-the-art CNN and Transformer methods on 3D CT/MRI organ segmentation, 2D instrument segmentation, and cell segmentation.
Publicly available code, models, and data.
Extensive evaluation across diverse modalities and tasks with per-organ results.
Efficient linear complexity compared to quadratic self-attention in Transformers.
weaknesses: Training from scratch may disadvantage Transformer baselines; no pre-training used.
No statistical significance testing (only standard deviations).
Relies on nnU-Net defaults for many hyperparameters, limiting reproducibility details.
Limited discussion of failure cases and edge scenarios.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: U-Mamba can be used for accurate organ segmentation in CT and MRI, instrument segmentation in endoscopy, and cell segmentation in microscopy, potentially improving clinical workflows by providing robust and efficient segmentation with fewer outliers.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: The paper curates a dataset of 11,454 CT scans, which is far above the 50-subject threshold.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Sources are clearly described, including in-house and public datasets (e.g., TCIA, MSD, TotalSegmentator, etc.) with a detailed table in the supplementary.
