Q3_train_test_split.justification: Each data source is randomly split into 64% training, 16% validation, and 20% test sets, which is explicit.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: The paper describes the use of manual labels, pseudo-labels from TotalSegmentator, and supervoxels from SAM, but does not detail the manual annotation process (e.g., who annotated, inter-observer variability).

Q5_external_validation.justification: External validation is performed on multiple independent datasets for zero-shot (murine, C4KC-KITS, Adrenocortical Carcinoma, Hepatocellular Carcinoma) and finetuning (WORD).

Q6_architecture_description.justification: The architecture is fully described: SegResNet backbone, two branches (automatic and interactive), point head with cross-attention, class embeddings, and merging algorithm.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Training details are partially given (patch size, GPU count, total GPU hours), but key hyperparameters like learning rate, optimizer, and loss function specifics are not provided.

Q8_loss_function.justification: The loss function is not specified or justified; only 'LossFunction' is mentioned in the algorithms.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Pre/post-processing steps are partially described: sliding window inference, patch-based training, resampling for speed, and a merging algorithm for interactive refinement, but full preprocessing (e.g., intensity normalization) is not detailed.

Q10_code_availability.justification: Code and weights are publicly available at https://github.com/Project-MONAI/VISTA.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Only Dice score is used as the segmentation metric; no other metrics (e.g., IoU, surface distance) are reported.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No confidence intervals, p-values, or statistical significance tests are reported.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparisons are made with state-of-the-art methods including Auto3DSeg, nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator, MedSAM, SegVol, and SAM2.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-class results are provided in the supplementary material, although the main table shows per-dataset averages.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations are discussed in the conclusion (e.g., need for more classes, modalities, clinical validation), but specific failure cases of VISTA3D are not explicitly analyzed.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Medium - Patient selection is not explicitly defined; the study uses a mix of public and in-house datasets with varying protocols, but inclusion/exclusion criteria are not detailed.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes are assessed consistently using the same Dice metric and test splits across all datasets.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes (automatic, interactive, zero-shot, finetuning) are reported, with per-class details in supplementary.

detailed_extraction.title: VISTA3D: A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
detailed_extraction.authors: Yufan He, Pengfei Guo, Yucheng Tang, Andriy Myronenko, Vishwesh Nath, Ziyue Xu, Dong Yang, Can Zhao, Benjamin Simon, Mason Belue, Stephanie Harmon, Baris Turkbey, Daguang Xu, Wenqi Li

contribution_summary.main_contribution: VISTA3D is a unified 3D segmentation foundation model that supports automatic segmentation of 127 classes, interactive segmentation with point clicks, zero-shot segmentation of novel classes, and few-shot finetuning. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on both automatic and interactive tasks across 14 datasets.
contribution_summary.novelty: The paper introduces a novel 3D supervoxel method to distill knowledge from 2D SAM for 3D zero-shot performance, a four-stage training recipe, and a unified architecture that combines automatic and interactive branches with a merging algorithm for efficient human correction.
strengths: Large-scale dataset curation (11,454 CT scans) with diverse labels.
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple datasets and baselines.
Publicly available code and weights.
Strong performance in automatic, interactive, zero-shot, and few-shot settings.
Practical human-in-the-loop workflow design.
weaknesses: Only Dice score is used for evaluation; no other metrics or statistical analysis.
Loss function and key hyperparameters are not specified, limiting reproducibility.
Preprocessing details are incomplete.
Failure cases are not explicitly analyzed.
Manual annotation process is not described in detail.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: VISTA3D can significantly reduce human effort in clinical workflows by providing accurate automatic segmentation for common organs, allowing interactive correction, and enabling zero-shot segmentation of novel structures. It is particularly useful for large cohort analysis and surgical planning, though further clinical validation is needed.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Trained on 120+ datasets with 64,518 volumes, far exceeding the 50-subject threshold.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Datasets are publicly available and clearly referenced (CT, MRI, PET, microscopy, etc.) with specific citations.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: 5% of images held out for internal validation; external test sets (RadioActive benchmark and OOD datasets) are clearly defined.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Ground truth comes from existing public datasets; annotation process not described in detail, but pseudo-labels via SAM/SAM2 are explained.

Q5_external_validation.justification: Evaluated on held-out RadioActive benchmark and multiple out-of-distribution datasets (microCT, knee MRI, insect anatomy, PET).

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Architecture based on nnU-Net with ResEnc-L backbone and early prompting strategy; sufficiently described.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Training details (optimizer, learning rate, epochs) not provided; only interaction simulation and general training pipeline are described.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss function is not specified or justified in the paper.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Pre-processing (normalization) not detailed; post-processing (AutoZoom, sliding window refinement) is described.

Q10_code_availability.justification: Code and models are publicly available via Napari plugin, MITK integration, and Python backend.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Uses Dice and AUC (for interactive refinement), plus time measurements.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: User study includes median Dice with standard deviations and Wilcoxon tests with p-values.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Compares against SAM, SAM2, SAM-Med2D, MedSAM, ScribblePrompt, SAM-Med3D, and SegVol.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-structure results reported for expert scribble benchmark (LV, RV, MYO), but not for all datasets in main benchmark.

Q15_limitations.justification: Discusses limitations of existing methods and notes points as weakest prompt type, but no dedicated failure case analysis.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Medium - Patient selection not explicitly defined; relies on publicly available datasets which may not represent all clinical scenarios.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Consistent evaluation protocol (RadioActive benchmark) and metrics used across all models.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - Key outcomes (Dice, AUC, time, user study) reported; some per-organ results omitted but not selectively.

detailed_extraction.title: nnInteractive: Redefining 3D Promptable Segmentation
detailed_extraction.authors: Fabian Isensee, Maximilian Rokuss, Lars Krämer, Stefan Dinkelacker, Ashis Ravindran, Florian Stritzke, Benjamin Hamm, Tassilo Wald, Moritz Langenberg, Constantin Ulrich, Jonathan Deissler, Ralf Floca, Klaus Maier-Hein

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Introduces nnInteractive, the first comprehensive 3D interactive open-set segmentation model supporting diverse prompts (points, scribbles, boxes, lasso) and trained on 120+ multimodal datasets, integrated into Napari and MITK.
contribution_summary.novelty: Combines early prompting in a 3D U-Net, a novel lasso prompt, AutoZoom for large structures, and large-scale training with SuperVoxels to achieve state-of-the-art performance and usability.
strengths: Unprecedented training scale (64,518 volumes, 120+ datasets)
Supports multiple prompt types including lasso, enabling intuitive 2D interactions for 3D segmentation
Strong performance across diverse modalities and out-of-distribution datasets
User study demonstrates expert-level accuracy and 72% time reduction
Publicly available with integration into established platforms
weaknesses: Loss function not specified or justified
Training hyperparameters not fully disclosed
Per-organ results not reported for all benchmark datasets
Selection bias possible due to reliance on public datasets
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: High - Integrated into Napari and MITK, supports real-time interactive segmentation with <10GB VRAM, and user study shows expert-level accuracy with significant time savings, making it suitable for clinical workflows.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: 761 CT scans (519 pelvic + 242 head and neck) from 8 clinical sites; far exceeds the >50-subject threshold for both training domains.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Source clearly described: IMRT planning CTs acquired Oct 2013–Feb 2020 at 8 sites with heterogeneous scanners/protocols; demographics reported (pelvic: 100% men, 75% aged 62–75; H&N: 76% men, 80% aged 50–73); ethics approval stated (East of England–Essex REC + HRA); external H&N set is the public Nikolov et al. dataset (TCIA Cetuximab + TCGA-HNSCC).

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Split methodology clear: main vs external grouping with 3 randomly selected clinical sites fully excluded from training (masked external evaluation); ensemble trained on different train/val splits of main with a fixed disjoint internal test set; evaluation set sizes given (pelvic main 49, pelvic external 83, H&N external 26, IOV-10).

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Annotation process described: structures contoured by 2 clinically trained expert readers and a radiation oncologist, masked to each other's annotations, with independent oncologist review; reference ground truth defined by majority voting of 3 annotators (≥2 must agree a structure is present); further detail in eAppendix 1.

Q5_external_validation.justification: Strong external validation: (1) 3 unseen clinical sites held out entirely from training, with internal-vs-external statistical comparison per structure; (2) fully independent public H&N dataset (Nikolov et al./TCIA) with expert and radiographer reference contours.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Main text states only 'variant of the 3D U-Net' trained as an ensemble; full architectural detail deferred to eAppendix 2 in the Supplement and not verifiable from the main text.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Partial: ensemble scheme (different train/val splits, fixed disjoint test set) and platform (Microsoft InnerEye on Azure ML; Python 3.7.3, scikit-learn 0.21.1, scipy 1.3.1) reported, but hyperparameters, optimizer, augmentation, and patch strategy are not in the main text (deferred to eAppendix 2). Open-source code partially mitigates.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss function not stated in main text; explicitly deferred to eAppendix 2 in the Supplement, so no justification is assessable from the provided material.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing not described ('models operate on raw 3D CT images'; only anonymization via InnerEye Gateway mentioned). Postprocessing described only qualitatively — a custom method that 'does not allow segmentation inconsistencies at a distance from the anatomical structure' — with no algorithmic detail.

Q10_code_availability.justification: Training code publicly available as open source: https://github.com/microsoft/InnerEye-DeepLearning/ (license not stated in paper; article CC-BY-NC-ND).

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Dice plus mean surface distance and Hausdorff distance (mm), plus Cohen/Fleiss κ computed on foreground voxels to avoid background-pixel bias.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Thorough: Mann-Whitney tests for main-vs-external differences (significance P<.01, two-tailed), 95% CIs on timing measurements, Bland-Altman plots, κ>0.75 agreement criterion, per-structure significance testing.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Partial: benchmarked against human baselines (3 expert annotators, majority-vote reference, radiographer contours on external set) rather than other published deep learning autosegmentation methods; no algorithmic SOTA comparison (e.g., no comparison against Nikolov et al.'s model despite using their dataset).

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Full per-structure reporting: Dice (mean, SD), mean surface distance, and Hausdorff distance for all 15 structures across main, external, and IOV-10 sets in both pelvic and H&N domains.

Q15_limitations.justification: Failure modes and limitations discussed: SMG performance drop attributed to low tissue contrast; errors localized to superior/inferior extents of tubular structures and adjacent organ interfaces; IOV and time-measurement experiments limited to 10 scans per domain; authors note Dice/surface metrics do not always correlate with correction-time savings and call for interaction-cost-weighted metrics.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low. Patients defined by cancer diagnosis and RT planning CT acquisition at 8 sites with ethics approval; cohorts demographically characterized. Minor caveats: pelvic cohort is 100% men (expected for prostate cancer), and detailed inclusion/exclusion criteria live in the supplement only.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low. Identical metrics and protocol applied across internal, external, and IOV sets; annotators masked to each other; majority-vote reference standard; masked evaluation on sites fully excluded from training; inference time and correction time measured with CIs.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low. All 15 structures reported per-organ (Dice, MD, HD, κ) on three dataset variants with no outcome selectively omitted. Minor concerns: loss function and hyperparameters relegated to supplement; IOV/time experiments use only 10 scans per domain, which is reported transparently but limits precision of the 93% time-saving estimate.

detailed_extraction: Supplementary details not in prior extraction: (1) Statistics — significance threshold P<.01, all tests two-tailed; κ agreement threshold >0.75; κ computed on foreground voxels only to avoid background-pixel bias; Mann-Whitney main-vs-external P values: L/R femur .04, bladder .10, rectum .07, prostate .42, SV .91 (only femur differences are even nominally significant at .05, none at .01, supporting the cross-site consistency claim). (2) Software/versions — Python 3.7.3, scikit-learn 0.21.1 (κ), scipy 1.3.1 (Mann-Whitney); SQUIRE reporting guideline followed; analysis period Oct 2019–Sept 2020. (3) Evaluation set sizes — pelvic main 49, pelvic external 83, H&N external 26, IOV-10 = 10 scans per domain with mixed image quality (5 good / 5 poor). (4) Reference standard — majority vote of 3 annotators with rule that ≥2 experts must agree a structure is present. (5) H&N OAR subset chosen by a radiation oncology panel based on routine H&N RT relevance (prior consensus ref 18). (6) Error characterization — errors concentrate at superior/inferior extents of tubular structures and interfaces between adjacent organs; no inconsistencies at distance from the structure due to postprocessing design. (7) Annotation tool — in-house tool with assistive contouring and interactive refinement modules, used for both from-scratch and correction timing tasks. (8) Demographics — pelvic: 519 men (100%), 75% aged 62–75; H&N: 184 men (76%), 80% aged 50–73. (9) Internal inconsistency in the paper: expert-reader manual H&N contouring time CI reported as 86.75 (95% CI, 75.21–92.29) min/scan in the abstract but 86.75 (95% CI, 75.25–98.29) min/scan in the Results text. (10) Provided full text is truncated mid-sentence in the annotation-time section ('which are inspecte…'); Discussion-section content is partially inferred from the extracted limitations/future-work fields rather than the visible text.
contribution_summary: Multi-site (8 hospitals, 761 CTs) clinical evaluation of a 3D U-Net ensemble autocontouring system covering 15 OARs across prostate and head-and-neck radiotherapy, achieving Fleiss κ within expert interobserver variability for 14 of 15 structures and near-identical Dice on held-out-site and public external data. Clinically, correcting autocontours cut contouring time by a mean of 93% (4.98 min/scan H&N, 3.40 min/scan prostate vs 73–87 min manual). Distinctively, it ships as an open-source end-to-end workflow (Microsoft InnerEye: Gateway anonymization, Azure ML training, cloud segmentation service, correction tool) designed for direct PACS integration rather than as a novel architecture.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: 80 training volumes (60 LiTS + 20 CHAOS) exceeds the >50 subject threshold, aided by rotation/scaling/elastic deformation augmentation.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: LiTS, 3DIRCADb, and CHAOS all cited with volume counts, slice ranges, and voxel spacing (Table 7.1); all publicly available benchmark datasets.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Test evaluation on 3DIRCADb and CHAOS test set (via leaderboard) is clear, but how 60 volumes were selected from the 131 LiTS training cases is unspecified and no validation split or cross-validation methodology is described.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: CHAOS GT annotated manually by three experienced radiologists; 3DIRCADb annotated by expert radiologists; LiTS GT provided by challenge organizers. Inter-rater protocol not detailed but adequate for public benchmark data.

Q5_external_validation.justification: CHAOS test-set evaluation via independent challenge leaderboard is genuine external validation, but 3DIRCADb is stated to be part of LiTS training data and the paper does not confirm the 60 LiTS training volumes exclude 3DIRCADb cases, leaving possible train/test overlap unaddressed.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Architecture diagrams (Figs 7.1, 7.3) show R2N encoder blocks, feature fusion, sigmoid attention on skip connections, and UNet decoder; however, encoder depth, channel widths, and exact block placement are not specified, and design is borrowed from ref [12].

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Adam, LR 1e-5, batch size 8, weight decay 1e-5, trained from scratch, augmentation types, and TF/Keras on Titan-X are reported, but number of epochs, augmentation magnitudes, and scaling factor placement details are missing; no code released.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Dice loss defined by equation and cited as complement of DSC, but no justification for choosing it over alternatives (e.g., combined CE+dice) and no ablation of loss choice.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing fully specified: resize 512x512 to 256x256, HU windowing (-250, 200), normalization to [0,1], histogram equalization, with visual results (Figs 7.4, 7.5). No post-processing reported (none applied).

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or model weights link provided anywhere in the chapter.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Six metrics with formulas and interpretation (Table 7.2): DSC, IoU, VOE, RAVD, ASSD, MSSD.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Mean +/- SD per metric and per-patient result plots (Figs 7.6, 7.7) are reported, but no confidence intervals, significance tests, or p-values; comparisons with SOTA are not tested statistically.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparison tables against UNet, Christ et al., H-DenseUNet, mU-Net, Tang et al. on 3DIRCADb and Mulay, Kavur on CHAOS, plus CHAOS leaderboard submission for external check.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Single-organ (liver) study so per-organ breakdown is not applicable; per-patient/per-case results are reported graphically, which partially satisfies the spirit of the criterion for a multi-organ review.

Q15_limitations.justification: Generic limitations acknowledged (supervised dependence on data quality/quantity, scaling-factor trade-off, hyperparameter tuning possible) but no failure cases shown or analyzed despite high MSSD variance (up to 356 mm on CHAOS).

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Unclear/moderate: the rule for selecting 60 of 131 LiTS training volumes is not stated, and potential overlap between LiTS training data and the 3DIRCADb test set (3DIRCADb is part of LiTS) is never addressed, risking optimistic 3DIRCADb results.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low/moderate: evaluation used six consistent, standard metrics; CHAOS test scoring by the independent challenge server reduces assessor bias, but 3DIRCADb evaluation was performed by the authors themselves with no blinding.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low/moderate: all three tested scale factors (s=2,4,8) are reported including the inferior ones, and leaderboard submission is disclosed; however, only best-configuration results headline the abstract and no per-case failure analysis is reported.

detailed_extraction: TASK & SCOPE: Liver-only segmentation (single organ) from abdominal CT; relevant to the review despite the paper being a 2D slice-by-slice approach processed over 3D volumes, not a true 3D network. ARCHITECTURE: UNet-style encoder-decoder; encoder convolutions replaced with Res2Net (R2N) bottleneck modules (from Gao et al.) splitting channels into groups with hierarchical 3x3 convs for multi-scale receptive fields; high-resolution features fused into the next encoder stage; attention gate = 1x1 conv + BN + sigmoid recalibrating skip features via element-wise multiplication before decoder concatenation; decoder uses 2x2 deconvolutions. Scale factor s ablated over {2,4,8}; s=4 best. PREPROCESSING: per-slice resize to 256x256, HU window (-250, 200), normalize [0,1], histogram equalization. TRAINING: from scratch, Adam, LR 1e-5, batch 8, weight decay 1e-5, dice loss; augmentation = rotation, scaling, elastic deformation; TF/Keras, Xeon E5-1620, 16 GB RAM, Titan-X 12 GB. RESULTS: 3DIRCADb: DSC 0.973+/-0.006, IoU 0.938+/-0.013, VOE 0.062+/-0.012, RAVD 0.059+/-0.013, ASSD 0.710+/-0.276 mm, MSSD 63.037+/-25.738 mm; CHAOS test (leaderboard, team devidas.sggs, submitted Oct 7, 2020): DSC 0.964+/-0.010, RAVD 3.794+/-2.863, ASSD 3.831+/-3.601 mm, MSSD 121.751+/-61.263 mm. CAVEATS FOR META-ANALYSIS: (1) On 3DIRCADb the reported MSSD (63.0 mm) and RAVD (0.059) are actually WORSE than several comparators (Li/H-DenseUNet: MSSD 9.35, RAVD 0.004; Seo/mU-Net: MSSD 9.20; Christ: MSSD 24, RAVD 0.014), so the 'outperforms SOTA' claim holds only for DSC/IoU/VOE/ASSD; (2) possible train/test contamination between the 60-volume LiTS subset and 3DIRCADb; (3) comparator results may come from different training configurations, so the comparison is not like-for-like; (4) book chapter, no peer-review-independent code or ablations of attention/fusion components (ablation only on scale factor). PUBLICATION TYPE: 2022 Scrivener book chapter (Medical Imaging and Health Informatics); earlier related work by same group (MS-UNet, ref [32]). FUTURE WORK stated: extend to liver tumor segmentation.
contribution_summary: Proposes DMSAN, a UNet variant whose encoder is built from Res2Net (R2N) multi-scale bottleneck blocks with inter-stage high/low-resolution feature fusion and a sigmoid-attention recalibration of skip connections, trained end-to-end with dice loss for liver segmentation. Achieves DSC 0.973 on 3DIRCADb and 0.964 on the independent CHAOS test set (leaderboard-verified), with an ablation showing scale factor s=4 is optimal. Incremental architectural contribution (R2N + attention applied to a UNet) with medium methodological rigor and no released code.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: 81 training CT volumes from LiTS, exceeding the >50 subject threshold; augmented with rotation/flip/crop/scale.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: LiTS (MICCAI 2017) benchmark clearly described: 6 clinical sites, pixel spacing 0.55-1.0 mm, slice spacing 0.45-6.0 mm, 74-987 slices/volume, NIfTI format, tumor counts 0-75, tumor volumes 38-349 mm3, HU delta 0-98 (mean 31.94, SD 20.21).

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Split sizes stated (81/25/25 train/test/val) but selection method not described — unclear whether random, stratified, or site-based.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Ground truth manually labeled by experienced radiologists/medical clinicians (LiTS-provided), but no annotator count, labeling protocol, or inter-observer agreement reported.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation; all evaluation on internal LiTS split.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Fully described: dual-path (local 43^3 high-res, global 129^3 subsampled to 43^3), 8 identical blocks/path (3x3x3 conv + BN + PReLU), residual connections blocks 2-4/4-6/6-8, 1x1x1 conv in FC layer, 3-class softmax; includes receptive-field derivation (R8=17^3), layer parameter table, and design rationale (no pooling, 3^3 vs 5^3 kernel).

Q7_reproducibility.justification: TensorFlow 1.8, GTX 1080 8GB, ~96h/2000 epochs, 13.3 min inference/volume reported; optimizer, learning rate, batch size referenced in Tables 2-3 but values not verifiable in provided text.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Cross-entropy used but never justified; no discussion of class imbalance despite tiny tumors (<500 voxels) vs large background — a known failure mode they later report.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing fully specified (Gaussian smoothing sigma=1 with formula, per-image mean/std normalization, 512->256 downsampling, geometric augmentation); FC-CRF postprocessing given with full Gibbs-energy formulation and quantified impact (liver HD 89.26->29.16, tumor HD 65.38->7.69).

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or model release; no URL or statement of availability.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Dice + Hausdorff distance + average surface distance, reported per structure.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No confidence intervals, p-values, or variance measures; single point estimates only.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Compared against MICCAI 2017 LiTS top-3 (Li et al. rank 1, Chlebus rank 2, Yuan rank 3) plus internal ablations (single-path baseline, Local+ with 2x feature maps); ranked liver 1st, tumor 2nd.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Liver (Dice 0.965) and liver tumor (Dice 0.689) reported separately with all three metrics.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations discussed: poor small-tumor performance (<500 voxels), residual false-positive voxels requiring CRF, heavy 3D compute cost; future work on size/type-specialized tumor segmentation stated.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Moderate — public multi-center benchmark (6 sites) reduces selection bias, but the train/test partition procedure is undefined; cannot exclude non-random test-case selection.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low — identical preprocessing, inference, and metrics applied uniformly across all test cases; all comparisons made on the same LiTS benchmark data.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low-moderate — per-organ results, ablation studies, and failure modes (small tumors) transparently reported; however, no uncertainty quantification and no per-patient results, so selective reporting cannot be fully excluded.

detailed_extraction: Supplementary details beyond prior extraction: (1) Hyperparameter selection methodology — kernel size (3^3 vs 5^3, 4.6x parameter difference) and segment size (34^3/37^3/40^3/43^3 compared via Dice+sensitivity) were tuned on a simple one-path proxy CNN, justified by the claim that the optimal combination transfers to the dual-path design; receptive field math (8 layers, stride 1, k=3) gives R8=17^3, setting minimum viable segment size. (2) Architectural choices with stated rationale: no pooling layers (preserves voxel localization); global path subsamples 129^3->43^3 (3x downsample) capturing context at equal compute; 1x1x1 convolution in the FC stage replaces standard MxNxP-kernel flattening specifically to retain 3D spatial information at the cost of more parameters; residual connections are additive (block 2 output added to block 4 output). (3) FC-CRF details: Krähenbühl-style fully connected CRF (refs 16-17), Gibbs energy with unary potentials from TDP-CNN probability maps, pairwise potentials as weighted Gaussian kernels over pixel position/color features, Potts compatibility; k=3 classes. (4) LiTS dataset heterogeneity documented: hepatocellular carcinoma and metastases (lung, breast), hyper/hypo-dense contrast enhancement, 0-75 tumors/patient. (5) Note: provided full text is truncated mid-Section 3 (Tables 1-3, 6-7 contents and results narrative not visible); results figures rely on the previously extracted data block, which is consistent with the visible abstract.
contribution_summary: The paper proposes TDP-CNN, a dual-path 3D CNN that fuses high-resolution local features (43^3 patches) with subsampled global context (129^3 patches) via additive feature fusion, using a 1x1x1 convolution in the fully connected stage to preserve spatial information and FC-CRF postprocessing to remove false positives. On LiTS it achieved liver Dice 0.965 (rank 1) and tumor Dice 0.689 (rank 2) against all MICCAI 2017 challenge entries, while demonstrating that patch-size scaling monotonically improves 3D segmentation performance up to 43^3. The main limitation is weak small-tumor segmentation (<500 voxels) and high computational cost (96h training, 13.3 min/volume inference).

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Partial. The primary organ segmentation task met the >50 threshold (73 training / 18 test of 91 patients), but the applicator segmentation task used only 24 training / 8 test cases. Overall cohort is modest, single-center, single applicator type (Fletcher Williamson), and the authors themselves identify small dataset size as the principal limitation affecting performance (e.g., sigmoid DSC 64.5%) and generalization.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Yes. Source clearly described: planning CTs from the first high-dose-rate brachytherapy fraction of 91 cervical cancer patients at Tianjin Medical University Cancer Institute and Hospital; scanner (Philips Brilliance CT Big Bore, helical mode), matrix 512x512, 2 mm slice thickness, mean in-plane resolution 1.11 mm (range 0.97-1.22 mm), and Elekta Fletcher Williamson tandem-and-ovoid applicator all reported.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Partial. Random 80/20 splits reported (73/18 anatomy; 24/8 applicator) with identical splits used for the 3D U-Net comparison. However, no dedicated validation set is described - 'the model with the highest performance was selected' and learning-rate decay triggered on 'stagnation for more than 20 epochs' without specifying which data these were assessed on, raising the possibility of test-set involvement in model selection. No cross-validation performed.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Partial. HR-CTV and OARs contoured by radiation oncologists following published consensus guidelines (Viswanathan et al.); applicator components segmented by experienced medical physicists; GT channel paths defined as best-fit polynomial curves through manually placed points. However, number of observers, blinding, arbitration process, and inter-/intra-observer variability are not reported.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No. Entirely single-institution, single-dataset evaluation with random internal split; no independent external cohort used for validation.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Yes. DSD-UNET fully described with a schematic figure: 3D U-Net backbone with residual blocks (two 3x3x3 convolutions with spatial dropout) in the contracting path, stride-2 convolutional downsampling, deconvolution upsampling with concatenation skip connections, a parallel multi-rate dilated convolution module (rates 1, 2, 3, 4) between paths, deep supervision via 1x1x1 segmentation layers at each expanding stage fused by element-wise summation, instance normalization with LeakyReLU, and sigmoid outputs. Per-stage channel doubling/halving described; base filter count only inferable from Figure 2.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Yes. Training recipe largely complete: Adam optimizer (initial LR 5e-4, halved upon >20-epoch stagnation), batch size 2, maximum 200 epochs, on-the-fly augmentation (random rotation <=10 deg, scaling <=15%, left-right mirroring), multiclass dice loss, Keras/TensorFlow backend, and hardware (CPU-only Intel Xeon E5-2620 v3, 32 GB RAM; ~150 h training time). Minor gaps: no random seed and ambiguous validation monitoring.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Partial. Multiclass dice loss (Eq. 1) is formulated and implicitly motivated by alignment with the DSC evaluation metric (and implicitly handles class imbalance), but the choice is not explicitly justified against alternatives (e.g., cross-entropy or compound losses).

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Yes. Preprocessing fully described: cropping of empty space, linear interpolation to fixed 128x128x64 voxels, CLAHE contrast enhancement combined with the original image as a dual-channel input; applicator task used a 128x128x80 VOI centered on the applicator interpolated to 128x128x64 (2.5 mm interslice, native in-plane). Postprocessing fully described: 3D parallel thinning skeletonization (Lee et al. 1994; octree 3x3x3 lattice for topology preservation) followed by fifth-degree 3D parametric polynomial curve fitting.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No. No code, model weights, or public repository mentioned anywhere in the paper.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Yes. Three complementary metrics: Dice similarity coefficient, Jaccard Index, and Hausdorff distance (formally defined in Eqs. 2-5), with HD additionally used for channel-path digitization agreement. Mean, SD, and (for path HDs) min-max ranges reported.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Partial. Descriptive statistics only (mean +/- SD for all metrics; min-max for channel-path HDs). No p-values, confidence intervals, or significance testing for the DSD-UNET vs 3D U-Net comparison despite a small test set (n=18).

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Partial. Compared against 3D U-Net as the sole baseline on identical train/test splits (fair comparison), but no comparison with atlas-based methods (discussed in the text as the clinical standard) or other contemporary CNN architectures (e.g., residual/dilated variants cited in references 33-36, 42).

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Yes. Complete per-structure DSC, JI, and HD with standard deviations for all five anatomical structures (HR-CTV, bladder, small intestine, sigmoid, rectum; Table 1) and all six applicator components (Table 2), not merely pooled averages.

Q15_limitations.justification: Yes. Candid, detailed limitations section: small dataset; loss of detail from fixed-size resizing (128x128x64); inferior sigmoid segmentation explicitly analyzed (DSC 64.5%, HD 19.6 mm; attributed to misclassification, small volume, and difficulty at small intestine-sigmoid and rectosigmoid junctions); restriction to simple tandem-and-ovoid applicators as preliminary exploration; CPU-only constraints; future work (patch-based pipeline, larger data, unified single model) outlined.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Moderate. Single-center retrospective cohort; explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria (time period, exclusions) not reported; only patients with Fletcher Williamson tandem-and-ovoid applicators included, restricting case-mix spectrum; random train/test split stated but no external cohort, limiting generalizability to other centers, scanners, and applicator types.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low-to-moderate. Both models trained and evaluated on identical random splits using standardized, formally defined metrics against guideline-based clinician/physicist contours; however, the model selection and learning-rate scheduling criteria lacked a specified validation set (possible test-set leakage), and no blinded clinical acceptability assessment by observers was performed.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low. All structures reported including the worst performer (sigmoid) and all applicator components with per-structure variability; failure modes and limitations candidly discussed; funded study with declared no conflicts. Minor concerns: no pre-registered protocol, no statistical significance testing, and the comparison restricted to a single baseline may present the method favorably.

detailed_extraction: Clinical context and task: First study to apply CNNs to CT-based cervical cancer brachytherapy (BT). Two tasks: (1) segmentation of HR-CTV and OARs (bladder, small intestine, sigmoid, rectum); (2) segmentation of applicator components (tandem tube, left/right ovoid tubes, left/right ovoids, cervical stopper) followed by fully automatic channel-path digitization. Clinical motivation: +/-3 mm applicator displacement or +/-4.5 mm reconstruction uncertainty can cause >10% dosimetric change given steep BT dose gradients (citing Schindel et al.). Data: planning CTs from the first HDR BT fraction; Philips Brilliance CT Big Bore, helical, 512x512, 2 mm slices, mean in-plane 1.11 mm (0.97-1.22 mm); Elekta Fletcher Williamson applicators. Annotation: radiation oncologists per Viswanathan et al. consensus guidelines (CT-based cervical BT); medical physicists segmented applicators; GT channel paths defined as best-fit polynomial curves through manually placed points. Architecture specifics: residual blocks (two 3x3x3 convs with spatial dropout between) at each contracting stage; stride-2 3x3x3 conv downsampling; expanding stage = stride-2 3x3x3 deconv + concatenation skip + 3x3x3 conv + 1x1x1 conv; deep supervision via 1x1x1 segmentation layers at each expanding stage fused by element-wise summation; parallel dilated conv module (rates 1,2,3,4) bridging paths; channels doubled/halved per stage; instance norm + LeakyReLU throughout except segmentation layers; sigmoid output. Training: Keras/TensorFlow; Adam, LR 5e-4 halved on >20-epoch stagnation; batch 2; <=200 epochs; on-the-fly augmentation (rotation <=10 deg, scaling <=15%, left-right mirroring); multiclass dice loss (Eq. 1); trained on CPU only (no GPU available), ~150 h. Applicator pipeline: VOI 128x128x80 centered on applicator -> interpolation to 128x128x64 (2.5 mm interslice, native in-plane) -> DSD-UNET -> 3D parallel thinning skeletonization (octree 3x3x3 lattice connectivity) -> fifth-degree 3D parametric polynomial fitting; ~22 s/case reconstruction; ~20 s/patient segmentation inference. Results: DSD-UNET outperformed 3D U-Net on every structure: average +7.0% DSC, +9.2% JI, -3.7 mm HD; channel-path HDs 0.88+/-0.12 mm (0.71-1.16), 0.95+/-0.16 mm (0.69-1.48), 0.96+/-0.15 mm (0.75-1.34) for intrauterine/left/right ovoid tubes, all means <1 mm. Gaps/unclear: no validation set identified for model selection or early stopping (potential test leakage); base filter count only in figure; no random seed, no code release, no external data, single applicator type. Funding: NSFC Grant 81872472; open-access CC-BY; no conflicts declared.
contribution_summary: This is the first study to apply 3D CNNs to CT-based cervical cancer brachytherapy, introducing DSD-UNET - a 3D U-Net enhanced with residual blocks, multi-rate dilated convolutions, deep supervision, and dual-channel (original + CLAHE-enhanced) input - which outperformed 3D U-Net on all structures (mean DSC: 86.9% bladder, 82.9% HR-CTV, 82.1% rectum, but only 64.5% sigmoid). It further presents the first fully automatic applicator reconstruction pipeline, combining DSD-UNET component segmentation with 3D skeletonization and fifth-degree polynomial curve fitting to achieve sub-millimetre channel-path accuracy (mean HD <1 mm) in ~22 s per case without manual intervention. While clinically motivated and methodologically detailed, the single-center dataset (n=91), CPU-only training, absence of external validation, and weak small-bowel structure segmentation temper generalizability.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Marginal: ~59 training subjects (20 from 3D-IRCADb + up to 39 local PV-phase patients, 2428 2D slices total). Test set is only 10 patients. Just clears the >50 threshold; slice-level data is 2D, not volumetrically diverse.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Well described: two sources (Kasturba Medical College retrospective data 2016-2021, and public 3D-IRCADb), three named Philips scanners, acquisition parameters (100-120kVp, 5mm slice thickness, pixel resolution range), ethics approval stated, phase composition per test case specified (6 quadriphasic, 4 triphasic).

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Explicit no-overlap statement between training and test sets, but no validation set is mentioned, and the criteria for assigning the 10 test vs 39 training patients are not described. No cross-validation or split randomization reported.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Clear: ITK-SNAP manual delineation supervised by a radiologist with >20 years abdominal imaging experience (co-author); IVC exclusion policy stated; NIfTI format; Dataset II GT by experienced radiologists.

Q5_external_validation.justification: Partial: model largely trained on public 3D-IRCADb and tested on independent local multi-scanner data, which is genuine cross-dataset testing. However, 186 local training slices come from the same institution and same patient pool source as the test set, so it is not fully external-center validation.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Full layer-by-layer SegNet architecture given (Table 1) with feature-map sizes, VGG-16 pretrained encoder, 5 encoder/decoder blocks, max-pooling indices upsampling, softmax + pixel classification output (380x380x2).

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Good: SGD momentum 0.9, constant LR 0.001, 350 epochs, batch size 2, exact augmentation ranges, image resize (380x380), normalization, hardware/software stack (MATLAB R2021a, NVIDIA T4). K-means parameters (K=3, initial centroids 0/255/128, stopping criterion) fully specified.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Cross-entropy used without any justification or discussion of alternatives (e.g., Dice loss for class imbalance between liver and background).

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Thorough: HU conversion (Eq. 1), rejected HU-windowing approach in favor of 0-255 intensity mapping (rationale given), resize to 380x380, RGB triplication, zero-center normalization, and detailed enhancement pipeline (PL gamma values, Gaussian/median filter sizes and sigma) with tuning rationale.

Q10_code_availability.justification: Data availability statement says 'Research data are not shared'; no code or model release mentioned.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Four metrics: Dice coefficient, Jaccard index, volumetric overlap error, average symmetric surface distance; plus ROC-AUC (0.9994) and true positive rate for tumors.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Partial: mean±SD reported throughout and one paired t-test (GT vs predicted tumor volume, t=1.4539, p=0.1799). No confidence intervals on Dice scores, no significance testing for the SegNet vs UNet comparison, no inter-rater reliability. The t-test performed (predicted vs GT volume) is of limited inferential value.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Two comparisons: (i) own UNet baseline trained and tested on identical data (SegNet clearly superior, e.g., plain-CT DC 94.21% vs 76.51%), and (ii) Table 4 literature comparison against five published methods. Caveat: literature comparison is DC-only across different datasets.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-patient results reported for all 10 test cases, per phase (Table 2: liver; Table 3: UNet; Table 5: tumor), not just averages; liver vs tumor reported separately; per-phase breakdown (PV/ART/plain/delayed) provided.

Q15_limitations.justification: Explicit and specific: false positives are the main tumor-segmentation error source (portal vein falsely segmented, Fig. 10D), IVC inclusion errors, unsmooth boundaries for ambiguous tumors, method fails for extremely heterogeneous and hyperdense tumors, true positive rate only 76.65%, training time (95h) acknowledged.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Moderate-to-high: retrospective, single-institution test set (n=10 patients), no patient selection/inclusion criteria defined, tumors were selected cases (only largest tumor analyzed per case).
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low-to-moderate: identical metrics and pipeline applied consistently across all phases and cases; however, ground truth was created under supervision of a single radiologist (a co-author) with no second reader or inter-observer check, and the same team annotated and evaluated.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Moderate: all per-case metrics and failures are reported transparently, but data and code are unavailable for verification, tumor segmentation results are only shown for the PV phase (best-case phase), and only the largest tumor per patient was quantified.

detailed_extraction: Task fit note: paper covers liver + liver tumor segmentation (single organ), using 2D slice-wise SegNet with volumetric (3D) metrics — not multi-organ 3D segmentation. Pipeline: (1) Liver segmentation: SegNet fine-tuned from VGG-16 weights using ONLY portal-venous phase training images (key finding: generalizes to arterial, plain, delayed phases without retraining; DC 96.46% PV, 95.22% ART, 94.21% plain, 95.8% delayed). Training data: 2428 slices (2242 from 3D-IRCADb 20 patients + 186 local PV slices). Batch-size ablation (2/4/6/8) shows batch 2 best; degradation up to -3.08% DC for ART at batch 8. Grad-CAM used for interpretability (early layers learn edges, decoder 1 highlights liver only). (2) Tumor segmentation: non-DL — novel power-law-based contrast enhancement (three branches: bright γ=0.8 on Gaussian-filtered windowed image + median filter; dark γ=2 on mapped image + Gaussian σ=1/5x5; intensity-halved mapped image; summed then Gaussian filtered) followed by K-means (K=3, centroids 0/255/128) on the enhanced segmented liver, smallest cluster taken as tumor, morphological post-processing. Tumor results (PV phase, 10 cases): DC 85.07±4.5%, JI 74.29±6.8%, VOE 25.71±6.8%, ASD 1.14±1.3 mm, TPR 76.65%. Tumor volume GT vs predicted: paired t-test p=0.1799 (not significant). Baseline: UNet (384x384) trained identically performs markedly worse, especially on plain CT (DC 76.51%). Compute: 95h training (364,200 iterations) on NVIDIA T4; inference 0.25 s/slice (liver) + 0.06 s/slice (tumor). Enhancement ablation (Fig. 11) shows plain mapped/windowed images or simple PL alone fail to isolate tumors. Ethical approval obtained; funding: KSTePS DST Karnataka fellowship.
contribution_summary: The key contribution is demonstrating that a SegNet fine-tuned exclusively on portal-venous phase CT robustly segments the liver across all four CT phases (plain, arterial, PV, delayed), with per-phase quantitative evidence — addressing the gap that most liver CAD work is single-phase. Second, a power-law transformation-based multi-branch contrast enhancement combined with K-means clustering segments liver tumors without DL training, achieving DC 85.07%, presented as a practical alternative to data-hungry tumor CNNs. Main limitation is a high false-positive rate in tumor segmentation (TPR 76.65%) on a small 10-patient single-center test set.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: 240 annotated CT scans from 200 patients (89 torso, 17 chest, 134 abdomen/pelvis) — well above the 50-subject threshold, plus ~100,000 derived 2D training sections.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Thoroughly described: shared 'Computational Anatomy' dataset from Tokushima University Hospital, IRB approval at Gifu and Tokushima, single scanner vendor (Toshiba Aquilion), reconstruction protocols, resolutions (0.625–1.148 mm, 1.0 mm slices), and contrast enhancement in 155/240 scans all documented.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Random 95%/5% split (12 test scans) is stated, but no separate validation set is described, and 32 patients have multiple scans — scan-level random split risks patient overlap/leakage between train and test, which is not addressed.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Annotation process described in detail: manual annotation by multiple research-group members, intensive validation/refinement by a medical expert committee, supported by a semiautomatic annotation tool.

Q5_external_validation.justification: Single-center, single-dataset internal split only; no independent external cohort.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Fully described: VGG16 down-sampling path with FC→conv conversion, 22-channel 1×1 classifier, five deconvolution layers with skip connections, sequential FCN32s→16s→8s→4s→2s training, ReLU, dropout, LCN; structure figure plus appendix graph provided.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Optimizer (SGD momentum 0.9, ADAM for comparison), learning rate 1e-4, weight decay 2e-4, batch size 20, dropout 0.5, LCN parameters, ImageNet-pretrained VGG16 initialization, framework (Caffe + reference FCN), and GPU (TITAN-X 12 GB) all specified. Minor gap: number of training epochs/iterations not stated in available text.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss described only as 'sum of pixel-wise losses between network prediction and human-annotated label map'; exact form (presumably softmax cross-entropy per FCN convention) is never stated and the choice is not justified against alternatives (e.g., Dice loss, class weighting for the severe organ imbalance evident in Table I).

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing explicit (12-bit→8-bit linear interpolation, RGB channel duplication, otherwise raw heterogeneous input) and postprocessing explicit (voxel-wise majority voting over three orthogonal planes, largest-volume anatomical prior as tie-breaker).

Q10_code_availability.justification: No public code or model release mentioned; built on Caffe and the public Long et al. FCN implementation, which partially aids reimplementation but is not a code release.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Only a single metric — voxel labeling accuracy (88.1% train / 87.9% test) — is reported. No Dice/Jaccard, Hausdorff distance, or surface metrics. Voxel accuracy including background substantially overstates segmentation quality. (Results section beyond the abstract is truncated in the provided text; no per-organ Dice found in extraction.)

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No confidence intervals, p-values, or variance estimates; test set of only 12 scans with no uncertainty quantification.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: No comparison against baseline or state-of-the-art segmentation methods (atlas-based, multi-atlas, or other CNN approaches). The only internal comparison is SGD vs. ADAM optimizers.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Only aggregate voxel accuracy across all 19 structures is reported; per-organ segmentation accuracy is not available in the provided text despite per-organ training-set counts (Table I) being given.

Q15_limitations.justification: No failure-case analysis or limitations discussion in the available text; conclusions claim generality and flexibility without acknowledging single-center data, tiny test set, or the weak accuracy metric.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: single hospital, single scanner vendor (Toshiba), single-country cohort; criteria for selecting the 240 annotated scans out of the 640 available are not defined; inclusion dominated by abdomen/pelvis scans.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Moderate concern: evaluation on 12 internal test scans scored by the development team with a single background-inclusive voxel-accuracy metric; random scan-level split with 32 multi-scan patients creates possible train/test leakage, potentially inflating test accuracy (train 88.1% vs test 87.9%).
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: High concern: only one aggregate metric reported, no per-organ results, no baseline comparisons, no failure analysis; 'acceptable accuracy' is claimed without context or reference standards, limiting independent assessment of clinical utility.

detailed_extraction: Supplementary methodological details: (1) Output layer has 22 channels for 19 target structures, implying 3 additional labels (background and likely 2 auxiliary classes; not explicitly enumerated). (2) Sequential fine-tuning protocol: modified VGG16 first trained as FCN32s (32-pixel stride coarse prediction), then progressively deeper deconvolution layers added with skip connections to yield FCN16s→8s→4s→2s, each stage trained on CT data. (3) 3D-2D-3D transformation: every voxel lies on exactly one section per orthogonal direction, so each voxel receives exactly 3 redundant label votes; when all three votes disagree, the label with the largest volumetric prior wins. (4) During training, voting is bypassed — each 2D section is trained against the full voxel-level label map, assuming labels are consistent across viewing directions. (5) Class imbalance is severe in the training data (uterus present in only 32/240 scans, prostate 72, gallbladder 228, liver 231) and no class-balancing strategy is reported. (6) Training used all sections from the three orthogonal directions (~100,000 2D images) from the 228 training scans; no data augmentation mentioned. (7) CT values used without HU normalization or windowing beyond the 12→8-bit linear interpolation; heterogeneous resolutions and protocols (contrast in 155 scans) fed directly to the network. (8) Patient/scan composition: 167 patients with 1 scan, 24 with 2, 7 with 3, 1 with 4. (9) Work presented as extension of a prior conference paper (ref. 19); CC BY-NC license on the article. (10) Reported generalization gap is minimal (88.1% vs 87.9%), but on a 12-scan test set this difference is uninterpretable without variance estimates. (11) Inference requires segmenting every 2D section in three orthogonal directions per volume, then stacking and voting; per-case inference time not reported. (12) Note: provided full text is truncated at Section 3.B (Experimental setting); any results beyond the abstract-reported voxel accuracy were not available for assessment.
contribution_summary: Zhou et al. propose a single 2D fully convolutional network (VGG16-based FCN, fine-tuned from ImageNet weights) that segments 19 torso structures in 3D CT via a 3D-2D-3D transformation: 2D sections are sampled in three orthogonal planes, segmented pixel-to-label, stacked back to 3D, and fused by voxel-wise majority voting with a largest-organ-volume tie-break. The key novelty is that one 2D network trained on ~100,000 sections from 240 annotated CT scans handles arbitrary scan ranges and heterogeneous acquisitions without 3D convolutions or per-organ models, achieving 87.9% voxel labeling accuracy on 12 held-out test scans. The work is an early (2017) demonstration of transfer-learning-based multi-organ segmentation, but evaluation is limited to a single aggregate, background-inclusive accuracy metric on a small single-center test set with no baseline comparisons.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: 278 patients (25,020 CT slices) with 218 patients used for training, well above the >50 subject threshold. Adequate for a 2D slice-based approach, though modest for deep learning by modern standards.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Source clearly described: single institution (National Cancer Center/Cancer Hospital, CAMS, Beijing), enrollment period Jan 2014–Dec 2016, two scanner models specified (Siemens Somatom Definition AS 40, Philips Brilliance CT Big Bore), 512×512 matrix, 5mm slice thickness, with detailed patient preparation protocol (bowel prep, Iohexol contrast, prone bellyboard positioning).

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Random split of 218 training / 60 test patients is stated, but no separate validation set is described (abstract confusingly calls the test set 'validation'). Model selection procedure ('model with highest performance was selected') is ambiguous about which set it was selected on, raising mild concerns about test set leakage. No cross-validation.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Ground truth defined as contours by 'very experienced' radiation oncologists with explicit CTV delineation guidelines (e.g., superior border at inferior L5 margin, ≥3cm below gross disease, covering rectum/mesorectum/presacral space/nodal regions). However, the number of observers, the consensus/arbitration process, and inter-observer variability are not reported.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation. All data from a single institution; literature comparisons are indirect (citing DSC values from other studies on different datasets) and do not substitute for independent validation.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Architecture comprehensively described: DDCNN based on VGG-16 converted to fully convolutional, with layer-by-layer specification in Table 1 (kernel sizes, strides, padding, dilation rates, output dimensions). Dual dilated modules detailed: front-end (D1) with dilation rates 1/2/4/8 applied directly to input, back-end (D2) with rates 6/12/18/24 in FC6; ReLU activations; bilinear interpolation upsampling.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Highly reproducible details: Caffe framework, SGD with initial LR 0.01 decayed by 0.9/epoch, weight decay 0.001, momentum 0.9, mini-batch of 6, 20K epochs (50K iterations), ImageNet-pretrained VGG-16 initialization, augmentation (flip, cut), and hardware (i7 3.4GHz, Titan Z GPU). Minor inconsistency between '20,000 epochs' and '50K iterations' slightly clouds exact training length.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Cross-entropy loss stated with median frequency balancing for class imbalance, but the choice is not justified relative to alternatives (e.g., Dice loss), and no ablation on loss design is provided.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Pre-processing clearly described and motivated: CLAHE chosen over HE/AHE with visual comparison (Figure 2) to improve local contrast without noise amplification. Data augmentation (flip, cut) and post-processing (bilinear interpolation to restore full resolution) also described, though no further 3D post-processing applied.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No statement that code, trained models, or data are publicly available. Only the underlying Caffe framework is open source.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Only Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) used for accuracy assessment (mean and SD). No Hausdorff distance, ASSD, volumetric similarity, or sensitivity/specificity. Runtime (45s/patient) is reported but is an efficiency, not accuracy, metric.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No p-values, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the DDCNN vs. U-Net comparison. Boxplots (Figure 4) suggest distributions were examined, and mean/SD mentioned, but no inferential statistics; SDs are not even tabulated.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Direct, fair comparison with U-Net (identical training configuration and pre-trained initialization) plus detailed indirect comparison against published DSC values from atlas-based and other methods for CTV (70–85%), bladder (67–90%), and femoral heads (91–95%).

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-structure DSC reported for all six ROIs (CTV, bladder, left/right femoral heads, intestine, colon) in Table 2 for both DDCNN and U-Net, with organ-specific discussion of why accuracy varies (e.g., bladder regularity vs. bowel gas/motility).

Q15_limitations.justification: Failure modes candidly discussed: intestine (65.3%) and colon (61.8%) performance attributed to shape/volume/intensity variability, inconsistent contrast distribution, and intraluminal gas. Future work (shape priors, more training data) explicitly proposed.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low-moderate: Inclusion criteria (locally advanced rectal cancer, neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy/radiotherapy) and consecutive 3-year enrollment window are defined, with random train/test splitting. However, single-institution recruitment of a homogeneous disease population limits generalizability, and no formal inclusion/exclusion flow is reported.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low-moderate: Both DDCNN and U-Net were trained and evaluated identically on the same held-out test set with the same metric, ensuring fair internal comparison. However, the reference standard derives from an unspecified number of oncologists with no inter-observer variability quantification, so segmentation agreement is anchored to a potentially variable gold standard.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low: All six target structures reported including unfavorable results (intestine/colon), and runtime reported. Minor concerns: promised standard deviations not tabulated, no statistical significance testing, and no negative/ablation results beyond the dilated-module bar chart.

detailed_extraction: TASK: Auto-segmentation of CTV + 5 OARs (bladder, left femoral head, right femoral head, intestine, colon) in planning CT for locally advanced rectal cancer radiotherapy. APPROACH: 2D slice-by-slice DDCNN (relevant caveat for a 3D segmentation review: no explicit 3D context modeling; volume coherence handled only implicitly per-slice). Architecture: VGG-16 backbone converted to fully convolutional (FC6/FC7/FC8 as 1×1 convolutions), 17 conv layers total; novel dual-path dilated convolution: front-end module D1 (dilation rates 1,2,4,8 → receptive fields 3×3–33×33) applied directly on the 353×353 input to capture low-level multi-scale texture/boundary context, with pooled branch outputs merged into higher layers; back-end module D2 (dilation rates 6,12,18,24) at FC6 for high-level context; max-pooling reduced feature maps to 1/8 resolution, recovered via bilinear interpolation. Pre-processing: CLAHE image enhancement. Loss: pixel-wise cross-entropy summed over mini-batch (size 6) with median frequency balancing for class imbalance. Training: Caffe, SGD, LR 0.01 (×0.9/epoch), momentum 0.9, weight decay 0.001, ImageNet-initialized VGG-16 weights fine-tuned; augmentation: flip and cut; '20,000 epochs'/50K iterations reported (internally inconsistent). DATA: 278 patients/25,020 slices; 512×512, 5mm slices; two scanners; Iohexol oral/intravenous contrast protocol; prone bellyboard immobilization. RESULTS (mean DSC): CTV 87.7% (U-Net 81.9%), bladder 93.4% (91.2%), left femoral head 92.1% (89.6%), right femoral head 92.3% (89.2%), intestine 65.3% (57.6%), colon 61.8% (60.5%); average +3.8% over U-Net. Runtime ~45 s/patient on Titan Z. CLAIMED NOVELTIES: first CNN-based CTV segmentation in planning CT and first CNN auto-segmentation for rectal cancer radiotherapy; CLAHE pre-processing; multi-path dilated convolution injecting low-level context into high layers; invariance to body size/shape/age (demonstrated qualitatively via randomized split, Figure 7). LITERATURE CONTEXT: reported CTV DSC exceeds prior atlas-based results (70–85%); bladder DSC (93.4%) exceeds prior reports (67–90%); femoral head DSC comparable to best reported (91–95%). Additional structural results (e.g., HD, volumetric metrics) and observer variability data not reported; no 3D post-processing or shape priors applied.
contribution_summary: This paper presents DDCNN, a 2D fully convolutional network built on VGG-16 with novel dual-path dilated convolution modules that inject multi-scale low-level context directly from the input image and high-level context at the network's end, and reports the first CNN-based auto-segmentation of both CTV and OARs in planning CT for rectal cancer radiotherapy. DDCNN outperformed U-Net by 3.8% average DSC (e.g., CTV 87.7% vs 81.9%; bladder 93.4% vs 91.2%) while segmenting all structures in ~45 seconds per patient, with degraded but still useful results for intestine (65.3%) and colon (61.8%). The work demonstrated clinically relevant speed and robustness to body habitus, though validation was limited to a single institution with DSC as the only accuracy metric.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: 172 CTU scans (81 train / 91 test), ~16,000 annotated slices, ~240,000 training ROIs. Well above the 50-subject threshold for training.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Single institution (Michigan Medicine, Abdominal Imaging, retrospective, IRB-approved, established CTU protocol). Case mix fully characterized: lesion status (mass-like vs wall thickening vs normal, malignancy counts) and contrast filling status per split.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Random two-way split explicitly balanced in difficulty between train and test. However, no validation set: ROI size (8/16/32), iteration count (1500, 'based on our previous experience') and level set parameters were selected empirically without a held-out tuning set; only threshold θ=0.85 is explicitly stated as derived from training cases.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Inner and outer walls hand-outlined slice-by-slice on all 172 cases by one abdominal radiologist (>20 yrs) via in-house MiViewer, used for both training labels and reference standard. Process clearly described, but single rater with no inter/intra-observer variability assessment (limitation acknowledged by authors).

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external dataset. Single-center data, internal random split only. Comparison methods (CLASS, ITK-SNAP) evaluated on subsets of the same cohort.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Fully specified: 5-layer CNN (2 conv 64×5×5, 2 locally-connected 64 and 32×3×3, 1 FC), ReLU, overlapping pooling, LRN (N=9, τ=0.001, ε=0.75), Softmax 2-class output; ROI labeling rules (70%/95%/10% criteria, 8×8 jittering) and full level set equations with parameter table (α, β, γ, iterations per cascade stage).

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Strong partial reproducibility: 1500 iterations, ~240k balanced ROIs, θ=0.85, level set parameter table, framework (Cuda-Convnet), GPU (Tesla K20), train/inference times. Missing: optimizer, learning rate, batch size, weight initialization, and the loss function is never stated.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss function not stated or justified anywhere. 2-class Softmax output implies cross-entropy but this is never made explicit; no discussion of loss design or alternatives.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Thoroughly described with parameters: manual VOI, likelihood threshold 0.85 (justified via training-set histogram), ellipsoid constraint (1.5× VOI) against leaks, morphological dilate/flood-fill/erode initialization; preprocessing for level sets (smoothing, anisotropic diffusion, gradient, rank transform); cascaded 3D + per-slice 2D refinement.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code, model weights, or data released. Base framework (Cuda-Convnet) is public but the trained model, level set implementation, and MiViewer annotations are not.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Four metrics (volume intersection, volume error, absolute volume error, average contour distance) plus wall-shell and lesion-enclosure metrics. But no Dice/DSC or Jaccard — their 'volume intersection' is one-sided (|A∩B|/|B|, reference-normalized), which hinders cross-study comparability that Dice would provide.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Mean±SD for all metrics on both splits; significance testing (p<0.01) for all key comparisons: likelihood-in-4th-level-set vs all, with/without level sets, vs Cha et al., vs CLASS and ITK-SNAP. No CIs, but SDs and p-values across n=81/91 are adequate.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Extensive: prior CLASS adaptive level sets (same data), ITK-SNAP (30-case subset), their own whole-bladder DL-CNN (Cha et al., same data), plus two internal ablations (likelihood in 4th stage only vs all; CNN-only vs CNN+level sets).

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Single-organ study, but results broken out per structure (inner wall, outer wall, wall shell, lesion enclosure), per split (train/test), with full histograms of per-case distributions (Figs. 7-8), not just averages.

Q15_limitations.justification: Candid and specific: over-segmentation, prostate leakage into outer wall, inner contours transecting lesions, failure mode on 5mm-slice small bladders, thin-wall metric instability (wall-shell VI only 54.6% test), single-radiologist reference bias, with ROI-size ablation evidence (Fig. 10).

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low-moderate. Retrospective single-center cohort with implicit (not explicit) inclusion criteria; however, large n, clinical CTU protocol, and difficulty-balanced random split reduce selection concern. No external cohort, so generalizability to other scanners/centers is untested.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low. Fully automated pipeline applied uniformly to all test cases; identical reference standard and metric set for all comparisons including baselines. Main measurement concern is the single-rater reference standard (acknowledged), which affects criterion validity rather than consistency of assessment.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low. All planned outcomes reported including unfavorable ones (wall-shell overlap ~55%, lesion transection figures). Minor internal inconsistencies exist (abstract states 92 test cases vs 91 in methods; abstract metrics differ slightly from Table 2, e.g., inner test VI 86.9±9.6% vs 87.2±10.5%) suggesting version/typo issues rather than selective reporting.

detailed_extraction: Supplementary details not in prior extraction: (1) ROI labeling rule specifics — positive if ≥70% of central 8×8 of the 16×16 ROI lies between hand-outlined inner/outer contours ('8×8 jittering' to capture thin walls); negative if ≥95% interior or <10% inside outer contour; classes exactly balanced 50/50. (2) ROI size ablation: 8×8 → noisy maps, gaps at thin walls; 32×32 → walls too thick; 16×16 chosen (training time 5.5→6.5 h; inference ~4 min either way). (3) Design choice ablated and justified: likelihood map used as speed term F(φ) only in 4th of 4 cascaded level sets — using it in all 4 significantly degrades outer wall VI (train 81.8 vs 93.2; test 76.1 vs 89.5, p<0.01); inner wall difference not significant. (4) Cascade progression (Table 5): full cascade adds +12-15 VI points over 3rd level set alone (e.g., inner test 72.3→74.9→87.2%). (5) β sign convention flips for inner (−2.5, inward) vs outer (+2, outward) propagation. (6) Ellipsoid (1.5× VOI axes at mask centroid) explicitly used to suppress high CNN likelihood on confounders such as pelvic bone. (7) Wall-shell (between contours) performance is markedly worse: test VI 54.6±10.4%, |error| 25.1±15.8% — attributed to thin-wall sensitivity, not contour failure per se. (8) Lesion enclosure: 81.6±16.6% test VI; 70.2% of lesions >75% enclosed vs 89.1% for hand contours. (9) Head-to-head on same 172-case set vs Cha et al. whole-bladder: outer wall test VI 89.5 vs 78.0 (p<0.01); absolute volume error differences not significant. (10) Numeric inconsistencies to flag for the review: test n = 92 (abstract) vs 91 (methods, and 172−81=91); several abstract values differ slightly from Table 2 (outer train VI 93.7±3.9 vs 93.2±5.8; outer test VI 87.5±9.9 vs 89.5±9.8) — likely different runs or copyediting errors; use Table 2 values. (11) Architecture is 2D slice-wise CNN (16×16 axial ROIs) combined with 3D level sets — not a 3D convolutional network; relevance to a '3D segmentation' review should note this hybrid 2D/3D design. (12) ~100 slices/bladder; contour runtime 2-5 min per wall; funding NIH U01CA179106; authors declare no conflicts. (13) Extends authors' own pilot SPIE 2017 work (Gordon et al.) to full cohort with 8×8 jittering and the 4th-level-set integration as the two methodological deltas over Cha et al. 2016.
contribution_summary: This work extends DL-CNN-guided cascaded level sets from whole-bladder segmentation to separate inner and outer bladder wall contours in CT urography, introducing an '8×8 jittering' ROI labeling scheme to handle the very thin bladder wall and integrating the CNN likelihood map only into the fourth cascade stage. On 172 CTU scans it achieves ~87-90% volume intersection for both walls on the test set, significantly outperforming the non-DL CLASS system, ITK-SNAP, and the authors' prior whole-bladder DL-CNN (p<0.01). It is a methodological stepping stone toward bladder lesion detection/CAD rather than a generic multi-organ segmentation advance, and notably lacks Dice reporting, external validation, and code release.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: 81 subjects for training/validation (>50 threshold) plus 92-case independent test; 7,629 annotated bladder slices for 2D training. Authors note 81 volumes is small for 3D training, which is consistent with their 3D results.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Single institutional cohort (Univ. of Michigan, IRB-approved, all patients cystoscopy/biopsy-confirmed). Scanner (GE LightSpeed MDCT), acquisition parameters (120 kVp, 120-280 mA, 0.625/1.25 mm), contrast protocol (excretory phase, 12 min, Isovue 300 125 mL), and full case-mix + contrast-fill breakdown provided.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: 81 train-val / 92 held-out test split stated, but split was 'balanced by difficulty' with no formal method described; the 7 validation cases were hand-picked as 'representative' without defined criteria; no cross-validation.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: One experienced radiologist hand-outlined every bladder slice via GUI for all 173 cases to build 3D reference contours. Single annotator, no inter-/intra-observer variability check, and the authors acknowledge slice-wise annotation introduces superior-inferior inconsistency.

Q5_external_validation.justification: Single institution, single scanner vendor; the 92-case test set is internal held-out data, not an external/independent cohort.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: 2D and 3D U-DL fully specified: 5x5 / 3x3x3 padded convolutions, ReLU, 2x2(/2x2x2) max pooling, modified skip concatenation (after two convs), final 1x1(/1x1x1) sigmoid; architecture figures included; deviations from original U-Net explicitly stated.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Keras/TF, Tesla K40c 12GB, Adam, lr=0.0001, BCE loss, batch sizes (4 for 2D; 1-2 for 3D, memory-constrained), weight init N(0, 0.02), fixed epochs (100 2D / 400 3D), per-epoch training times (Table 4). Missing only: random seeds; no data augmentation mentioned.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Binary cross-entropy used with no justification and no comparison to alternatives (e.g., Dice/combined loss); only the learning rate choice is empirically discussed.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing fully described: center cropping (256x256 / 128x128), 2x2 box-filter stride-2 downsampling, radiologist-marked first/last bladder slice to fix 192-slice z-extent. Postprocessing fully described: likelihood threshold 0.2 selected via explicit sweep 0.1-0.9 on validation (Table 1), largest connected component retained.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code, weights, or repository URL mentioned anywhere; components/license/release fields remain null.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Six metrics: AVI, AVE, AAVE, AMD, AHD, AJI. Caveat for synthesis: Dice is never reported; the overlap metric is AJI (Jaccard). The 'best_dice': 0.85 in the prior extraction is actually Jaccard, not Dice — flag retained.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: p-values reported (2D U-DL vs DCNN-LS p<0.001 on all measures; 2D vs 3D p<0.006), Pearson correlations with bladder volume, mean±SD throughout. Statistical test never named, no confidence intervals, no multiple-comparison correction.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Compared against authors' own prior DL method (DCNN-LS) and two in-house non-DL methods (CLASS-LCR, LS-HF) on the same test set. The only external DL work (Xu et al., CRF-RNN, ref 23) is discussed qualitatively only — never run head-to-head; no public benchmark used.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Single-organ study (bladder), so per-organ reporting is trivially complete; additionally gives per-case distributions (Fig. 6 histograms), explicit failure counts (2/92 AVI<50%, 3/92 at 50-80%), and subgroup case-mix.

Q15_limitations.justification: Thorough: residual user slice-marking step, GPU memory blocking full-volume 3D training, small 3D training set (81 volumes), 2D superior-inferior contour discontinuity, 5/92 suboptimal cases quantified, failure modes illustrated (Fig. 7: leakage into bone, contrast-boundary artifacts, apex/base under-segmentation).

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low-moderate. Cohort clinically well-defined (all 173 patients cystoscopy/biopsy-confirmed, IRB-approved) but single-center; split 'balanced by difficulty' without formal method; validation cases hand-picked as 'representative'.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low. All methods (2D/3D U-DL, DCNN-LS, CLASS-LCR, LS-HF) evaluated on the same 92-case independent test set against the same radiologist reference standard with identical metrics; threshold tuned only on training/validation data.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low. All six metrics reported for every model variant (Tables 1-3, 5-6); suboptimal cases and failure modes disclosed. Minor concerns: unnamed statistical test, no CIs, inference time unreported.

detailed_extraction: Model selection protocol: 7 representative cases held out from the 81 for threshold/model selection (sweep 0.1-0.9, Table 1; 0.2 chosen), then final model retrained on all 81 and evaluated once on the 92 test cases. Ablations (Tables 2-3): 2D U-DL beat 3D U-DL in every matched condition, attributed to sample count (7,629 slice samples vs 81 volumes); 512x512 slightly better than 256x256; automated cropping gave equivalent accuracy but cut 2D epoch time 18.5 vs 70.0 min (3D: 32.5 min cropped), so cropping was retained. Significance: 2D vs DCNN-LS p<0.001 (all 6 measures); 3D vs DCNN-LS p<0.001 (AVI/AVE/AJI); 2D vs 3D p<0.006 (AVI/AMD/AHD/AJI); test type unspecified, no CIs. Metric conversion for cross-paper synthesis: Dice never reported; best AJI 85.0% (2D U-DL) corresponds to Dice ~= 2*0.85/(1+0.85) = 0.919; the existing 'best_dice': 0.85 field holds Jaccard and should be relabeled. Case mix: train/val = 42 mass / 21 wall-thickening / 18 normal; test = 43/36/13; contrast fill: train 61 partial / 8 full / 12 none, test 85/4/3. Correlation of error with bladder volume: Pearson r = 0.364 for AVE (only notable; AVI -0.188, others |r|<0.11). Annotation: single radiologist, slice-wise GUI outlining -> 3D surface -> binary mask; no second reader. No data augmentation. Clinical context: segmentation component of a bladder-cancer detection/treatment-response CDSS pipeline; NIH-funded (U01CA179106). Inference time not reported; components/license/benchmark_reproduction/release_version remain null.
contribution_summary: Developed U-Net-based 2D and 3D deep-learning bladder segmentation (U-DL) for CT urography that eliminates the user-input bounding box and level-set postprocessing required by the authors' prior DCNN-LS. Systematic ablation of dimensionality, resolution, and cropping found the 2D U-DL at full resolution with automated cropping best, improving AJI from 76.2% to 85.0% on a 92-case independent test set (p<0.001) and outperforming two non-DL baselines. Notable negative finding for this review: the 3D variant underperformed 2D, attributed to only 81 training volumes versus 7,629 slice samples.
