Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Every experiment was repeated three times with different random seeds and mean performance reported, but no confidence intervals, standard deviations, p-values, or significance tests appear in the provided text, so improvements over baselines are not statistically qualified.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Baselines include CNN, MLP, and ResNet (eGFR prediction) and U-Net variants plus 'state-of-the-art segmentation models' (segmentation), evaluated under an explicit fairness protocol (official implementations or faithful reimplementation; identical splits, preprocessing, hardware, metrics; FAIR principles). Caveats: actual comparison tables fall outside the truncated text, and no modern segmentation SOTA (e.g., nnU-Net) is named in the visible portion.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: The results section states that metrics are reported 'across cortex, medulla, and pelvis regions' (per-compartment rather than pooled), but the provided text truncates before any results tables; the abstract reports only pooled Dice 0.94 and HD95 9.8 mm. Per-structure numbers could not be verified from the available text.

Q15_limitations.justification: Section 4 is announced as covering 'clinical implications and limitations' but is not included in the provided text. The only visible limitation is the acknowledgment of the small MRI cohort; no failure-case analysis or discussion of the CT-mask absence is visible.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Unclear/moderate. Public datasets with defined composition (50/50 healthy-CKD MRI) support reproducibility, but inclusion/exclusion criteria, recruitment pathway, patient demographics, and CKD stage distribution are unreported; the CT set is class-imbalanced (5077 normal vs 1379 stone); split ratios are unstated, so subgroup and split representativeness cannot be judged.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low-to-moderate. On MRI, outcomes appear consistently assessed: uniform metrics, identical training/evaluation conditions for all baselines, 3-seed repetition. However, outcome assessment on the external CT set cannot be judged consistent or valid because CT lacks ground-truth masks and the paper internally contradicts whether CT was used in training; no blinding/reader study is described.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Moderate/unclear. Abstract reports only favorable pooled results (Dice 0.94, r 0.92); alpha/beta loss weights, split ratios, and per-compartment tables are not visible; a direct contradiction exists about CT usage (evaluation-only in Sec. 3.1 vs. encoder enrichment in Sec. 3.2); no CT quantitative results are visible despite abstract claims of 'experiments on... colorized CT datasets'. Completeness is unverifiable because Results (mid-Section 3.5), Discussion, and Limitations are truncated in the provided text.

detailed_extraction:
STUDY DESIGN: Methodological development and retrospective evaluation on public data; no prospective/patient-level recruitment; single research group (Altinbas University).

DATASETS: (1) T2-weighted Kidney MRI Segmentation dataset [ref 20]: 100 subjects (50 healthy controls, 50 CKD), manual kidney masks, subject metadata CSV, separate CKD/control archives, 10 subjects scanned 5x in one session for precision assessment; sole dataset for ALL training (segmentation, biomarkers, eGFR) and primary evaluation. (2) Kidney CT Colorized dataset [ref 21]: ~12,446 colorized kidney CT images, 4 image-level classes (5077 normal, 3709 cyst, 2283 tumor, 1379 stone; per ref 9, Dhaka, Bangladesh), ~150x150 px average, NO segmentation masks; claimed use = external structural/cross-modality evaluation only.

CRITICAL DATA-USAGE CONTRADICTION: Section 3.1 states CT was used 'solely as an external evaluation set' with 'no CT images used for training, fine-tuning, or learning'; Section 3.2 states CT images 'were used primarily to enrich the anatomical variability available to the encoder and assist the model in learning diverse renal structures.' These statements are mutually inconsistent and materially affect interpretation of generalization claims.

ARCHITECTURE (FG-CKD-UNet): Shared 4-level residual encoder (3x3 convs, InstanceNorm, ReLU, max-pool; residual shortcuts) -> bottleneck -> (a) segmentation decoder (transposed-conv upsampling, skip concatenation, two 3x3 conv refinements per level, 1x1 conv + Softmax, classes: background/cortex/medulla/pelvis), (b) functional head (global average pooling + MLP, dropout 0.15) predicting eGFR, (c) embedded differentiable morphological biomarker extractor: per-class binary masks -> volumetric sums; mean cortical thickness via Euclidean distance transform; cortex-medulla ratio CMR = Vc/(Vm + eps); biomarker vector B = [Vc, Vm, Tc, CMR, ...] fed to auxiliary regressor g(.) producing y_morph.

LOSS: L_seg = Dice + cross-entropy; L_func = 0.7*MAE + 0.3*MSE; L_sf = alpha*|y_morph - y| + beta*|y_hat - y_morph|; total L = 1.0*L_seg + 0.75*L_func + 0.25*L_sf. Alpha/beta final values unreported; weights chosen by empirical tuning with ablation support (5 ablation runs implied; excessive consistency weight reported to destabilize training).

TRAINING: AdamW (lr 1e-4 cosine-annealed to 2e-6, warm restarts, 5-epoch warm-up; beta1 0.9, beta2 0.999; wd 0.01); batch 8 (MRI slices)/16 (CT); 120 epochs; grad clip 5.0; FP16; 3 seeds, means reported; ~14.7 h on RTX 4090 (24 GB), i9-13900K, 64 GB RAM; Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.2.1, CUDA 12.2, Docker 24.0; TorchIO/SimpleITK/scikit-image/OpenCV for imaging; TensorBoard logging.

PREPROCESSING: MRI - corrupted-slice/out-of-kidney-region removal, uniform resampling, z-score normalization, abdominal cropping, mask cleaning; CT - resize 150x150, [0,1] normalization, per-channel mean-variance standardization. Augmentation (on-the-fly): rotation, H/V flips, affine, zoom, elastic deformation, brightness perturbation, Gaussian noise, contrast jitter.

EVALUATION: Segmentation - DSC, IoU, Pixel Accuracy, HD95; Function - MAE, RMSE, Pearson r, R2; Consistency - CE = mean |y_morph - y|. HEADLINE RESULTS (abstract): Dice 0.94, HD95 9.8 mm; eGFR MAE 0.039, RMSE 0.058, r 0.92; CE reduced 0.071 -> 0.042 with consistency loss; claims superiority over CNN/MLP/ResNet (function) and U-Net variants (segmentation). Detailed tables, per-compartment numbers, and ablation results are NOT present in the provided (truncated) text.

GAPS/CONCERNS FOR THE REVIEW: (1) eGFR ground-truth provenance is unclear - the MRI dataset is described as having 'CKD stage information', but how continuous eGFR labels were obtained/derived is never stated; (2) processing appears 2D slice-based (MRI 'slices'), so the mm-unit HD95 (9.8 mm) and any 3D volume aggregation are unexplained; (3) CT external validation is compromised: no GT masks, colorized 2D images rather than native CT volumes, contradictory usage statement; (4) 2D architecture limits direct comparability with 3D CT segmentation methods (e.g., nnU-Net-style volumetric pipelines); (5) kidney-only scope with per-compartment (cortex/medulla/pelvis) labels - relevant to multi-organ reviews only as a single-organ, multi-structure method; (6) no code release. RELEVANCE VERDICT: tangential to the review topic '3D Organ Segmentation from CT Scans' - primarily a 2D, MRI-driven multitask method; the CT component lacks masks and 3D volumetric processing. Recommend flagging as low-relevance/medium-quality if the review strictly requires 3D CT segmentation.
contribution_summary: This paper proposes FG-CKD-UNet, a dual-headed multitask U-Net that jointly performs multi-compartment kidney segmentation (cortex/medulla/pelvis) and eGFR prediction, coupled through a novel structure-function consistency loss and an embedded differentiable morphological biomarker extractor (cortical thickness, compartment volumes, cortex-medulla ratio). On a 100-subject T2-weighted MRI CKD dataset it reports Dice 0.94 / HD95 9.8 mm and eGFR MAE 0.039 / Pearson r 0.92, with the consistency loss reducing consistency error from 0.071 to 0.042. For a review focused on 3D CT organ segmentation, its relevance is limited: the method is 2D slice-based, primarily MRI-driven, and its CT 'external validation' uses colorized 2D images without segmentation masks.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Primary training on LiTS with 91 training patients (>50 threshold), plus 20 validation and 20 test patients. AMOS-CT (>500 volumes) used for multi-client simulation; 3D-IRCADb (20 volumes) used only as external test. Training size clearly exceeds adequacy threshold.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Three public datasets (LiTS, 3D-IRCADb, AMOS-CT) thoroughly characterized: scanner vendors (Siemens, GE, Philips, United Imaging), slice thickness ranges (0.7–5.0 mm), in-plane resolution (0.56–1.0 mm), contrast phases, number of acquiring hospitals (6 for AMOS), and rationale for each dataset's role (training, external test, collaborative simulation).

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Exemplary split methodology: strictly patient-level partitioning (no slice leakage), fixed random seed (42), explicit LiTS split of 91/20/20, IRCAD held out entirely as external test, AMOS partitioned into mutually exclusive virtual clients. Summarized in Table 1; test set touched only for final reporting.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Ground truth described only at dataset level ('expert-annotated liver and tumor masks', 'detailed manual annotations'). The annotation process itself (number of annotators, delineation protocol, inter-observer agreement, arbitration of disagreements) is not described; relies on the original dataset documentation.

Q5_external_validation.justification: Strong external validation: 3D-IRCADb (20 volumes) used strictly as an unseen external test domain, plus cross-domain testing on AMOS-CT, both reported in a dedicated cross-domain generalization section (Table 4) with Dice and HD95.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Architecture fully specified: 5-stage residual encoder with explicit feature dimensions (256×256×64 → 16×16×512 bottleneck), 3×3 convs with normalization/ReLU, residual blocks with 1×1 shortcut convs; server decoder with parallel dilated convolutions (rates 1, 2, 4), residual refinement block, bilinear progressive upsampling with 3×3 smoothing convs, and 1×1 prediction layer. Supported by six architecture figures (Figs. 2–7).

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Highly reproducible: Adam (lr=1e-4, β1=0.9, β2=0.999), batch size 16 per client, 150 epochs, early stopping patience 20, loss weights (λD=0.5, λCE=0.2, λB=0.3), fixed seed 42, exact augmentation parameters (±15° rotation, 0.9–1.1 scaling, ±10% intensity), software versions (Python 3.14.2, NumPy 2.4.2, PyTorch 2.10), and identical baseline training protocol (including constrained nnU-Net v1 2D config).

Q8_loss_function.justification: Composite loss (Dice + Cross-Entropy + Boundary-Aware) with mathematical definitions (Eqs. 1–4) and explicit per-term justification tied to the skip-free design (e.g., boundary loss compensates for lost high-frequency edge information from skips). Weights reported and stated to be empirically selected on validation data; ablation confirms boundary loss contribution (tumor Dice drops 0.737→0.700 without it).

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing exceptionally well described and supported by a sensitivity analysis (HU clipping [-200, 250], min-max normalization, 1 mm³ resampling, threshold-based ROI cropping to 256×256; crop-size and resampling ablations in Section 3.4). However, post-processing steps are not mentioned at all—it is unclear whether none were applied or simply unreported.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code repository, GitHub link, or model availability statement found anywhere in the provided text. Reproducibility relies solely on the written description.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Dice Similarity Coefficient plus 95th-percentile Hausdorff Distance (HD95), reported for both liver and tumor across all main tables (in-plane overlap and boundary precision), plus communication payload and estimated latency as systems-level metrics.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Beyond mean ± std across patients, the paper reports paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (significant vs U-Net tumor Dice at p<0.05; not significant vs nnU-Net), Cohen's d effect sizes, and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (1000 iterations)—unusually rigorous statistical treatment for this literature.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Dual comparison strategy: (1) five baselines (U-Net, ResUNet, Attention U-Net, DenseNet-UNet, nnU-Net) retrained under identical preprocessing/splits/optimization to eliminate confounds; (2) literature comparison with recent SOTA (T-MPEDNet, Rahman et al., Manghi et al.) in Table 3, with appropriate caveats about 2D vs 3D and centralized vs collaborative differences.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Liver and tumor results consistently reported separately (never averaged) in all quantitative tables, with per-structure HD95, standard deviations, and structure-specific discussion (e.g., higher tumor variability, small/low-contrast lesion challenges).

Q15_limitations.justification: Dedicated failure-case section (Section 3.3) with qualitative examples showing under-segmentation of small/low-contrast tumors; frank acknowledgment of privacy limitations (no formal DP or cryptographic guarantees; susceptibility to advanced inversion/membership inference attacks deferred to future work); transparent reporting when baselines outperform FF-ResUNet.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low-to-moderate. Patient-level splits with fixed seeds and pre-registered-style partition discipline minimize leakage-related selection bias, and public benchmark datasets are used. However, patient inclusion criteria are inherited from dataset design rather than author-defined, and 'multi-institution' collaboration is simulated by partitioning AMOS-CT into virtual clients within one computational environment—not real hospitals—which limits external validity of the collaborative claims.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low-to-moderate. All baselines share identical preprocessing, splits, augmentation, and optimization settings, and evaluation metrics are applied consistently; outcome assessors are not applicable (automated metrics). Concerns: the collaborative setting is simulated (no real distributed deployment), communication payloads and latency are analytically computed from tensor dimensions and assumed bandwidths (100/20 Mbps) rather than measured, and DenseNet-UNet HD95 values are missing ('—') in Table 2, creating slight comparison asymmetry.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low. Reporting is comprehensive: per-structure metrics with variance, statistical tests, ablations of every component, a controlled skip-vs-skip-free experiment (Table 7), and preprocessing sensitivity analysis. Authors candidly report inferior results where they occur (FF-ResUNet liver Dice lowest among compared methods on LiTS; nnU-Net superior cross-domain). Caveat: the provided full text truncates mid-sentence in Section 3.6, so multi-client scaling results (mentioned in abstract), conclusion, and full limitations could not be verified.

detailed_extraction: TASK & SCOPE NOTES FOR REVIEW: (1) Although the review topic is 3D organ segmentation, this method is deliberately 2D slice-based (axial), justified by communication/memory constraints of collaborative learning; no inter-slice 3D context is exploited. (2) Task is liver + tumor only (binary/multi-class per slice), not multi-organ. Both points affect applicability to the review's core question. ARCHITECTURE: Client-side 5-stage residual encoder (channels 64/128/256/512/512; spatial 256→16), each stage = conv block + residual refinement with 1×1 shortcut alignment; bottleneck 16×16×512 is the sole transmitted tensor. Server-side decoder: (a) multi-scale dilated convolution module (parallel 3×3 convs, dilation rates 1/2/4, ASPP-like), (b) residual refinement block, (c) progressive upsampling via bilinear interpolation + paired 3×3 smoothing convs (avoids checkerboard artifacts), (d) 1×1 conv classifier. COLLABORATIVE PROTOCOL (split-learning variant): encoders initialized identically across clients; bottleneck features sent client→server; loss and backprop computed server-side through decoder and ONLY the top encoder block connected to the bottleneck; lightweight gradients returned to clients. Earlier encoder layers receive no server-side gradient updates—their training mechanism (or freezing) is not fully explained, a methodological ambiguity. Privacy position: reduced inversion risk by design (low-res abstract features, no skips), but explicitly NO formal differential-privacy or cryptographic guarantees; authors cite prior feature-inversion attack literature as motivation. KEY QUANTITATIVE RESULTS (LiTS test, n=20): FF-ResUNet liver Dice 0.952±0.015, tumor Dice 0.737±0.060, liver HD95 4.2±1.3 mm, tumor HD95 10.9±4.1 mm. Baselines: U-Net 0.958/0.682 (HD95 5.6/20.1), ResUNet 0.961/0.705 (4.9/15.2), Attention U-Net 0.969/0.734 (4.4/13.1), DenseNet-UNet 0.955/0.760 (HD95 n/r). Note FF-ResUNet has the LOWEST liver Dice of all compared methods; its edge is tumor HD95 (best boundary error) and communication efficiency, not raw Dice. Cross-domain (trained on LiTS): IRCAD liver 0.93/tumor 0.61/tumor-HD95 15.2 mm; AMOS-CT liver 0.94/tumor 0.57/17.4 mm; nnU-Net best overall (IRCAD 0.94/0.63/14.3). ABLATIONS (LiTS test): full 0.952/0.737; w/o multi-scale dilation 0.945/0.690; w/o residual refinement 0.946/0.670; w/o boundary loss 0.948/0.700; w/o progressive upsampling 0.945/0.680. CONTROLLED SKIP ABLATION (Table 7): identical architecture with full skips achieves 0.960/0.753/9.8 mm vs skip-free 0.952/0.737/10.9 mm → quantified privacy–accuracy trade-off of ~1.6 tumor Dice points for >10× communication saving. COMMUNICATION ANALYSIS: skip-based baseline = 7,864,320 elements/sample × FP32 × batch 16 ≈ 480 MB/iteration vs FF-ResUNet bottleneck 131,072 elements ≈ 8 MB/iteration (98% reduction; 92–98% across batch sizes/FP16). Estimated transfer latency: 38.4 s vs 0.64 s per iteration at 100 Mbps; 192 s vs 3.2 s at 20 Mbps. PREPROCESSING SENSITIVITY: resampling vs native spacing changes Dice <0.6% (liver) / <1.2% (tumor); crop size 224/256/320 → 0.947/0.952/0.953 liver, 0.724/0.737/0.739 tumor. OTHER: baselines include nnU-Net v1 2D with auto-configuration disabled for protocol parity; abstract reports improved multi-client performance with increasing client count before saturation, but detailed multi-client results fall in the truncated portion of the provided text; publication metadata (2026) and software versions postdate current releases as stated in the manuscript.
contribution_summary: This paper proposes FF-ResUNet, a privacy-preserving split-learning segmentation framework in which each institution runs a residual U-Net encoder locally and transmits only a compact 16×16×512 bottleneck tensor to a central server, eliminating the high-resolution skip-connection features that dominate both privacy leakage risk and bandwidth cost in collaborative U-Nets. A purpose-built server-side decoder (multi-scale dilated convolutions, residual refinement, progressive bilinear upsampling, boundary-aware loss) compensates for the absent skip fusion, achieving LiTS liver/tumor Dice of 0.952/0.737 with the best tumor boundary error (HD95 10.9 mm) while cutting per-iteration communication by 92–98% (~480 MB → ~8 MB), at a quantified cost of ~1.6 tumor Dice points versus a full-skip equivalent. Cross-domain evaluation on 3D-IRCADb and AMOS-CT under simulated multi-institution partitions demonstrates robust generalization, positioning the work as a practical privacy–bandwidth–accuracy compromise for multi-center deployment rather than an accuracy-maximizing method.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Only 20 CT volumes total (~15 train / 5 test after 75/25 hold-out), far below the >50 subject threshold. Extremely small dataset severely limits statistical power and generalizability.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Source clearly described: Ma et al. COVID-19 CT Lung and Infection Segmentation Dataset, comprising 20 scans from RAIOSS (n=14) and Radiopaedia (n=6), with a per-patient table detailing in-plane resolution (512x512 or 630x630), slice depth (39-418), and infection severity (mild/moderate/severe).

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Hold-out validation with 75% train / 25% test is stated, but no randomization/stratification details, no explicit patient counts per split, and critically no separate validation set described despite early stopping (patience=250) being used — raising the possibility that the test set served for model selection (leakage risk).

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Annotation process described (inherited from Ma et al.): masks manually annotated by two radiologists and verified by an experienced radiologist. Three mask types provided (lung, infection, lung+infection).

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external/independent validation. All training and testing performed on the single 20-scan dataset; no second cohort or cross-dataset experiment.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: 3D UNet described at block level (encoder: conv+batch norm+ReLU+max-pooling; decoder: upconvolution with skip concatenation; dropout added for regularization) with a figure, plus clear description of encoder replacements (3D ResNet152, 3D VGG19, 3D DenseNet201) and reference to Appendix A for detailed specifications.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Key hyperparameters given: ADAM optimizer, learning rate 1e-4, max 5000 epochs, early-stopping patience 250, input size 128x128x128, hold-out 75/25, Google Colab Pro GPU. However, batch size, deep learning framework, and random seeds are not reported, and no code is released.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Total loss = Dice loss + focal loss (equal class weights for Dice term). Justification is purely empirical ('after several experiments... better than using only Dice loss or only focal loss') with no theoretical rationale or reported ablation table; no weighting scheme analysis.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing thoroughly described: resampling to 128x128x128 via ImageJ (average up/downsampling, bilinear interpolation in depth), min-max scaling to [0,1], CLAHE for noise/intensity inhomogeneity with before/after visual comparison, and explicit mask label unification (left+right lung merged; multi-class labels remapped to background/lung/infection).

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code, model weights, or repository link provided anywhere in the paper.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Six metrics formally defined with equations: IoU/Jaccard, Dice, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score — exceeding the Dice+1 requirement.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No confidence intervals, p-values, significance tests, or variance estimates. With only 5 test volumes, single-point metric reports are highly unstable; absence of statistical analysis is a major weakness.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparison against six published methods on the same Ma et al. dataset (DMDF-Net, UNet, SSA-Net, CHS-Net, SD-UNet, UNet-EfficientNetB0) with their reported metrics tabulated, plus internal comparison of 7 architecture variants. Caveat: external comparisons use literature-reported numbers, not reimplementation under identical conditions.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Results reported per segmentation task (binary lung: Dice 97.05%; multi-class lung+infection: Dice 88.61%) rather than per anatomical structure — left/right lungs were deliberately merged into a single class, so per-organ breakdown is absent. Per-class (lung vs. infection) results in the multi-class case are only partially visible due to truncation.

Q15_limitations.justification: Partial: the paper acknowledges higher computational cost of 3D vs. 2D architectures and that vanilla 3D UNet needs more iterations to converge. However, the small dataset size — the most critical limitation — is not discussed as such, and no formal limitations section or failure case analysis appears in the provided text (truncated before Discussion/Conclusion).

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: High — all 20 volumes are COVID-19-positive patients sourced from two online repositories (RAIOSS/Radiopaedia); no healthy or non-COVID pathology controls; no description of how patients were assigned to train/test splits, so split composition could favor particular severity levels.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Moderate/Unclear — identical preprocessing, input size, loss, and evaluation protocol applied consistently across all seven model variants; however, unclear whether early stopping/model selection relied on the test set (no dedicated validation set), and only 5 test volumes make outcome assessment sensitive to individual cases.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Moderate — all six defined metrics reported for the internal model comparison, but no per-class/per-organ breakdown, no failure case examples, no code release, and external SOTA comparisons rely on selectively quoted literature values rather than standardized re-evaluation; some result tables truncated in the provided text.

detailed_extraction: Supplementary methodological details: (1) The 'multi-class' segmentation is a 3-class problem (background/lung/infection), created by relabeling the original 4-label mask (0=bg, 1=left lung, 2=right lung, 4=infection) to (0=bg, 1=lung, 2=infection); lung-class merging is justified by authors as having no significant visual difference between lungs. (2) Split arithmetic implies 15 training and 5 test volumes, though exact counts are not stated. (3) Backbone selection rationale: ResNet (>142,000 studies) and VGG (>119,000 studies) chosen for ubiquity and ImageNet 2014/2015 wins; DenseNet201 chosen over DenseNet169 (used in prior 3D DenseUNet work by Alalwan et al. for liver/tumor segmentation) as the deepest available 3D variant, motivated by reduced vanishing gradients, feature reuse, and compact parameters. (4) Transfer learning applied to encoder only, initialized from ImageNet-pretrained weights; each modified backbone trained both with and without transfer learning, yielding 7 models per segmentation case. (5) Training regime: ADAM, lr=1e-4, max 5000 epochs, early stopping patience 250; combined Dice+focal loss selected empirically without reported ablation. (6) Dataset heterogeneity: RAIOSS scans 512x512 with depth 70-301; Radiopaedia scans 630x630 with depth 39-418; severity spans mild/moderate/severe — all resampled to 128^3. (7) Baseline literature values on the same dataset: DMDF-Net Dice 75.7%/IoU 67.22%; Mahmoudi et al. UNet Dice 98% (lung)/91% (infection); SSA-Net avg Dice 75.4%; CHS-Net Dice 81.6%/Jaccard 79.1%; SD-UNet Dice 86.96% binary vs. 59.36% multi-class; UNet-EfficientNetB0 Dice 65% — the proposed 3D UNet's 97.05%/88.61% outperforms most, though Mahmoudi's 2D UNet lung Dice of 98% is comparable on the binary task. (8) Clinical application emphasized: 3D infection projections exported as 3D files to visually grade COVID-19 severity (mild/moderate/severe), presented as the key translational advantage of the volumetric approach. (9) Minor reporting inconsistency: contributions section claims 'five evaluation metrics' but names four (IoU, Dice, accuracy, F1-score), while Section 3.4 formally defines six. (10) Hardware: Google Colab Pro with GPU accelerator and high-RAM runtime; GPU model, framework, batch size, and training/inference times unreported. (11) Open access under CC BY 4.0; no declared funding/conflict details relevant to extraction; relevance to review scope: single-organ (lung) segmentation plus pathological (infection) region segmentation, fully volumetric 3D processing — relevant as a representative 3D UNet-family lung segmentation study.
contribution_summary: This study benchmarks the original 3D UNet against three encoder-modified variants (3D ResUNet/ResNet152, 3D VGGUNet/VGG19, 3D DenseUNet/DenseNet201, each with and without ImageNet transfer learning, totaling 7 models per task) for lung (binary) and lung+infection (3-class) segmentation on COVID-19 CT volumes, using a combined Dice+focal loss and fully volumetric 128^3 processing to avoid 2D slicing. Surprisingly, vanilla 3D UNet achieved the best results (Dice 97.05% lung; 88.61% lung+infection; IoU 94.32%/81.58%), outperforming all modified backbones, and the authors highlight 3D infection projections for clinical severity grading as the practical benefit. The evidence base is weak, however: only 20 CT volumes (5 test), no external validation, no statistical testing, and no code release limit the reliability and reproducibility of the conclusions.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: 112 CT scans total; ~60 NIH scans per fold used for training (>50 threshold met). D1/D2 (15 each) used only for external testing, not training.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Public NIH Pancreas-CT (82 healthy, contrast-enhanced, cited to TCIA/Roth et al.) plus two in-house CSMC datasets (15 pre-cancerous, 15 cancerous; predominantly portal venous phase). Resolutions, slice counts, IRB approval, and de-identification all described.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Split is stated (4-fold CV, ~60 train/~20 test per fold) but no independent validation set exists — test folds double as validation, and the model ran to 500 epochs 'to obtain best performance on the training data' with no held-out data guiding model selection. Validation/test conflation is a methodological gap.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Exemplary annotation protocol: two radiologists (>12 years experience) independently labeled all 112 scans, 84% initial overlap, reviewed to 96% consistency, final 4% resolved by mutual agreement. Three-step consensus process explicitly reported.

Q5_external_validation.justification: Two independent external datasets (D1 pre-cancerous, D2 cancerous) with zero training overlap; final model retrained on all 82 NIH scans before external testing. Covers both healthy and diseased populations.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Standard 3D U-Net (Çiçek et al.) with 3 down/3 up sampling steps via MONAI 0.7; two input channels (normalized intensities + subregional labels); Bayes fusion mechanism (per-pixel joint probability, renormalized) fully specified. Standard architecture + citation is sufficient.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: All key hyperparameters reported: Adam, lr 1e-4, batch size 2, max 500 epochs (~200 convergence), Dice+focal 1:1 loss, 4-fold CV, MONAI 0.7/PyTorch 1.8.0, MATLAB 2021b for Bayes, 2080Ti GPU, ~8h training time. Would likely reproduce modulo code absence.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Dice loss choice justified (class imbalance, small pancreas volume vs. imaging volume); Tversky loss considered and explicitly rationale given for omitting (low variation in subregional boundary difficulty).

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Fully described and deliberately minimal: crop to pancreas bounding box using reference labels (fixed 218×239×288, no pancreas voxels removed), non-pancreas voxels zeroed, intensities linearly scaled to 0–1, 'no other preprocessing'. Post-processing explicitly none (joint-probability normalization is inside the model). Nothing hidden.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or trained model released. Subregion labels for NIH only 'available in their next study or can be requested from authors' — labels, not code, and not deposited.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: DSC only. No HD95/ASSD, no precision/recall, no VOE. For boundary-sensitive subregion splitting, a distance metric is a notable omission.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Mean ± SD across 4 folds reported per subregion (Table 1) — descriptive only. No confidence intervals, no significance tests (e.g., paired test U-Net vs. proposed per fold), no per-case distribution.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Only internal ablation (U-Net without Bayes, ~8% DSC gap). Defensible — first method for this task, no prior CT subregion method exists — but whole-pancreas methods [14–16] could have been adapted or a multi-class nnU-Net baseline attempted.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Full head/body/tail breakdown per dataset (Table 1) plus per-region baselines; tail consistently weakest (92.9 NIH), consistent with failure localization at body/tail border.

Q15_limitations.justification: Both quantitative failure analysis (~67% of errors at body/tail border, U-shaped morphology worst cases) and honest limitations (requires complete pre-delineated pancreas; may fail post-pancreatectomy/Whipple, inflammation; small datasets; single-institution external sets).

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low-moderate. NIH cohort is public and unselected for healthy pancreas; but inclusion/exclusion criteria for the 15-subject D1/D2 CSMC cohorts are not stated (how were pre-cancerous/cancerous cases sampled?), and all external data is single-institution.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low. Identical DSC definition (one-vs-rest per subregion) applied across all three datasets; labels created under one documented two-reader consensus protocol; no outcome cherry-picking evident — worst-case examples shown alongside best.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low. Per-subregion results, ablation, failure localization, and limitations all reported; inference time is the only conspicuously missing outcome. Label release deferred to a 'next study' slightly reduces transparency.

detailed_extraction: Supplementary details beyond prior extraction: (1) Naive Bayes internals — feature α = pixel-wise shortest Euclidean distance to y_f expressed as percent of total pancreas length l (α=α/l), where y_f is the head pixel farthest from body/tail; feature β = count of pixels between x_i and y_f on all three axes normalized by total pancreas pixel count A (β=β/A); per-subregion Gaussian parameters (μ,σ) learned fully supervised; priors P(s)=0.33 for all classes. (2) Fusion rule — per-pixel per-class product of U-Net probability Y and Bayes probability X gives Ŷ=Y∗X, then renormalized so the three class probabilities sum to 1; applied every training epoch and at inference. (3) DSC computed one-vs-rest per subregion (e.g., head = positive, body+tail = negative). (4) For D1/D2 external testing, model retrained on all 82 NIH scans (no D1/D2 images in training). (5) No inference time reported. (6) Authors claim and document novelty: first automated CT pancreatic subregion segmentation; only prior comparable work is one MR method (Bagur et al.). (7) Subregional reference labels for the full NIH dataset created as a byproduct — a reusable community resource — but release deferred ('next study' or on request). (8) Input channel 2 during training uses subregional labels (not just pancreas mask), meaning the second channel carries soft-label information at train and test via Bayes maps. (9) Funded by NCI/NIH R01 CA260955; retrospective CSMC data IRB-approved, identifiers removed.
contribution_summary: First automated 3D method for segmenting pancreatic subregions (head/body/tail) in contrast-enhanced CT, using a naïve Bayes model over anatomical priors (subregion length and volumetric proportions) to generate soft-label probability maps that are fused per-epoch with a 3D U-Net via joint-probability renormalization. The anatomy guidance yields ~8% mean DSC improvement over plain U-Net, reaching 94.5/95.6/89.9% on healthy (NIH), pre-cancerous (D1), and cancerous (D2) cohorts, with cross-dataset transfer demonstrating robustness to pancreatic pathology. Also contributes new expert subregional reference labels for the entire public NIH Pancreas-CT dataset.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: 307 pooled cases (NSCLC-Radiogenomics 211 + MSD Task06 Lung 96), 215 training cases — well above the >50 threshold. Caveat: only 144 NSCLC subjects have segmentation maps (144+96=240 annotated cases), and only tumor-containing slices were retained (8,992 slices), so effective training data may be smaller than the headline 307 cases.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Two well-established public datasets (TCIA NSCLC-Radiogenomics, MSD Task 06 Lung) with citations; Table 1 details demographics, acquisition parameters (slice thickness, kVp, mA). Minor weakness: some MSD technical parameters are marked as 'typical' (asterisked) rather than verified, and the 307-case figure conflicts with the 144 NSCLC cases having masks.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Explicit 70/10/20 split (215/31/61 cases) with fixed random seed for reproducibility, held-out test set plus 3-fold cross-validation; splits are described at case ('case') level. Minor gap: no explicit statement that all slices from one patient remain in one fold (a key leakage risk for 2D slice pipelines), though 'cases' wording implies patient-level splitting.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Ground truth comes from dataset-provided annotations (RTSTRUCT clinical contours parsed via rt-utils for NSCLC; pixel-level masks for MSD), but the annotation process itself (observers, protocol, inter-observer variability, verification of RTSTRUCT quality) is not described; readers are referred to the original dataset publications.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation. Both public datasets are pooled and randomly split; the 'five clients' are simulated virtual clients drawn from the same pooled data. No independent third dataset (e.g., LIDC-IDRI) or real multi-site evaluation.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Very thorough: ViT encoder specs (12 layers, 768 dim, 12 heads, MLP 3072, 16×16 patches, learnable positional embeddings), ASPP dilation rates [6,12,18], per-stage decoder channel table, attention gates, Algorithm 1 pseudocode, and architecture figures; LAURA variants described via width-scaling with depthwise separable convolutions. Inconsistency: abstract claims ~136M parameters while ablation tables list 29.4M for the 'Proposed' model — not reconciled in text.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Excellent: complete hyperparameter table (Table 4) covering architecture, augmentation, centralized training (AdamW LR 2e-5, batch 4, 200 epochs, AMP, grad clipping 0.5, warmup 15 + cosine annealing, early stopping patience 20) and FL settings (5 clients, 100 rounds, µ=0.01, α=0.3, local epochs, LR multipliers); software versions (PyTorch 1.12.0, MONAI 1.0.0) and hardware (NVIDIA T4) reported.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Dice-CE loss with smoothing (ε=1e-5) and numerical safeguards is used, with a brief justification (region-based loss mitigates background dominance under class imbalance), but no systematic justification or comparison against alternative losses; Eq. 3 is essentially a placeholder.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing is clearly described (rt-utils/Nibabel parsing, extraction of tumor-containing axial slices only, HU clipping [-1000,400], normalization to [0,1], resize/pad to 256×256) along with a fully specified MONAI augmentation pipeline; however, no post-processing steps are described (not even a statement that none were applied).

Q10_code_availability.justification: Public GitHub repository (https://github.com/Mohamed-Alaa-1/AuraVIT/) with stated installation/run instructions; datasets are public (MSD, TCIA).

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Dice plus sensitivity/recall and specificity for all experiments; additionally GFLOPs, parameters, VRAM, inference time, per-round training time, and communication volume for efficiency analysis.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Paired t-tests (centralized vs. FL: p=0.0271 MSD, p=0.0429 NSCLC), Wilcoxon signed-rank tests vs. FedAvg and SCAFFOLD (both p<0.001), ablation p-values (e.g., ViT_Tiny on NSCLC p=0.0017), and standard deviations on held-out results. No confidence intervals or multiple-comparison correction, but statistical testing is substantive.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Partial: fair internal FL baseline comparisons (FedAvg, SCAFFOLD) with significance testing, but cross-study comparisons (nnU-Net 69.2%, Carvalho 70.9%, Hossain 65.77%, Pang 77.67%) are taken from literature under different protocols — 2D slice-level Dice on tumor-containing slices is not directly comparable to 3D volumetric Dice (e.g., nnU-Net MSD challenge result), and no modern transformer baselines (TransUNet, UNETR, SwinUNETR) are empirically compared despite being cited.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Single-structure task (lung tumor), so per-organ breakdown is not applicable; the paper instead reports results per dataset (MSD vs. NSCLC), per model variant, per input type (full lung vs. bounding-box masks), plus per-sample statistical analysis and volumetric failure thresholds — adequate granularity for this task design.

Q15_limitations.justification: Strong: dedicated qualitative error analysis (Section 3.4) with quantified failure cases (missed 434.88 mm³ nodule, over-segmentation of 1808.17 mm³ tumor into chest wall, under-segmentation of 4529 mm³ mass; degraded performance for pleural/peripheral tumors) and a limitations section (2D loss of volumetric context, simulated FL, single T4 GPU, edge validation pending).

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low-to-moderate. Public datasets with clearly characterized demographics reduce selection concerns. However: (1) only tumor-containing slices are included (no negative slices/healthy controls), which inflates apparent difficulty-adjusted performance and prevents assessment of false-positive behavior on normal anatomy; (2) handling of the 67 NSCLC subjects lacking segmentation maps is unclear despite the 307-case claim; (3) federated 'clients' are simulated partitions of public data, not real institutions.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low-moderate. Outcomes measured consistently (same preprocessing, metrics, held-out test set) with statistical testing, and evaluators are automated metrics (no human reading variability). Risk arises from cross-study comparisons under non-uniform protocols (2D slice Dice vs. 3D challenge Dice) used in headline claims of superiority over nnU-Net.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low. All outcomes reported including failure cases, ablations with negative findings (attention gates unnecessary), efficiency trade-offs, and author-stated limitations; code released. Minor issues: unexplained discrepancy between claimed ~136M parameters and 29.4M in tables; 307-case count vs. 144 NSCLC annotated subjects; some MSD acquisition parameters labeled as 'typical' rather than exact; no per-case or volume-level Dice distribution reported.

detailed_extraction:
SCOPE NOTE: This paper addresses lung TUMOR (lesion) segmentation, not multi-organ segmentation; relevance to an organ-segmentation review depends on whether thoracic tumor tasks are in scope.

TASK & INPUT: Binary lung tumor segmentation from CT. 2D slice-based design: 3D volumes reduced to tumor-containing axial slices only, resized/padded to 256×256 (224×224 for LAURA-Mobile); HU clipping [-1000, 400], normalization to [0,1].

DATASETS: (1) NSCLC-Radiogenomics (TCIA): 211 subjects, 144 with 3D RTSTRUCT tumor maps; age 24-86 (mean ~67-68), 135 M/76 F, CT + PET/CT, slice thickness 0.625-3 mm. (2) MSD Task06 Lung: 96 CT volumes, thin-section (<1.5 mm). Pooled: 307 cases; 70/10/20 split = 215/31/61 (fixed seed); 3-fold CV also reported. 8,992 total slices (NSCLC 7,335; MSD 1,657). NOTE: 144+96=240 annotated cases vs. 307 claimed — internal inconsistency.

ARCHITECTURE (AuraViT): ViT encoder (patch 16×16, 12 layers, hidden 768, 12 MSA heads, MLP 3072, dropout 0.1/block dropout 0.05, learnable positional embeddings) → ASPP at bottleneck (dilations 6/12/18) → U-Net-like decoder, 4 stages with attention-gated skip connections (channels 512/256/128/64), residual blocks with dropout, 1×1 conv + sigmoid. Parameter count conflict: ~136M (abstract) vs. 29.4M (ablation tables).

LAURA VARIANTS (width-scaled, depthwise separable convs, 8 layers/512 dim): Small ~30M/11.46 GFLOPs; Tiny ~14M/8.46; Mobile ~5.5M/5.14 GFLOPs (224×224 input). Pruning/quantization listed as intended optimizations but not evaluated.

TRAINING: PyTorch 1.12.0/MONAI 1.0.0, NVIDIA T4, AMP; AdamW (LR 2e-5, WD 1e-5), batch 4, 200 epochs centralized / 100 FL rounds; Dice-CE loss (ε=1e-5); 15-epoch warmup + cosine annealing; grad clipping max-norm 0.5; early stopping (patience 20 epochs/20 rounds); augmentation: random 90° rotations, H/V flips, affine (translate ±5 px, rotate ±5°, scale ±5%) each p=0.3; Gaussian noise p=0.1 (std 0.005); intensity scaling p=0.2.

FEDERATED SETUP (simulated, 5 virtual clients): FedProx (µ=0.01); adaptive weighted aggregation blending cosine-similarity and data-size weights (α=0.3); dynamic virtual client partitioning — datasets exceeding 0.3×median are split into ceil(N/median) virtual clients (NSCLC→6, MSD→2), reducing imbalance 4.43:1→1.48:1; heterogeneous local epochs [10,8,8,6,6]; client LR multipliers [1.2,1.0,1.0,1.0,1.0]. No formal privacy mechanism (no differential privacy) — privacy relies solely on raw data non-sharing in simulation.

RESULTS: Centralized — MSD: Dice 84.24% (3-fold CV) / 84.01±0.23% (held-out), Sens 91.09±0.39%, Spec 99.90%; NSCLC: 81.09% (CV) / 80.53±0.19% (test), Sens 90.14±0.14%, Spec 99.72%. FL: global Dice 80.81%, Sens 90.19%, Spec 99.75% (<1% drop vs. centralized; paired t-test p=0.0271/p=0.0429). FL baselines: FedAvg 80.06%, SCAFFOLD 74.33% (Wilcoxon p<0.001). LAURA — MSD: Small 82.19%, Tiny 82.35%, Mobile 82.96% (Mobile exceeds standard model); NSCLC: Small 80.20%, Tiny 80.06%, Mobile 78.64%. Bounding-box-mask experiments: MSD Tiny 84.47%, NSCLC Tiny 80.58%. Ablations: attention-gate removal → no significant difference (p=0.26/0.77); ViT_Tiny (13.9M) statistically equivalent on MSD, significantly better on NSCLC (+0.65%, p=0.0017). Efficiency: VRAM 3196→2809.8 MB; inference 17/14/15 ms; FL communication 1123.8→211.2 MB/round; training 1601.8→1117.7 s/round. CRITICAL CAVEAT: all Dice computed at 2D slice level on tumor-containing slices only — not comparable to 3D volumetric Dice in cited SOTA; headline comparison vs. nnU-Net (84.24% vs. 69.2%) mixes protocols.

FAILURE ANALYSIS: missed small nodule (~435 mm³/152 px, false negative), over-segmentation of medium tumor (1808 mm³) into chest wall, under-segmentation of large mass (4529 mm³); degraded performance for peripheral/pleural tumors (HU similarity to chest wall); central/hilar tumors segmented well; small-structure failures attributed to ViT patch-embedding downsampling. Data heterogeneity characterized: raw intensity means 55.72±38.94 (MSD) vs. 99.37±68.38 (NSCLC); tumor size distributions right-skewed, MSD smaller tumors (~1000 px mean) vs. NSCLC larger/more variable.

LIMITATIONS (author-reported): 2D processing discards volumetric context; FL simulated on public data (no asynchronous updates, uptime/firewall realities); single T4 GPU; no edge-hardware validation; planned 2.5D extension.

REPRODUCIBILITY: Code public (github.com/Mohamed-Alaa-1/AuraVIT); data public (MSD, TCIA); hyperparameters comprehensively tabulated. Overall borderline-High quality (24/30): strong methodology/reproducibility and error analysis, weakened by absent external validation, slice-level metric comparability issues, and internal reporting inconsistencies.
contribution_summary: The paper introduces AuraViT-FL, a resource-efficient 2D hybrid Vision Transformer–CNN segmentation framework (ViT encoder + ASPP + attention-gated U-Net decoder) trained with a FedProx-based federated learning pipeline featuring adaptive weighted aggregation and dynamic virtual client partitioning for privacy-preserving lung tumor segmentation, achieving 80.81% mean Dice with <1% degradation versus centralized training. It further proposes lightweight LAURA variants (down to ~5.5M parameters, >96% reduction) that retain competitive Dice (up to 82.96% on MSD Lung), with ablations showing smaller encoders can match or beat the full model. The evidence supports decentralized training feasibility, though slice-level evaluation, simulated federation, and non-comparable cross-study baselines temper the strength of the SOTA claims.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training sizes exceed the >50 threshold on both benchmarks: NIH uses 65 cases in 5-fold CV (+16 held-out test; 2 scans excluded for missing masks), and MSD uses 230 cases in 5-fold CV (+51 held-out test). NIH is only modestly above threshold and single-center/benchmark-scale, hence not full headroom, but clearly satisfies the criterion.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Both datasets are well-established public benchmarks, clearly identified (NIH Pancreas-CT via The Cancer Imaging Archive/TCGA; MSD Task01 Pancreas) with acquisition details (contrast-enhanced CT, DICOM/NIfTI formats, 512×512 slices, slice thickness 1.5–2.5 mm NIH / 2.5 mm MSD, in-plane ~0.5 mm, slice counts). Direct data access URLs provided in the Data Availability Statement.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Split methodology explicitly described: random partition into 5 disjoint folds with no patient overlap (NIH: 5×13 cases; MSD: 5×46 cases), plus an independent held-out test set never used in training/CV (NIH: 16; MSD: 51). Identical pipeline applied to both datasets. Minor caveat: an internal numeric inconsistency exists (intro cites 82 NIH scans; methods state 81 with 2 excluded, yet folds+test sum to 81).

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Partial: NIH masks were provided by 'trained radiologists' and released in NIfTI, but no annotation protocol details (number of annotators, consensus procedure, inter-rater agreement) are given; MSD ground truth is inherited from the Decathlon challenge without discussion of its annotation quality. Annotation process is attributed to the source datasets rather than described.

Q5_external_validation.justification: No external validation. NIH and MSD are evaluated in separate experiments (train/test within each benchmark); there is no cross-dataset generalization test (train on NIH → test on MSD or vice versa). The authors themselves list cross-dataset/domain-shift validation as future work.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Architecture fully specified: symmetric 3D encoder-decoder, 4 downsampling blocks (two 3×3×3 convs each, BN, ReLU, stride-2 max-pooling), channels 2→16 in deepest encoder and mirrored 16→2 in decoder with 3D transposed convolutions; attention gates at every skip connection described mathematically (1×1×1 projections, Layer Normalization, ReLU fusion, C/2-reduction subnetwork, sigmoid voxel-wise attention map). Architecture figure (Fig. 1) included.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Partial: TensorFlow 2.16.1, Adam optimizer, initial LR '6×10^4' (apparent typo, likely 6×10^-4), ReduceLROnPlateau with 100-epoch patience, 3D on-the-fly augmentation (rotations ±10°, flips p=0.5, shifts ≤10%), and hardware (NVIDIA T4 16GB, 48GB RAM) are reported. However, batch size, total number of epochs, and the focal loss focusing parameter γ are not specified, hindering exact reproduction.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Strong: Dice+Focal combination is explicitly motivated (class imbalance, small organ), formally defined (Eqs. 1–3), and empirically validated via a 3-way ablation (Dice-only vs Dice+CE vs Dice+Focal) with Friedman test (p=0.0224 MSD; p=0.0408 NIH) and post-hoc pairwise tests (p=0.03 Dice+Focal vs Dice-only on both datasets).

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing thoroughly described with rationale: HU windowing [-100, 240], min-max normalization to [0,1], resampling to 1.0×1.0×1.0 mm³, and a fixed mask-independent center crop to 224×224×128 voxels explicitly designed to avoid label leakage. MSD pancreas+tumor label merging stated. No postprocessing is applied/reported (a limitation, but the described pipeline itself is clear and reproducible).

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or trained model release. Data Availability Statement points only to the public source datasets; generated segmentation masks are 'available upon request' only. No repository link, license, or release version provided.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Three complementary metrics: DSC (volumetric overlap), ASSD, and HD95 (boundary accuracy, in mm), all reported with mean ± SD, and DSC additionally with per-case min–max ranges on both datasets.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: Friedman test across loss configurations with explicit p-values (p=0.0224 MSD, p=0.0408 NIH) and post-hoc pairwise comparisons (p=0.03 Dice+Focal vs Dice-only on both datasets); SDs and per-case ranges reported. Caveats: no confidence intervals, and the attention-vs-no-attention gain (80.8% vs 77.6%) is not significance-tested.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparison tables against multiple published methods on both benchmarks (NIH: Giddwani et al. 83.31%, Boers et al. 78.10%, Jain et al. 81.75%; MSD: Li et al. 80.24%, Zhang et al. 82.47%, Chen et al. 76.60%) plus an internal 3D U-Net ablation baseline (77.6%). Comparisons are literature-based on possibly different splits/preprocessing rather than re-implementations, and the paper candidly notes missing variance data in competitors — a minor weakness but the comparison effort is substantial.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Single-organ study (pancreas), so per-organ reporting is trivially complete; the target organ's results are reported in full detail with mean ± SD and per-case ranges on both datasets (NIH 80.8±2.1% [78.6–84.1]; MSD 78.1±1.1% [76.2–79.1]) plus surface metrics. Note that MSD results include tumor voxels merged into the pancreas mask, which slightly complicates cross-study organ-level comparability.

Q15_limitations.justification: Explicit limitations section with three concrete limitations (limited dataset size/heterogeneity, sensitivity to anatomical variability, restricted out-of-distribution generalization). Discussion also interprets the moderately high HD95 relative to low ASSD as localized errors in pancreatic head/tail. Qualitative figures include a challenging low-contrast case, though dedicated failure-case examples are not shown.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low-to-moderate. Case selection is defined by established public benchmarks with an explicit exclusion rule (2 NIH scans removed for missing masks) and random patient-disjoint fold partitioning. However, convenience sampling inherent to public benchmarks, no clinical/inclusion criteria (e.g., contrast phase, body habitus), and the small NIH cohort limit generalizability; the healthy-patient NIH set vs. tumor-bearing MSD set also differ systematically.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low. Identical preprocessing, training pipeline, and metric computation (DSC, ASSD, HD95 in physical units) applied consistently across both datasets with a held-out test set untouched during model selection. Minor concern: it is not fully explicit whether headline numbers are 5-fold CV averages or held-out test-set results (ranges suggest per-case test-set variability), and literature comparisons use heterogeneous splits/preprocessing.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low. All planned metrics, the full loss ablation (including small/nonsignificant effects on MSD), per-case ranges, inference times, and explicit limitations are reported; no evidence of selective outcome reporting. Minor gaps: no parameter count/FLOPs or training time despite the efficiency motivation, no failure-case visualizations, and the architecture gain lacks a significance test.

detailed_extraction: Supplementary methodological details: (1) Reproducibility gaps — focal loss focusing parameter γ value never specified despite the formula; initial learning rate printed as '6×10^4' (apparent typo for 6×10^-4); batch size and total epochs unreported; ReduceLROnPlateau patience = 100 epochs on validation loss. (2) Model efficiency design — unusually narrow feature channels (2→16 deepest layer) deliberately chosen to reduce computational burden for deployment on modest hardware (~2.7 s/case inference on an NVIDIA T4), though parameter count/FLOPs and training time are not reported. (3) Attention-gate variant — uses 1×1×1 convolutions with Layer Normalization and a C/2-reduction two-layer subnetwork, applied at every skip connection; differs in normalization details from the original Oktay et al. Attention U-Net. (4) Label-leakage-safe preprocessing — fixed anatomically-centered crop (224×224×128 voxels) independent of ground-truth masks, explicitly to avoid label leakage; risk of clipping atypical anatomy is not discussed. (5) Label semantics — MSD pancreas and tumor labels merged into one binary mask, so the reported 78.1% MSD DSC is 'complete pancreas incl. tumor' and is not strictly comparable to literature MSD numbers segmenting pancreas only; authors frame this as a binary benchmarking step before future multi-class tumor extension. (6) Numeric inconsistency — intro cites 82 NIH scans, methods state 81 with 2 excluded (→79), yet splits sum to 81 (5×13 + 16). (7) Ambiguity in reported metrics — unclear whether headline results are 5-fold CV means or held-out test-set results (per-case min–max ranges suggest the latter). (8) Statistical testing scope — restricted to the loss ablation; the attention mechanism's contribution (80.8% vs 77.6% for plain 3D U-Net on NIH) is not significance-tested, and no confidence intervals are given. (9) Ablation asymmetry — Dice+Focal gain over Dice-only is large on NIH (+6.0 points) but modest on MSD (+1.4 points); Dice+CE is never significantly better than Dice-only. (10) Context — builds on the authors' prior 2.5D attention model (BIOSTEC 2025); this work is the 3D counterpart. Article is open access (CC BY 4.0); predictions available on request; code not released; no external/cross-dataset validation or postprocessing (e.g., largest-connected-component filtering) performed.
contribution_summary: This paper proposes a lightweight 3D Attention U-Net (channels 2→16) with attention gates at all skip connections, trained with a Dice+Focal loss for binary pancreas segmentation in contrast-enhanced CT, achieving 80.8±2.1% DSC (ASSD 2.1 mm, HD95 8.1 mm) on the NIH dataset and 78.1±1.1% DSC (ASSD 3.3 mm, HD95 12.3 mm) on MSD with fast inference (~2.7 s/case). Its key contributions are demonstrating that a computationally frugal attention-gated 3D architecture reaches competitive benchmark accuracy, and a statistically rigorous (Friedman + post-hoc) loss-function ablation showing Dice+Focal significantly outperforms Dice-only. Limitations include lack of code release, no external/cross-dataset validation, and non-comparable MSD label merging (pancreas+tumor).

Q1_dataset_size.justification: StructSeg 2019 has 50 training patients (at the threshold) and SegTHOR has only 40 labeled scans. Both are small datasets, typical for this domain but below ideal for training deep networks; the authors themselves acknowledge small dataset challenges and rely on transfer learning to compensate.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Both datasets clearly described: SegTHOR from ISBI 2019 challenge (40 scans, 4 OARs: heart, esophagus, trachea, aorta) and StructSeg 2019 (50 training + 10 test lung cancer patients, 6 OARs: left/right lung, spinal cord, esophagus, heart, trachea). Example visualizations of both datasets provided.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Split methodology explicit: 5-fold cross-validation on StructSeg (50 patients) and 4-fold cross-validation on SegTHOR (40 scans). SegTHOR results computed via official CodaLab challenge server on held-out test set. Minor limitation: StructSeg results reported on cross-validation of training set rather than the 10 held-out test patients.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Partial: For StructSeg, 'each scan is annotated by one expert and verified by another one' is stated. For SegTHOR, annotation process not described by authors (relied on challenge-provided labels). No details on annotation protocol, inter-observer variability, or delineation guidelines.

Q5_external_validation.justification: Partial: Evaluated on two independent public datasets demonstrating cross-dataset applicability, and SegTHOR results obtained from official held-out test set via online server. However, separate models were trained per dataset (no single model tested across institutions), and StructSeg performance was only reported on cross-validation of the training set, not the independent test patients.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Architecture thoroughly described: U-Net variant with ImageNet pre-trained encoders (ResNet34: channels 64/64/128/256/512; SEResNext50: 64/256/512/1024/2048), decoder channels (256/128/64/32/16), dual-branch decoder blocks, custom spatial attention module (SAM) with equations and figures, group normalization placement, and skip connections all specified.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Good but incomplete: Adam optimizer, 30 epochs, loss weights (θ=0.9, σ=0.1), per-class CE weights, augmentation types (horizontal flip, elastic transform, rotation), HU windowing values, hardware (GTX 2080Ti 11GB), and training times provided. Missing: learning rate, learning rate schedule, batch size, and input slice/patch resolution — preventing full reproduction.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Combined loss (0.9×Dice + 0.1×weighted Cross-Entropy) presented with mathematical formulations and class-specific weights addressing imbalance. However, the rationale for the specific weighting values is not justified and no loss ablation is performed; group normalization choice is better justified (batch-size independence, stability) than the loss design.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Clearly described: 3D-to-2D slice extraction, HU intensity normalization with explicit boundaries ([-1000, 400] for StructSeg; [-400, 400] for SegTHOR), and detailed STAPLE post-processing pipeline (per-organ 2-class map conversion, k-fold candidate fusion, map reassembly) with figures.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or trained model release mentioned. Only data availability statement referencing the SegTHOR challenge download is provided.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Two complementary metrics used: Dice score (overlap) and Hausdorff Distance / HD95 (boundary distance, in mm), both formally defined with equations.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No confidence intervals, p-values, standard deviations across folds, or significance testing. All results are single point estimates; differences from competing methods (e.g., 0.8690 vs 0.8594 Dice) not tested for statistical significance.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Extensive comparisons: 7 published methods on SegTHOR test set (via challenge leaderboard values), MTL-WMCE on StructSeg, plus internal ablations over attention mechanisms (CBAM, SCSE, none, proposed SAM), backbones (ResNet34 vs SEResNext50), and normalization (BN vs GN).

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Esophagus-specific results (the paper's focus organ) reported separately on both datasets with per-fold breakdown in Figure 7. However, the model segments all thoracic OARs (multi-class task) and results for the other organs (heart, trachea, aorta, lungs, spinal cord) are not reported.

Q15_limitations.justification: No limitations section or failure case analysis. Discussion is limited to claiming multi-dataset robustness; no discussion of 2D approach drawbacks (loss of 3D context for a tubular structure), small dataset constraints, or example failure modes.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low-to-unclear: Patient cohorts are predefined by public challenge datasets (StructSeg: lung cancer patients; SegTHOR: thoracic CT), but the authors provide no inclusion/exclusion criteria, scanner/protocol details, or patient demographics — limiting assessment of cohort representativeness.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Moderate: SegTHOR evaluation used the official online challenge server (consistent, unbiased assessment), but StructSeg results are cross-validation results on the training set without held-out test evaluation, creating risk of optimistic performance estimates. Same metrics/protocol applied consistently across compared methods on SegTHOR.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Moderate: Only esophagus results reported despite a multi-organ model and multi-organ benchmarks; no variance/uncertainty reporting; discrepancy between abstract (claims atrous spatial pyramid pooling module) and methods section (ASPP never described in architecture details); no negative results or failure cases presented.

detailed_extraction: TASK & CONTEXT: Automated esophagus segmentation (organ-at-risk) from chest CT for radiotherapy treatment planning; framed as a multi-class OAR segmentation task (7 classes on StructSeg, 5 classes on SegTHOR) but evaluated only on esophagus. ARCHITECTURE: 2D slice-based U-Net variant (explicitly chosen over 3D to save computational resources) with ImageNet pre-trained encoders (ResNet34 and SEResNext50 tested; SEResNext50's SE blocks provide channel attention while the proposed SAM provides spatial attention). Decoder: two branches per stage — main branch [2×(Conv3×3→GN→ReLU) + SAM], auxiliary branch [1×1 Conv→GN] inspired by Inception/ResNet downsampling, merged by element-wise addition. Atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP) is claimed in the abstract to enlarge receptive field but is not detailed in the methods (internal inconsistency). Group Normalization used throughout, replacing BatchNorm (ablation on SegTHOR test: GN Dice 0.8690/HD 0.2527 vs BN Dice 0.8667/HD 0.2748). STAPLE POST-PROCESSING: k-fold ensemble fusion via Simultaneous Truth and Performance Level Estimation instead of mean/max voting — fold-level esophagus Dice on SegTHOR test ranged 0.8547–0.8598, improving to 0.8690 after STAPLE fusion; applied per-organ on binary maps then reassembled into multi-organ image. TRAINING: PyTorch; Adam; 30 epochs; augmentation = horizontal flip, elastic transform, rotation; ~20h (StructSeg) / ~16h (SegTHOR) on a single GTX 2080Ti 11GB; ~20s inference per patient. RESULTS: SegTHOR official test set — Dice 0.8690, HD 0.2527 (best among 11 compared methods; next best He et al. 2020 Dice 0.8594/HD 0.2590; Han et al. 2019 Dice 0.8651). StructSeg 5-fold CV (training set) — Dice 0.7784, HD95 11.28mm vs U-Net-scse-seresnext50 (0.7762/11.31) and MTL-WMCE (0.6055/28.96). Attention ablation (StructSeg): proposed SAM > SCSE > CBAM > no attention for both backbones. RELEVANCE TO REVIEW SCOPE: Addresses a single small/tubular thoracic organ (not a large parenchymal organ); uses a primarily 2D strategy with 2.5D-style STAPLE ensemble across folds — relevant as an example of computationally lightweight alternatives to 3D networks and of esophagus-specific handling, a challenging OAR with low contrast and ambiguous boundaries. FUNDING: National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF-2020R1A4A1019191; NRF-2019M3E5D1A02067961).
contribution_summary: This paper proposes a fully automated 2D U-Net variant for esophagus segmentation in chest CT that combines ImageNet-pretrained encoders (ResNet34/SEResNext50), a custom spatial attention module in the decoder, and group normalization, with a STAPLE-based fusion of k-fold cross-validation predictions as post-processing. Evaluated on both SegTHOR and StructSeg 2019, it achieves the best reported esophagus Dice (0.8690) and HD (0.2527) on the SegTHOR test set versus prior challenge methods, and demonstrates via cross-dataset experiments and ablations (attention type, backbone, GN vs BN) that the approach is effective and not overfit to a single dataset. The key insight is that lightweight 2D processing plus attention and probabilistic multi-fold label fusion can match or exceed 3D methods for a small, low-contrast organ while drastically reducing computational cost.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Main scenarios train on 600 TS CT scans and target AMOS (500 CT / 100 MR); >1800 total subjects across five public datasets. Small-sample scenarios (BTCV 20, MMWHS 12 CT train) are an intentional part of the evaluation design (low-sample generalization test), not a shortfall of the primary experiments.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: All five datasets are public and cited. Appendix Table A1 reports date ranges, modalities, patient counts, sites, scanners, sex, age statistics, and clinical characteristics (e.g., BTCV = colorectal chemo trial + hernia study; SPINE = healthy volunteers; AMOS includes tumor/abnormality cases).

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Figure 1 flowchart fully specifies splits (BTCV 20/10, AMOS 10 MR test, TS 600 train / 10 test, MMWHS 12/6); splits drawn randomly and held fixed across all methods for fair comparison; MMWHS split explicitly avoids paired CT-MR cases leaking across train/test. Caveat: target test sets are small (n=6-10), which limits estimate precision though not split clarity.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Partial: annotation process is explicit only for TS (semi-automatic with clinician review) and SPINE (manual); for BTCV, AMOS, and MMWHS the paper cites the original dataset publications ('previously reported'). The authors' own GT harmonization (spinous-process cropping for TS>SPINE) is transparently described, lifting this from 0 to 1.

Q5_external_validation.justification: Every reported result is an external, cross-dataset, cross-modality, cross-scanner evaluation (CT source to MR target: BTCV>AMOS, TS>AMOS, TS>SPINE, TS>MMWHS MR, MMWHS CT>MR). Test scans are unseen by training by construction; this is the paper's core setting.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Built on the referenced, self-configuring nnUNet framework; all modifications fully specified: BN-layer variant, 12-channel SSC descriptor input, two-branch TTA with inverse transforms and consistency masking, 3-fold TTA ensemble, partial-layer adaptation ablations (norm-only, encoder-only). Code release covers remaining architecture detail.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Public code (GitHub); optimizer, lr, weight decay, step count, gradient accumulation over 16 patches, resampling grid, SSC patch parameters, hardware, and software versions (Python 3.11, scipy 1.14.1) all reported. Minor gaps: no random seeds; GIN hyperparameters deferred to ref [15].

Q8_loss_function.justification: Explicitly justified: soft Dice consistency loss with exponent d=2 chosen over d=1 via a loss-landscape analysis (Figure 4) showing d=2 yields zero loss along the consistency diagonal without forcing overconfidence. Supervised pre-training loss is the standard nnUNet default.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Fully described: resampling to 1.50x1.50x1.50 mm3; GIN augmentation and SSC descriptor application to inputs; GT label harmonization (5-voxel-dilated spinous-process exclusion); postprocessing prediction correction to match label definitions; consistency masking of inverse-transform border artifacts; 3-fold ensemble inference.

Q10_code_availability.justification: Code publicly available at https://github.com/multimodallearning/DG-TTA (stated in Data Availability, accessed 31 Aug 2025). Trained model weights not explicitly stated as released.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Dice plus 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) for all scenarios, plus runtime measurements (pre-training 15.3 h; TTA 1.7 min/scan/fold, 5.2 min with ensemble).

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: One-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on paired predictions with significance levels (* p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001) reported per method; mean +/- SD and boxplots with median/mean. Deduction-free per rubric since p-values are present; note: no confidence intervals despite small per-scenario test samples (n=6-10).

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Four cross-domain competitors (Tent, TTA-RMI, RSA, AdaMI) evaluated under a unified setting, plus internal ablations (GIN-only, SSC-only, GIN+SSC, partial-layer adaptation, 56 TTA configurations) and an in-domain target-training upper-bound reference (84.5 Dice / 8.8 mm).

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Tables 1-2 report per-structure Dice and HD95 for all 10 abdominal classes (spleen through pancreas) for every method; visual per-class overlays in Figure 7. Spine (L1-L5) and cardiac scenarios report means only.

Q15_limitations.justification: Dedicated Section 4.3 plus conclusions: TTA adds little when GIN pre-training already generalizes (+0.2 to +1.6%, one case -0.4%); adaptation step count empirical with no convergence criterion; residual orientation/resolution domain gaps; persistent gap vs in-domain training (78.6 vs 84.5 Dice); failure regions explicitly contoured in Figure 7.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low. Inclusion criteria explicitly defined (e.g., BTCV subset restricted to 10 uniformly labeled classes; AMOS test scans required to contain all 10 reference substructures; random subsampling with fixed source:target ratios); all data from public benchmarks with cohort characteristics tabulated. Residual concern: very small random target test sets (n=6-10) and a healthy-volunteer SPINE cohort limit representativeness of clinical populations.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low. Identical splits, ground truth, resampling, and metrics (Dice, HD95) applied to all methods; Tent and AdaMI re-implemented inside the same nnUNet pipeline; label-definition corrections applied uniformly to predictions; automated, reproducible outcome assessment; no human readers whose assessment could vary.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low. Negative and modest results disclosed (TTA decreases Dice by 0.4% in one scenario; RSA underperforms baseline; TTA gains marginal when pre-training generalizes); per-organ tables, ablations, and a dedicated limitations section included. Conflicts of interest (industry employment: EchoScout, Dampsoft, Draegerwerk) declared with no commercial relationship to the method declared.

detailed_extraction: Data composition beyond the summary: BTCV restricted to 10 uniformly labeled classes; AMOS target test = 10 randomly selected MR scans containing all 10 reference substructures; TS training subsampled to 600 CT; MMWHS 12/6 split constructed to prevent paired CT-MR cases leaking across train/test. Method detail: GIN(x) = alpha*g_rho(x) + (1-alpha)*x with a shallow conv net re-initialized every iteration; SSC expands input 1-to-12 channels via 6-neighborhood patch SSD distances (patch size and distance 1 voxel); optimal TTA configuration from a 56-combination ablation (Experiment III): affine spatial augmentation in both branches, gradient backpropagation only in branch A, no intensity augmentation at test time; TTA gains up to +30.1 Dice for non-generalized NNUNET vs max +1.6 for already-generalized GIN model; only classes of interest are optimized. Baseline integration: Tent and AdaMI re-implemented inside nnUNet (AdaMI class-ratio prior estimated from training-set voxel counts); TTA-RMI and RSA run in their original pipelines; RSA is 2D and produced scattered 3D masks. Efficiency comparison vs ref [28]: 126.6 h training + 82 min adaptation (RSA-style pipeline) vs 15.3 h + 5.2 min per scan here. Reference upper bounds: in-domain target training reaches 84.5 Dice / 8.8 mm HD95 (abdominal) vs best cross-domain 78.6 Dice / 17.2 mm. Statistics: one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, mean +/- SD; software Python 3.11, scipy 1.14.1. Declarations: BMBF-funded (MEDICARE 01IS21094; Medic V-Tach 01KL2008, ERA-CVD); CC BY open access. Minor internal inconsistency: Section 2.2.1 states AOR omitted from the BTCV 10-class subset, yet Tables 1-2 report AOR results, and the text says '14 organs' while listing 13. Review relevance: no novel segmentation architecture - the contribution is a training/adaptation protocol on top of nnUNet; organ sets are standard benchmarks (10 abdominal structures, L1-L5 vertebrae, 7 cardiac structures), so cross-study per-organ comparability is good, but reported Dice values are cross-domain (CT-to-MR) and must not be pooled with in-domain CT segmentation results in meta-analysis.
contribution_summary: DG-TTA combines domain-generalized nnUNet pre-training (GIN intensity augmentation plus SSC self-similarity context descriptor inputs) with a source-free, two-branch augmentation-consistency test-time adaptation (soft Dice loss, d=2) applied per unseen scan, integrated entirely within the standard 3D nnUNet pipeline. Across five public datasets and five CT-to-MR cross-domain scenarios (abdominal, lumbar spine, cardiac), it significantly improves over base nnUNet (up to +64.0% Dice on non-generalized models; p<0.001) and outperforms Tent, TTA-RMI, RSA, and AdaMI, reaching 78.6-82.6% mean Dice while closing most of the gap to in-domain training with minimal assumptions and released code.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: 389 training scans (KiTS23), 100 internal validation, 592 external validation = 1081 total, far exceeding the >50 subject threshold; largest reported set is the external validation cohort.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Both sources explicitly described: public KiTS23 (GitHub link with access date; corticomedullary + nephrogenic phases; 0.5-5.0mm slice thickness; full histological subtype breakdown incl. ccRCC 63.49%, papillary 10.03%, chromophobe 8.48%) and private MSKCC cohort (592 CECT, nephrogenic-only, 1.0-7.5mm, ccRCC-only).

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Clear 80/20 split of KiTS23 (389 train / 100 internal validation) plus fully independent 592-scan external test set; randomization method for the split not specified (minor).

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Manual annotations stated as reference standard for all evaluations, but the annotation process is undescribed: no annotator expertise, rater count, inter-observer agreement, or arbitration procedure reported for either dataset.

Q5_external_validation.justification: Strong external validation on 592 independent institutional scans from a different source than training, explicitly reported per tumor size with detection and segmentation metrics.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Both stages fully specified: Stage 1 SwinUNETR (shifted-window self-attention, non-overlapping 128^3 patches, 4-stage encoder with 2 transformer blocks each, CNN decoder with residual blocks, instance norm, deconv upsampling, pointwise conv + sigmoid); Stage 2 custom 6-stage 3D UNet (RBs per stage 1,3,4,6,6,6; feature maps 32-320; attention gates; LeakyReLU; patch 192x128x128); architecture figures provided.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Optimizers (AdamW lr=3.5e-4 / SGD lr=0.001), batch size 5, patch sizes, DiceCE loss, pretrained-weight source [42], PyTorch 2.2/Python 3.10/CUDA 11.1, A40 GPU all reported; missing epochs, LR schedule, weight-decay value, and augmentation parameter ranges prevent exact reproduction.

Q8_loss_function.justification: DiceCE used for both stages and its composition stated, but no explicit justification for the choice (e.g., class imbalance handling for small tumors) versus alternatives.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Preprocessing fully specified (HU clipping to 0.5-99.5 percentiles, isotropic 1.0mm resampling, zero-mean/unit-variance normalization; augmentation list with quantified +5.5% Dice gain); authors explicitly state no postprocessing is used, and the 25% VOI expansion between stages is described.

Q10_code_availability.justification: No code or trained model released; Data Availability Statement covers only the KiTS23 dataset.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Extensive metric suite: Dice, precision, Volumetric Distance, OSR, USR (all formally defined with equations) plus detection sensitivity and FPC per patient; exceeds Dice + one other requirement.
